POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Thu, 01 Oct 2026 13:31:48 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.9 Trump’s energy chief asked Europe to release more than a third of its diesel reserves https://www.politico.eu/article/trumps-energy-chief-asked-europe-to-release-more-than-a-third-of-its-diesel-reserves/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 01 Oct 2026 12:51:01 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9091757 BERLIN — The Trump administration has circulated a proposal to European governments asking them to release a large portion of the bloc’s strategic diesel reserves to ease soaring fuel costs, according to four officials in European and U.S. governments.

The plan, put forward by U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright, was pitched as an alternative to President Donald Trump’s threat of a blanket ban on diesel exports from the U.S.

Under the proposal, EU governments would release 120 million barrels of diesel from their national strategic reserves over 180 days, a government official from a European country told POLITICO. The official, like others in this story, was granted anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the proposal’s details publicly.

That would account for well over a third of the approximately 315 million barrels of diesel EU countries held in reserve as of June this year, according to Eurostat figures. Among EU countries, Germany, France, Italy, Spain and Poland hold the largest reserves of the essential transport fuel.

POLITICO reported Tuesday that the White House was floating the idea of asking the EU to use its diesel reserves to bolster global supply and thus lower prices. A German government official on Thursday confirmed that the United States had contacted Berlin in the matter. 

Germany was not the only country approached by the U.S. Reuters reported that France had been approached about the plan, while a third major EU member was also approached bilaterally in the U.S. last week, according to another senior European energy official.

“It was very hypothetical: ‘What do you think about Europe releasing some of the reserves in order to decrease prices, put pressure on supplies?'” the official said of the approach. “‘It could also help our government not to continue the discussion on the export ban.'”

Wright, along with the U.S. oil and gas industry, opposes an export ban on one of the world’s most in-demand petroleum products, and the proposal is seen as an attempt to find an alternative to such a drastic measure.

At a press conference Thursday, Commission spokesperson Anna-Kaisa Itkonen wouldn’t confirm whether the EU had received Wright’s request but said that any stock releases would only be agreed through the International Energy Agency, a Paris-based institution which coordinates energy policy among rich countries and oversaw an earlier stock release this year. She added that the Commission was in close contact with EU member countries and Washington.  

Meanwhile, President Trump on Wednesday confirmed that a diesel export ban by his administration was still on the table. “I’m thinking about it,” Trump said of the export ban at an Oval Office event. “I speak to [Energy Secretary] Chris [Wright] and [Interior Secretary] Doug [Burgum] about it a lot — they sort of think it’ll help diesel, but it might raise the price of other things.”

Trump declined to rule out restricting diesel shipments. “It’s something that we think about and we talk about every day,” he said. “But it just seems that it would have a negative impact on gasoline, so that would go up a little bit, and diesel would come down a little bit.”

Wright, who was with Trump in the Oval Office on Wednesday, said the administration would soon announce measures aimed at bringing down diesel prices. Europe would also be announcing moves to add supply to the market, he said.

“You will hear announcements from our friends in Europe about new diesel supplies that’ll come to the market that’ll meaningfully push diesel prices down,” Wright said.

The French government will present later on Thursday a 2027 budget that earmarks €63.4 billion for military expenditures, compared with €57 billion this year. About 12% will be dedicated to nuclear deterrence and 43% to the purchase and maintenance of military equipment.

That’s in line with increases foreseen by the military planning law adopted over the summer.

“To ensure our sovereignty, the government plans to strengthen our military capabilities through additional orders for major equipment (surface-to-air defense systems, anti-drone systems, and artificial intelligence),” the document reads.

This means France’s defense budget will have doubled under French President Emmanuel Macron’s two terms, which started in 2017.

The defense ministry is one of the very few to benefit from a budget increase in 2027. The government has announced a deficit target of 5% of GDP for next year, and the freeze on most other ministerial budgets at their 2026 levels has been confirmed.

But many of the countries who didn’t receive an invite — such as the United Kingdom, France and the Baltic countries — are big defense spenders and play key roles in the alliance, leaving their diplomats wondering why they’re being frozen out.

They question whether the administration is playing favorites in a way that could further splinter an alliance already struggling with increasing Russian aggression and depleted weapons stockpiles.

“We’re doing everything that is being asked of us,” said an official from an excluded ally nation. “We’re trying to understand what the criteria is and what the purpose of these meetings are. Not much has been passed on to us yet.”

The White House did not respond to a request for comment, and the Pentagon declined to comment.

President Donald Trump and his top lieutenants have relentlessly criticized NATO since returning to power, on everything from members’ refusal to back the Iran war to the failure of some countries to spend 5% of their GDP on defense.

“I always considered NATO, where we spend Hundreds of Billions of Dollars per year protecting these same Countries, to be a one way street — We will protect them, but they will do nothing for us, in particular, in a time of need,” Trump railed in a Truth Social post this year. Last month, he snubbed another ally — South Korea — by abruptly scaling back a planned joint military exercise while complaining about Seoul’s refusal to join the war against Iran.

In April, as POLITICO first reported, the White House came up with something akin to a who’s-in-and-who’s-out list while it looked for ways to punish allies who didn’t adhere to Trump’s wishes.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has echoed that vision. He has encouraged “model allies” and warned that those that do not support U.S. interests will suffer consequences.

While details on the new NATO working group are still vague, it follows the threat of rewarding some at the expense of others.

Colby has held two similar meetings with invitees Norway, Sweden, Finland, Poland, Germany and the Netherlands. The countries involved in the meeting — known as the Bergen Group format — insist it’s not meant to rupture the alliance, said a diplomat from one of the invited nations, who like others, was granted anonymity to discuss internal deliberations. Instead, the group intends to come up with ideas it can bring to the full alliance for more stress-testing.

“This can be an engine for transformation,” for the whole alliance, the diplomat said. The person acknowledged that some allies are frustrated by the exclusion, especially since many have hit or surpassed the spending targets demanded by the Trump administration.

The U.S. might add Denmark to the exclusive club next given the agreement reached between the two countries to expand the American military footprint in Greenland, according to another person familiar with the planning.

Colby, who has been the catalyst for the initiative, held a first meeting of its kind in Bergen, Norway, in June and invited the six favored allies. “NATO allies that are rapidly meeting their Hague spending commitments, have the scale to contribute, and are ready to get down to practical business,” he wrote on social media after the meeting.

He noted this month at a conference in Washington that “the idea is to pull the whole alliance along,” adding that it “will be a better and stronger NATO that is more durable” and give Europe more military capacity.

Colby has taken a longtime interest in smaller format talks between NATO nations. He has focused in previous years on reviving Germany as a military power to contain Russia and dedicating American troops to deal with China’s rise.

But even invited allies question why Colby and other defense officials have cherry-picked attendees and left out some of the continent’s largest defense powers, such as Britain.

“If they try splitting NATO into the good ones and the bad ones, it is dangerous for the U.S.,” said another of the six diplomats. “But for Europe, this is existential.”

with DOMINIC GIANNINI

SNEAK PEEK

— Europe must band together to tackle drug pricing pressures rather than being picked off one by one, Spain’s Health Secretary Javier Padilla Bernáldez tells Morning Health Care.

— Parliament’s environment committee will vote on its opinion for the Biotech Act.

— EU health ministers meet in Dublin.

Welcome to Thursday’s Morning Health Care! Kudos to all those who made it to the 6am hike ahead of another jam-packed day at the European Health Forum in Gastein. I won’t throw Claudia under the bus, but I, for one, proudly took the lie-in. For those who opted for the walk, at least their stride shouldn’t have been impacted by this news that air pollution can impact marathon times — thanks to the clear air of the Austrian Alps.

Get in touch: cchiappa@politico.eu, dgiannini@politico.eu. Follow us on X: @chiappa_claudia, @domgiannini_

DRIVING THE DAY

LET’S COME TOGETHER: Spain’s Health Secretary Javier Padilla Bernáldez has called for Europe to band together in the face of U.S. drug pricing pressures rather than seeking bilateral agreements. As pressure mounts on Germany to strike a deal with the Trump administration, Padilla Bernáldez argues any such deal risks weakening the European market.

Right now: “When [most favored nation] emerged, there was a consensus that the main strength of the European Union was being more people with a higher degree of universal health coverage, and the weakness was having a fragmented market,” Padilla Bernáldez told Morning Health Care at the European Health Forum in Gastein, Austria. “If you go bilateral, you are losing this main strength.”

The context: Europe is grappling with how to respond to the Trump administration’s most-favored-nation drug pricing policy, which risks delaying the launch of new medicines in Europe. Companies fear launching in Europe will risk a lower matched price in the U.S., limiting profits in that lucrative market. 

Is the breakfast club no more? Countries initially seemed to be on the same page about the best way to respond to the pressure — as a team. Back in June, 11 countries, led by Sweden, first met to debate how to protect EU prices and agreed they were stronger when working together rather than pursuing individual deals. The Beneluxa group — a health care alliance uniting Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Austria and Ireland — also urged Europe to protect its solidarity-based health systems and warned against “uncoordinated, individual national responses.” 

Sweden continues to lead discussions on drug pricing and reimbursement amid geopolitical pressure, within an EU alliance of authorities that carry out this work known as NCAPR. (The next meeting is Oct. 9.) But some may be breaking ranks.

Art of the deal: U.S. diplomats and pharma companies are eyeing deals with EU countries similar to the one Washington struck with the U.K., which will see the National Health Service pay more for medicines.

Germany has been in talks with U.S. officials over the price of its medicines, following the Section 301 investigation. It has not announced an agreement but is considering rewarding drugmakers with higher prices if they invest locally.

France this week announced a new deal with the pharmaceutical sector on drug pricing, to provide “more clarity and predictability to pharmaceutical companies.”  “France is making a clear choice to invest in the future,” the government said Tuesday. Health Minister Stéphanie Rist said access to medicines was at the heart of the policy, while Public Accounts Minister David Amiel said “the resources released throughout the life cycle of medicines must make it possible to finance innovation and the treatments of tomorrow.”

Bad idea? Padilla Bernáldez warned that countries are giving up Europe’s main strength, its potentially large market, by thinking that they will be treated “in a positive way by the bully government of the United States” — but “I don’t think it’s going to happen.”

No comment, but: The U.S. government didn’t respond to a request for comment, but when it announced its trade probe into Germany’s drug pricing policies, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said the U.S. was “calling on Germany to pay its fair share for the innovative treatments its people use.”

We’ve seen this film before: “When we talk about procurement in Europe, there are always countries with big economies that think — and maybe that’s true — that they are … going to get a better price if they are going on their own,” Padilla Bernáldez said. “Maybe France and Germany think they are going to calm the United States by going on their own. It doesn’t work like that.”

Muddy deals: Yannis Natsis, head of the European Social Insurance Platform, representing payers, agreed that “going it alone is no solution.” “It remains unclear what French patients and taxpayers will get in return for accepting higher prices,” he said. “Even less clear is what pharmaceutical companies are committing to in return, beyond benefiting from those higher prices.”

Yes, but: Renew MEP Stine Bosse said the new French deal has “the right instinct.” But she warned that Europe should act as one in rewarding innovation and manufacturing. Her fear is that multiple sets of rules or bilateral deals will make the EU “more vulnerable” — “we become an even less predictable place for the companies we want to invest here.” Patients will pay the price, she said, and Europe’s competitiveness will suffer.  “Europe must act as one, or we will be picked off, one by one.”

It’s a common sentiment in Gastein: Valentina Strammiello from the European Patients’ Forum supported the European Commission coordinating a discussion that included patients’ voices, saying it was important that stakeholders were brought together to find a solution. “Otherwise, keeping working in isolation doesn’t lead to any solution,” she said. 

Also pro-EU: Nathalie Moll, head of pharma lobby EFPIA, said that Europe risks losing out “as a whole” if countries put policies in place to attract manufacturing to their country. “The problem in Europe is … that there isn’t enough Europe. And here we need to be smart as a region in how we consider competitiveness and what tools we put in place to attract the investment, and not fragment ourselves even further than we are today.”

What now? Ministers had asked the Commission to conduct an impact assessment of Trump’s policies at their last meeting, which Health Commissioner Olivér Várhelyi handed back to member states in August — although it found it was too early to assess the impact on Europe. The ball is now in the Council’s court.

Rolling coverage: EFPIA’s Moll said it was “really important” the impact of MFN on Europe is “monitored very closely, so that we can respond to it in the right way,” adding there needs to be “continuous assessment.” Europe also had to look at solutions it could implement quickly, and this should include scrapping clawbacks and cost containment measures, she added.

BIOTECH ACT

TIME TO VOTE: The environment committee is set to vote on its opinion on the Biotech Act today. Socialists and Democrats MEP Nicolás González Casares, who wrote the draft opinion, has called to scrap or limit the proposal to extend some biotech patents. This is only an opinion since the health and industry committees lead on the proposal.

Talking about the Biotech Act: Padilla Bernáldez has used his appearance at Gastein to defend Spain’s proposal to create a “European Coordinated Market Access Toolbox” to help drugs reach the market earlier. Countries could work together to estimate demand and coordinate negotiations with companies or launch collaborative procurement.

But: Companies could have commitments such as ensuring supply continuity, maintaining European manufacturing capacity, submitting national pricing and reimbursement applications on time, and ensuring equitable launch and access. 

Reciprocal commitments: Moll at EFPIA said there also needed to be reciprocal commitments on the part of states. “One of the commitments has to be to increase the value that is given to innovative medicines, so there needs to be a recognition that these products bring value beyond the value to the patient, but also to the economy and in the socio-economic context,” she told Morning Health Care.

Speed up access: Moll has another proposal — an agreement to make medicines available on the market while national pricing and reimbursement negotiations are ongoing, meaning patients would have faster access to drugs. Companies would set an initial price before discussions would start, and if negotiations stalled, patients would be able to keep using the medicine through a non-reimbursed route. Moll admitted the idea was in its early phases and hadn’t been brought to governments.

COUNCIL

WELCOME: Ireland’s Health Minister Jennifer Carroll MacNeill will chair an informal meeting of EU health ministers in Dublin today, which will also include the EU health commissioner, the World Health Organization’s Europe director and the head of the European Medicines Agency.

Smile: Ministers were shown around Dublin’s National Institute for Bioprocessing Research and Training on Wednesday afternoon, and today’s meeting will kick off with a family photo. 

On the agenda: They’ll hold closed-door discussions on innovation and improving patient outcomes; integrating care across the EU and strengthening medical ecosystems; and, of course, discuss global pressures and collective action. 

Sneak peek: The Irish Council of the EU presidency wants to lean into Europe’s commitment to universal access to health for the whole population, rather than people’s ability to pay. “There’s huge strength in that,” Muiris O’Connor, assistant secretary at the Department of Health, told Gastein via videolink. “We retain a core belief in science, and we purchase medicines and medical products at national scale right across the European Union. So I really think we have to remember just what is really strong about us and shore up the vulnerabilities.” A press conference is scheduled for 3.30 p.m. 

UCPM

SANT, ENVI VOTE ON UCPM PROPOSAL: Lawmakers in the public health and environment committees will vote today on an EU proposal for a union civil protection mechanism, or UCPM, for health emergency preparedness and response.

What’s this about? In the next multiannual financial framework proposal, the Commission wants to expand the civil protection mechanism — created to strengthen cooperation for disasters — to include health emergency preparedness and response. The proposed budget for this was €11 billion, though it’s unspecified how much will go to the civil protection department DG ECHO versus the health preparedness authority DG HERA.

Behind the report: The health and environment committees are leading on this file. Their compromise proposes increasing the budget to over €12 billion and allocating funds across sectors: 40% for civil protection, 40% for health emergencies, and 20% for flexibility.

Some of the changes: The committee draft proposes a new focus on climate-risk assessment, scenario planning and stress testing; emphasizes a One Health approach and measures to build public risk awareness and community preparedness; calls for action to fight disinformation; and expands support for resilient health care systems and workforces, cross-border medical teams, patient evacuation and stockpiling of medical countermeasures.

Smooth sailing: Lawmakers are expecting a “straightforward” vote, after reaching a “balanced agreement” supported by EPP, S&D, ECR, Renew, Greens and The Left, said S&D’s Leire Pajín, a co-author with ECR’s Aurelijus Veryga.

WHAT WE’RE READING

The FT looks at how Australia is battling a black market for cigarettes after a decade of tax rises.

Patients switching to Novo’s Wegovy pill from shots lose more weight, Reuters reports.

POLITICAL ADVERTISEMENT

**A message from EFPIA: The Biotech Act can help create the conditions for European breakthroughs to be developed and scaled-up in Europe. Promising science needs capital to grow. More ambitious and accessible EU funding can help biotechnology companies scale in Europe, rather than looking elsewhere for the investment they need. Strategic Projects can help bring together the expertise, infrastructure, investment and talent needed to turn scientific breakthroughs into new medicines and strengthen Europe’s industrial capacity. And as AI transforms medicine research and development, Europe needs rules that enable innovation. Trusted testing environments, interoperable data and coherent, proportionate governance can help unlock AI’s potential while maintaining trust and safety for people. Read more.**

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Thu, 01 Oct 2026 11:51:49 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.2 [Interview] Le Pen and Mélenchon are ‘economically illiterate’ and weaponising migration, says French scholar ahead of 2027 race https://euobserver.com/238893/interview-le-pen-and-melenchon-are-economically-illiterate-and-weaponising-migration-says-french-scholar-ahead-of-2027-race/ Thu, 01 Oct 2026 13:20:43 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=238893 French political scientist Jacques Rupnik says the economic illiteracy of Marine Le Pen and Mélenchon is astonishing. He anticipates that in the first round of France's presidential election, most voters will back a candidate they believe can stop Le Pen. A Mamdani moment could happen, since people feel that politics has exhausted itself.]]> “Marine Le Pen has reinvented herself. Her style now is more moderate,” reckons Jacques Rupnik, a French political scientist, ahead of the country’s widely anticipated battle for the presidency.

Many voters in France will vote for the candidate they see as having the best chance of defeating the far-right leader, Rupnik explains.

“All polls show that if the far-left Jean-Luc Mélenchon faced Marine Le Pen in the second round of France’s presidential election, Marine Le Pen would win,” he says, explaining that many French votes are unwilling to back Mélenchon.

In his interview with Denník N, Rupnik claims Mélenchon is the first French presidential candidate to seek support from immigrants so explicitly.

Find out:

  • How Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon have used the migration debate for their campaigns.
  • Why the presidential frontrunners do not understand economic issues.
  • Rupnik’s assessment of Emmanuel Macron’s two presidential terms.
  • Who does Marine Le Pen look up to?

Polls suggest that if France held a presidential election now, far-right Marine Le Pen and far-left Mélenchon would make the second round. What does this tell us about France?

France is divided and polarised. Young people in particular tend to lean towards more radical parties. Establishment parties are old and worn; they have lost their appeal. They have little to say, except for claiming that others are dangerous or worse. But you must bring something new to an election. But after ten years of Macron, that is very difficult.

And it is not entirely true that all polls predict Mélenchon will reach the second round; they often place former prime minister Edouard Philippe ahead of him. Mélenchon is powering ahead in polls because he has launched his campaign and is very good at it. But, nothing is decided.

In French presidential elections there are two rounds. In the first round, you vote for your preferred candidate; in the second, you vote for the lesser evil. So, for most voters, the question will not only be whom they prefer, but also who has the best chance of defeating Le Pen in the second round.

And that is very important. All polls say that if Mélenchon faced Le Pen in the second round, he would lose. Many people are not willing to vote for Mélenchon. A centrist candidate has the best chance of defeating Le Pen, so for now it looks like former prime minister Philippe.

But only if another former prime minister, Gabriel Attal, withdraws his candidacy.

Yes. We have two strong parties at the extremes, and the space in the centre has shrunk. The narrower it becomes, the more candidates appear within it. Every week, another politician tells media: “You know what, I would give it a go.”

Attal, of course, wants to win over Macron supporters — that is, voters on the centre left. The fact he is in the race matters even if he withdraws and endorses another candidate. That may prove a good strategy.

Read more

Can new French PM ‘Baby Macron’ help beat Le Pen?

If Le Pen and Mélenchon reach the second round, many would vote Le Pen. Why?

Marine Le Pen has reinvented herself. Not in the sense that she has been thinking about what new ideas to bring forward, but now her style now is more moderate. It is no longer the brash style associated with her father.

Perhaps she took her cue from Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni, seeing a candidate whom everyone feared, but no radical changes followed her election because she adapted quickly to European realities.

Le Pen points out that in several European countries, including Finland and Sweden, the far right has been in government and nothing has happened.

At the same time, Marine Le Pen managed to break through a certain barrier, and some moderate rightwing voters have shifted to her side.

Read more

Le Pen and Farage – the far-right always play the ‘victim’ card

How did that happen?

Previously, the moderate right was stronger and Le Pen’s camp was weaker. The type of rightwing voters who voted for Jacques Chirac have now shifted their weigh behind more radical options. The balance has shifted, and right-wing voters are saying: “Why should we, the right, be excluded from politics simply because Macron has failed and the Le Pen has grown stronger?”

Immigration is another reason behind growing support for Le Pen. Mélenchon is also capitalising on the immigration debate, but in the opposite way to her.

Please explain that.

Mélenchon opposes Le Pen’s position by arguing that immigrants integrate. The Le Pen camp says: “No, they have come from a different culture and their attitude is anti-French.” Le Pen’s camp says that integration works poorly, that immigrants do not even want to integrate instead preferring to live in their own communities.

“Mélenchon has therefore adopted the theory of grand remplacement, but instead of presenting it as a threat, he has turned it into a huge opportunity.”

And Mélenchon argues that it is fine for immigrants to remain in their own communities, practise their own religions, for women to wear headscarves and so on.

The great replacement conspiracy theory (“grand remplacement“) should be mentioned since the far right embraced it long ago. It is the idea that the native French population will gradually be replaced by new immigrants.

And Mélenchon now says: “What great replacement? On the contrary, it is an opportunity for France. He says: “The more of us there are, the better.”

Mélenchon has therefore adopted the theory of grand remplacement, but instead of presenting it as a threat, he has turned it into a huge opportunity. Of course, everyone knows what he is aiming for. It is an election campaign, and he is appealing to voters who are themselves immigrants.

Previously, no one focused on immigrants in elections except Le Pen who used them as a bogeyman. And now Mélenchon says: “We are appealing to Muslims.” He says Muslim headscarves are fine and religious symbols are fine. He says anyone who opposes this is racist.

In August, Le Pen announced her intention to ban headscarves in public spaces. Will her anti-Islamic agenda help her win?

On the contrary, such statements mainly play into Mélenchon’s hands. Of course, calling a referendum on the issue in France is not so simple since such laws already exist. The law states clearly that you can do what you want at home, but if you work in the public sector you must refrain from displaying your religion. There are laws covering this, and there is absolutely no need to devise new ones. Le Pen’s ideas in this regard seem to be mere campaign slogans; we cannot take them literally.

Read more

Islamic veil can be banned in workplace, says EU court

Yet, a major Le Monde poll shows the French are more concerned about the economy than immigration. Immigration ranks fourth, after social issues and ecology.

That is true, but other polls show that, for many voters, the issues of migration and safety overlap considerably.

So, as concerns about security become increasingly prominent, people are more concerned about security and often link it to migration. Marine Le Pen will certainly try to make it one of the key issues, alongside the economy.

]]> Listen: How does Trump’s AI pact compare with the EU? https://euobserver.com/240706/listen-how-does-trumps-ai-pact-compare-with-the-eu/ Thu, 01 Oct 2026 11:51:49 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240706 Donald Trump is betting on voluntary commitments from AI companies. On Tuesday (29 September), he unveiled a self-regulatory agreement drawn up with some of the biggest names in the AI industry.]]>

Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

Find the full transcript below: 


Donald Trump is betting on voluntary commitments from AI companies. On Tuesday (29 September), he unveiled a self-regulatory agreement drawn up with some of the biggest names in the AI industry.

What does it mean, and how does it differ from the EU’s Code of Practice for general-purpose AI?

On Tuesday, September 29, Trump brought together the CEOs of some of the biggest AI companies. Together, they signed what could be described as a self-regulation pact: a short list of non-binding commitments called the White House Accord on Super Intelligence.

Read more

AI chatbots turn users’ most intimate data into a potential goldmine for advertisers, researchers warn

That’s the other novelty: Trump no longer wants to talk about artificial intelligence, but about “super intelligence”. The term AI apparently has negative connotations.

So, what exactly have these companies committed to? The CEOs of OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, SpaceX and Nvidia have pledged to put safeguards in place, quickly detect and fix problems, and have their systems checked by independent auditors.

The principle of voluntary commitments may sound familiar to Europeans: They echo the EU’s Code of Practice for general-purpose AI — which, like the White House agreement, is not legally binding.

So what’s the difference? First of all, OpenAI, Anthropic and Google have also signed the EU code, while Meta, SpaceX and Nvidia have not.

And, more importantly, the EU does have binding rules in place: the AI Act, which is already in force. As part of this regulation, the European Commission developed the Code of Practice to help companies comply with the rules.

You could think of it as a checklist for AI companies, to help them make sure they are complying with the law.

Read more

Let’s not allow AI firms to use fears of future dystopias to distract Europeans from existing problems

Another difference is the sheer volume of recommendations. The document published by Trump is just one page long. The European Code of Practice runs to more than 60 pages and was prepared with the help of dozens of independent experts.

It is also more comprehensive, covering not only safety, but also transparency and copyright. But this raises another question: if both documents are voluntary,  how effective can they actually be?

When the European Code of Practice was published, some civil society organisations criticised it, arguing that voluntary commitments are not enough and that concrete obligations are needed.

Read more

EU states urged to ‘go beyond’ AI Act to protect people from abusive surveillance

There are binding obligations under the AI Act. But they are not as precise as what is in the code of conduct.

Similar criticisms have emerged since the White House agreement was published on Tuesday. And it is worse in the US case, since companies are absolutely not legally bound by the commitments they have made.

The United States has generally been less inclined towards binding regulation of the sector. Trump has argued that rules can hinder the development of companies, and has promoted a national framework that is as minimally restrictive as possible.

The White House document does leave the door open to legislation in the future. It says that, over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into lows or regulations.

But for now, they remain voluntary commitments. If you are interested in this topic, there will be a live event on Tuesday next week about AI and its safeguards, organised by VoxEurope.

 It will be online and you can find all information on Vox Europe website. 

]]> EU accession of Moldova and Ukraine is alternative to Nato, as Russia draws new Iron Curtain in Europe https://euobserver.com/239313/eu-accession-of-moldova-and-ukraine-is-alternative-to-nato-as-russia-draws-new-iron-curtain-in-europe/ Thu, 01 Oct 2026 10:03:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=239313 With Nato doors closed to Ukraine and Russia pushing a new Iron Curtain across the Black Sea, an “urgent” EU expansion toward Kyiv and Chișinău is emerging as Europe’s main tool to defend its eastern flank and preserve its global clout. ]]> “What is remarkable is that Ukraine and Moldova, despite finding themselves in a very tense situation regarding their security, are extremely keen to move closer to the EU and have therefore already begun negotiations and opened the first cluster.”

These are the words of the deputy director of the European Council on foreign relations (ECFR), Vesela Cherneva, and they come just as the official negotiation process for the two countries’ accession to the European Union has begun.

With this, the EU embarked on a truly geopolitical enlargement – driven not only by the pursuit of shared values, a larger market, and stronger common institutions, but also by the need to safeguard the continent’s security in a shifting environment.

Ukraine: a battle-hardened nation’s journey from the post-Soviet world to the EU

According to Cherneva, the EU’s upcoming enlargement is the only way to institutionally anchor Ukraine within a serious and lasting framework, given that the US position has remained clear under both presidents Donald Trump and Joe Biden: Nato enlargement to include Ukraine is not possible.

“Currently, EU membership is the only way to integrate Ukraine’s and Europe’s security systems. This is an entirely different discussion from negotiations on chapters, clusters, sanitary standards and other accession requirements. We are talking about security guarantees, but also about the transfer of military technologies from Ukraine to Europe and, more broadly, about how Ukraine – which currently possesses the strongest and most combat-capable army in Europe – can, while defending Europe, also become part of the European security debate,” Cherneva says.

Ognyan Minchev, political scientist, professor and executive director of the Institute for Regional and International Studies, an independent think-tank in Bulgaria, also believes that Ukraine’s importance is substantial and that the questions surrounding its integration are highly complex.

“Ukraine currently possesses the only genuinely combat-capable army on the European continent. Western European armies have very limited personnel numbers and, until recently, received extremely low levels of funding. The lack of real resources, including weapons, to address the challenges of military security makes Ukraine a more attractive partner,” he says.

Although many experts would point to Ukraine’s contribution to European security as the greatest benefit of its accession to the EU, the country can also contribute to development in other areas. There is undoubtedly great potential for development in the fields of agriculture and farming.

The country has a vast area of cultivated land and is among the world’s leading producers of a number of cereal crops such as wheat, maize, barley, rice, and others. It exports these products to third countries, and membership would increase the EU’s economic influence in these regions.

Ukraine’s accession could also lead to cooperation between different sectors and result in an increase in meat and dairy production as a consequence of increased cereal production.

Beyond agriculture, Ukraine’s pharmaceutical industry could offer the EU an opportunity to reduce its reliance on imports of generic medicines from China and various Asian countries. Thanks to its favourable climate, Ukraine also has great potential for various types of renewable energy.

Deposits of gallium, rutile, graphite, magnesium ores, lithium and other minerals vital to the green transition could contribute to European production and help the EU compete with China.

According to Minchev, integrating Ukraine represents a major challenge because it involves a large country that is institutionally weak, with high levels of corruption, poor economic organisation and significant shortcomings in the functioning of public life.

Read more

What JK Rowling’s Voldemort can teach us about Ukraine war

“Ukraine has been forced to transform itself into an effective fighting machine, but in other respects it remains a post-Soviet society with serious problems in the areas mentioned above. This makes its rapid integration into the EU extremely difficult,” Minchev says.

Moldova: a key piece in Europe’s security architecture continues to struggle under Russia’s shadow

“For Moldova, we can say that it is a small but significant element in the broader domino effect of Black Sea security, which is becoming an increasingly crucial aspect of overall European security. This is because the confrontation between the Kremlin regime and Europe is effectively unfolding along the line of a new Iron Curtain being formed across Ukraine and the Black Sea region,” Minchev says.

According to Cherneva, Moldova’s accession is also crucial precisely because the country is a buffer state, and Russia has demonstrated that it does not tolerate buffers.

Read more

[Interview] Moldova races for EU membership by 2030: ‘We owe this chance to Ukrainians’, minister says

“Russia seeks to conquer and control such buffer zones. If Moldova does not want to share the fate of Belarus or Georgia, it must take rapid steps towards European integration,” Cherneva says.

For years, Moldova has served as a testing ground for Russia’s hybrid warfare. As Western European countries are only now confronting the full scale of Russian hybrid attacks, Moldova has already spent years developing its own resilience and countermeasures.

The country brings to European security valuable expertise gained from combating Russian disinformation and resisting repeated attempts by the Kremlin to interfere in its domestic political processes.

Yet Moldova’s accession would have implications extending far beyond security. Although it possesses far less agricultural land than Ukraine, the country has the potential to make a meaningful contribution to the European agricultural sector. Moldova has been gradually integrating into the EU’s Single Market through the Deep and Comprehensive Free Trade Area (DCFTA).

]]> Europe’s children will inherit public-health crisis from new EU pesticide approvals https://euobserver.com/240266/europes-children-will-inherit-public-health-crisis-from-new-eu-pesticide-approvals/ Thu, 01 Oct 2026 09:37:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240266 By extending pesticide approvals and keeping hazardous products on the market, Brussels is bending to Big Pharma and causing a food-system and public-health burden for decades to come.]]> The European Union once prided itself on leading the world in protecting children. Today, policymakers backed by big polluters are betraying that promise in the name of “competitiveness”. 

In June 2026, Florence, Franck, and Isabelle packed their bags and headed to Brussels. Why? Because their children have all suffered serious harm from pesticides. 

These children have endured physical pain and heavy medical procedures, including repeated chemotherapy treatments. And their families have shouldered both the financial and emotional burdens alongside them.

As Isabelle puts it: “It destroys a family.” Her own daughter has been fighting leukaemia for the last seven years.

And they are not alone. In 2024, almost one in 20 children in the EU were exposed to dangerous levels of pesticides; that’s 380,000 kids. Now these parents have a clear message for policymakers: prioritise public health and stop dismantling the rules that protect children against harmful substances. 

In 2024, around 316,000 tonnes of toxic pesticides were sold in the EU to be sprayed across our countryside, risking not only the health of farmers but also polluting our soil, air and water.  

The European Environment Agency in Copenhagen has reported environmentally unsafe levels of pesticides in about a quarter of Europe’s rivers. In groundwater – which supplies 65 percent of the water we drink in Europe – unsafe levels were detected in 11-18 percent of water bodies. 

In the same year, trifluoroacetic acid, a harmful “forever chemical” that forms when ‘PFAS’ pesticides and F-gases break down, showed up in 94 percent of drinking water samples tested across 11 EU countries. 

We are surrounded by pesticide pollution. It’s even in our homes. 

But what’s happening in Brussels?

In December 2025, the European Commission proposed a legislative package that would remove fundamental environmental and health protections against pesticides in the EU.

Among other changes, the proposal – ironically labelled the ‘Food and Feed Safety’ Omnibus – suggests extending pesticide approvals indefinitely and relaxing the rules to allow pesticides already identified as hazardous to remain on the EU market. 

Let that sink in, no pun intended.

These proposals are a political choice to prioritise short-term profits for Big Polluters over children’s lives, people’s health, and the nature and ecosystems we need to survive.

Human health is at stake, and children are at particular risk – as they absorb substances more easily and are less able to excrete them. 

Pesticide exposure is linked to the development of childhood cancers, hormone disruption, neurodevelopmental impairments and birth defects. And prenatal and early childhood exposure can permanently alter development, with consequences that can be irreversible – and deadly.  

Under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, as well as the UN-declared human right to a healthy environment, all EU countries must commit to protecting children from environmental harm and ensure the highest attainable standard of health.

These principles must guide the work of EU institutions. 

Yet, instead of strengthening protections, the EU is moving backwards at a worrying speed. This is largely due to intense (and repeated) lobbying from multi-billion euro corporations, which includes the pesticides industry. Corporate chemical giants now spend €46m a year just to lobby the EU; that’s over 60 percent more than in 2020. 

Make it make sense

The incoherence of current EU policy is troubling. On the one hand, the EU Commission is celebrating its new Intergenerational Fairness Strategy – a framework that is meant to ensure today’s policies do not disadvantage future generations. On the other, the same institution is actively seeking to relax controls of harmful substances. 

Ripping up rules that protect people and the planet only benefits Big Polluters, industries that already make billions in profits at the expense of children’s health.

What’s more, an independent assessment found that the measures the EU institutions propose “will not accelerate innovations and authorisations”. In short, these proposals would actually make Europe less competitive.

Children’s rights and youth organisations have warned that deregulation exposes children to serious (and preventable) health risks. And the international scientific community recently stressed that robust environmental risk assessments cannot be optional.

Ultimately, Europe should widen and accelerate its access to pesticide-free alternatives. It must also support farmers in their efforts to transition away from pesticides, towards a more sustainable and resilient model.

So, what can be done? First, the EU must close the tap on pesticide use and production, and support farmers transitioning to safer alternatives. Second, it’s time for leaders to hold Big Polluters accountable for the damage they cause – not force the bill onto regular taxpayers and families harmed by these toxic substances.

Florence, Franck, and Isabelle’s children are among the hundreds of thousands already affected by pesticides. And they show that victims of pesticides are not just a statistic.

The ‘Food and Feed Safety Omnibus’ raises fundamental questions. Who exactly is the EU’s food policy supposed to protect? How many more children need to be harmed for politicians to act? And what kind of future do EU institutions want to build? 

Should pesticide protections be treated as obstacles to short-term profits, or should children be able to grow up safely? 

Politicians should reject this devastating Omnibus proposal and work instead to support the EU’s transition to safe, sustainable, and resilient farming.

]]> Inside Poland’s fake student scheme: cheap labour, bogus visas and Russian ties https://euobserver.com/239684/pro-russian-figures-linked-to-polish-universities-selling-paperwork-for-schengen-visas/ Thu, 01 Oct 2026 08:34:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=239684 In Poland, student status has become a sought-after commodity that employment agencies exploit for gains. Many foreign workers were unaware they were enrolled in fake schools associated with pro-Kremlin figures.]]> Maria, a Colombian woman, thought she was going to Poland to work at one of the country’s biggest meat-processing plants. Instead, the employment agency that arranged her job had quietly enrolled her in school.

She discovered this only after translating the papers she had been given. One said she was a student at an adult secondary school in Sieradz, another enrolled her at a Polish university. But Maria had never applied to either institution, attended a class or even heard of them.

Her case is part of a wider trade in fake student documents that exploited Poland’s labour and immigration systems. Employment agencies used fictitious student status to make foreign workers cheaper to employ, while private universities issued certificates that could help foreigners obtain visas or legalise their stay.

An investigation by the Polish publication Onet found the same schools and universities repeatedly appearing in documents issued to foreign workers from around the world. Some institutions existed largely on paper; in other cases, fraudsters forged documents in the names of legitimate schools without their knowledge.

The schemes went beyond fake student cards. Private universities also issued certificates used to obtain visas, enter the Schengen area or legalise residency.

They cost Poland’s social-security system millions of zloty and left some migrants facing job losses, residency problems and possible deportation – while people linked to the schools have established ties to Poland’s pro-Russian organisations and media.

Read more

EU’s new cross‑border work rules favour recruitment, not workers, say critics

Fake students cheaper for employers

Polish labour laws incentivise employment of students aged up to 26 under so-called agreements to perform a job. It means employers do not have to pay social security or health insurance contributions for them. The workers cost less than regular employees.

So, student status has become a sought-after commodity that employment agencies have exploited for gains.

A central figure in the case is Dariusz M., a school head in Sieradz detained by police in late May. When reporters from TVN24 posed as employers looking for a way to legalise the employment of foreign immigrants, M. offered to enrol them as students for 750 zloty (around €175) per person.

Prosecutors suspect him of participating in an organised group that allegedly issued around 2,500 false study certificates, costing the Polish state nearly six million zloty (more than €1.4m) in unpaid contributions.

Documents were often arranged by employment agencies with foreign workers unaware they had formally been enrolled at a school.

“In most cases, they do not even know they are involved in something illegal. They trust the employment agency,” said Rocio Flores, president of the Union of Latin American Workers in Poland.

When an inspection uncovers the fraud, the foreign workers face losing their jobs, residency problems and, in some cases, deportation. “We migrants suffer most as a result,” Flores said.

Inspections carried out by Poland’s social insurance authority confirmed there were many such cases.

In August, Dziennik Gazeta Prawna reported that Poland’s social insurance body (ZUS) stepped up inspections of companies employing foreigners with pupil or student status.

]]> AI chatbots turn users’ most intimate data into a potential goldmine for advertisers, researchers warn https://euobserver.com/239963/ai-chatbots-turn-users-most-intimate-data-into-a-potential-goldmine-for-advertisers-researchers-warn/ Thu, 01 Oct 2026 06:51:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=239963 Researchers found that even when users rejected non-essential cookies, Perplexity, DeepSeek, Gemini, Copilot, ChatGPT and Claude still connected to Google Ads.]]> Six out of nine of the most popular AI chatbots routinely exposed user input to third parties, new European research reveals.

Multiple chatbots disclosed sensitive user data to advertising companies through trackers – a piece of code used to identify and target users on the web with customised advertisements, which are widely used across the web.

And tech companies may have been able to link conversation summaries with personal identifiers, allowing users to be targeted based on their conversations with AI.

The researchers aimed to establish the connection between existing tracking technologies and AI advertising. “We basically connected the dots, and wanted to test whether and how AI bots integrate tracking and advertising services,” said Narseo Vallina-Rodriguez, who led the study.

Vallina-Rodriguez is part of a group of researchers who investigated the use of ad trackers in the most popular AI providers with colleagues at Imdea, a public research institute in Madrid.

Their findings warn of “tensions” between tech company practices and obligations to users under privacy laws.

Sensitive user-data shared 

“We already knew that tracking is pervasive, even without AI. But now you have the most super-invasive phenomena on the internet, which is AI,” said Itxaso Domínguez de Olazábal, a policy adviser at digital rights group Edri.

Users often share information about their health, psychological state, finances, and other intimate matters in AI prompts. The study shows how users who asked AI questions about such matters could have sensitive details summarised in a chat title shared with third parties. 

“Now, big tech has access to much more intimate information which users tell AI. It’s crazy, the details are so intimate. My friends ask AI bots about relationships, or they use ‘doctor AI’,” said Domínguez de Olazábal.

GDPR rules require companies to make clear how users’ data is harvested, but researchers question “ambiguous expressions” used to explain the role of trackers in T&Cs.

And the ePrivacy directive requires users to consent to cookies unless they are “strictly necessary”, but researchers found that even when users rejected non-essential cookies, AI bots Perplexity, DeepSeek, Gemini, Copilot, ChatGPT and Claude still connected to Google Ads.

All of the top nine most popular chatbots were found to integrate at least one third-party advertising or tracking service.

Consent and transparency ‘shortcomings’

A preview of the study, released in May, prompted the Spanish privacy watchdog AEPD to request for the European Data Protection Committee (EPDC) to share preliminary findings with European counterparts “for knowledge and assessment”.

The final paper, titled ‘Prompt like a Butterfly, Sting like a Tracker’, has been accepted for publication at an academic forum in Delft next year.

Findings “highlight tensions between current practices and obligations under the GDPR and ePrivacy Directive, exposing broader shortcomings in consent, access control, and transparency mechanisms,” the paper reads.

It reveals that Grok, operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceXAI, exposed public links to conversations by default, allowing trackers to routinely access whole conversations, with TikTok also processing screenshots of Grok conversations.

Meanwhile, Mistral, France’s flagship AI firm, did not offer users a choice to reject non-essential cookies.

    • The Ukrainian army stays in control of front lines, but safety in cities deteriorates. The war has reached a stage in which two separate conflicts appear to be taking place simultaneously.

    While Ukraine is currently losing the battle in the air and its cities are continually suffering missile and strikes by jet drones, the situation on battlefields is far better.

    Last week, Denník N spent time in Ukraine with former chief of the general staff Daniel Zmeko. During the trip, reporters met commanding officers from several brigades and battalions operating from the Izium area to Zaporizhzhia, and all of them said they had the situation under control.

    Yet official Russian maps persist with utterly nonsensical lines. We do not know to what extent this is an effort to deceive domestic and foreign audiences, and to what extent they genuinely believe it in Moscow. It is worth looking at how the regime wants the situation to appear, and what it is really like.

    The first map in the overview was produced by the Russian state news agency RIA Novosti and depicts the area around Lyman, on the northern flank of the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk direction, as of 29 September. On the eastern flank, it uncritically accepts every claim by the Russian defence ministry and, with equal lack of scrutiny, considers captured every small village where a Russian soldier raised a flag during a suicidal mission, even several months ago.     No update on Wednesday.

    Note: Neither side regularly reports its own deaths or equipment losses. Ukraine publishes daily figures for Russian casualties and destroyed equipment, which cannot be independently verified. In this overview, we use data from the Oryx project, which has compiled a list based exclusively on photographically documented equipment losses since the start of the war.

    ]]>         Let’s not allow AI firms to use fears of future dystopias to distract Europeans from existing problems https://euobserver.com/240465/while-ai-companies-keep-us-talking-about-the-future-were-ignoring-the-damage-theyre-doing-now/ Wed, 30 Sep 2026 14:17:26 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240465 As Big Tech companies dramatise rogue AI and China fears, the real fight is over who pays the price for today’s fraud, failures and job threats — and who pockets the productivity gains.]]> “Imagine a zombie that does not hunt you, but rings your doorbell and speaks so persistently and fluently that it finally arrives at a convincing argument for feeding it your brain.”

    Salvaggio’s zombie helps explain what gets lost when people say an AI “went rogue.” In his reading of the Hugging Face incident, a system set to never give up encountered a task it couldn’t complete.     The inadequately closed-off environment in which the models operated is crucial to explain what happened. But so is the person who created the goal, the conditions they (did not) give the AI system, as is the company that employs that person and presumably knows what they’re up to, the owners of that company who demand progress and the investors in that company who want to see returns. 

    And yet, all we seem to talk about is whether it’s correct to say a machine ‘decided’ to disobey.

    Conveniently, that story shifts attention away from the people who chose to reward persistence, provide access, and failed to contain the consequences.

    It also raises a question: where does the economy of an illegal Israeli settlement end?

    Most emerging measures follow economic relationships towards illegal Israeli settlements: do not buy goods produced there, invest there or provide services that enable their construction. 

    Norway’s proposed legislation is seemingly comprehensive, covering property purchases and services connected to construction and property transactions.

    The UK has also announced a ban on advertising property in illegal Israeli settlements, after such property had been advertised at a London real-estate event.

    But this all still largely considers illegal Israeli settlements within their territorial bounds.

    The problem is treating a spatial category as though the economic relationships producing it share the same boundary. We all know the world does not work like that.

    Kinnula, a municipality in central Finland, is now facing this reality: when money from the illegal settlement economy moves into public land in Europe. It is a small case, but it makes the problem unusually visible.

    On its own website, Dror Bonim Atid presents its Finnish development alongside a development in Efrat, an illegal Israeli settlement in the occupied West Bank, as well as a development in Dror-Hiran in the Negev.     One company website therefore takes us from an illegal Israeli settlement, through the site of a demolished Bedouin village, to holiday accommodation beside a Finnish lake.

    Finland’s ministry of defence must still approve the acquisition because the purchaser comes from outside the EU and EEA. But that system principally examines questions such as national security and defence.

    Involvement in illegal Israeli settlements does not fit neatly into the categories through which the transaction is being examined.

    Kinnula exposes a gap in the emerging European restrictions on trade with illegal Israeli settlements. Those restrictions follow economic relationships from Europe towards the settlements.

    Here the relationship points the other way. What happens when the economies of illegal Israeli settlements come to Europe to acquire public assets, invest and make money here?

    There is also now the fact that Europe accepts that it should not economically support illegal Israeli settlements, meaning it should also accept that companies involved in illegal settlements should not be able to come to Europe for public land, contracts and investment.

    “The situation at the Ceuta border had been genuinely critical for years, and crossings had occurred frequently — just never on this scale.”.

    Look at the current situation around the world. For instance, many people in Morocco face severe economic hardship, unemployment and so on. This leads to the younger generation seeking a better life. In this way, we are all in the same boat and I think many of us would make the same decision as them.

    This crisis was compounded by other factors. The media played a role. Some say it was a network of people smugglers. I am not particularly convinced by that argument, since smugglers typically aim to make money. Here, it appears that people migrated alone, so it is not clear how a smuggling network could have made much money. Others claim the surge was linked to the legalisation of undocumented migrants in Spain, or that a court ruling in Spain had “opened people’s eyes”.

    Some politicians have claimed that the legalisation of undocumented migrants automatically grants them EU citizenship.

    No one in their right mind would claim that – it’s utter nonsense! There is research and a substantial body of academic work examining the impact of granting residency status.

    Italy has run several immigration regularisation programmes in the past, something its politicians seem to forget when they argue against new ones. The US did the same under Ronald Reagan in the 1980s. There is no solid evidence that these programmes encourage more people to try to enter the country irregularly in the future. In fact, the opposite has often happened: irregular migration numbers have tended to fall, because giving people legal status and stability reduces the incentive to live and work in the shadows.

    Read more

    Sánchez and the EU have decided that Morocco relations are too big to fail

    Moreover, under this specific Spanish programme, people can apply for regularisation only under very specific circumstances, applying only to a group of people who entered the country at a very specific point in time. It was a one-off measure. Based on the facts examined by researchers, it is unlikely to have had anything to do with this.

    How do you respond to right-wing politicians who say Spain opened Europe’s borders?

    They are like kindergarten children. What we are really seeing here are political actors such as EU migration commissioner Magnus Brunner exploiting the situation to point the finger at Spain, which has taken a somewhat different path from other European countries. Ceuta was a welcome opportunity to say, “you are wrong, this is your fault,” and thereby justify a hardline approach.

    There were calls to exclude Spain from Schengen…is that even possible?

    No. The EU’s Schengen Borders Code, means everyone who is part of Schengen is bound by it. And there is no exclusion clause. Sometimes I do not know whether it is ignorance or simply deliberate deceit, but excluding a country from Schengen is simply not possible. What you can do is introduce border controls. However, the code contains a provision stating that, under strict circumstances and in the event of an emergency, border controls may be introduced for a very limited period.

    Read more

    The EU’s 15 year self-declared war against migrant smugglers is a deadly joke

    Border controls between Schengen countries should be temporary, but controls at the Slovakia-Austria and Germany-Austria borders have been in place for months or years. Is that even legal?

    “Any reasonable lawyer looking at this would ask: where do you see the emergency?”

    It is a breach of EU law. It is clear and everyone knows it, but the Germans deny it. Ceuta, too, was a welcome opportunity for Schengen members to say: “Another emergency, great! Let us use this to justify more border restrictions.” Any reasonable lawyer looking at this would ask: “Where do you see the emergency?” The overwhelming majority of people in Ceuta were sent back, with only a very small number who will make it to the mainland at all. Being in Ceuta does not mean you can access mainland Spain.

    You can only reach mainland Spain by sea. It is not as though you can get there by land.

    Indeed, just look at a map. Ceuta has a specific role and legal regime. Being in Ceuta does not mean that you have freedom of movement when travelling. If, for example, you apply for asylum in Ceuta, that does not automatically give you the right to enter Spain. And when you leave Ceuta to enter Spain, you are checked again, and if you do not have documents, you will not be allowed in. So saying, “they are all here in Europe now,” is a populist statement.

    “The only group likely to end up in Spain — and hopefully they will — are unaccompanied minors, who require special protection under European and national law.”

    These migrants are hundreds of kilometres away. They do not suddenly have the right to enter the mainland. The only group likely to end up in Spain — and hopefully they will — are unaccompanied minors, who require special protection under European and national law. Ceuta is not a place where Spain can guarantee that special protection, so it will probably have to transfer them to the mainland.

    EUobserver reported that thousands of children had been left living on the streets.

    Spain is thereby violating international law, EU law and national law every single day, because it has an obligation to immediately assess all minors and provide them with accommodation, food, psychological support and healthcare. They should not be there for even one day.

    Ceuta has been problematic for many years, with people climbing over the fences there virtually every day. And the EU has been unable to resolve the migration problem more widely, not only in Ceuta, but in other countries too. Why, in your view, is the system not working?

    Hundreds of people were still camping yesterday at Puerta del Sol in Madrid. They were demanding action on housing, as rents and property prices continue to rise.

    Did they take the protesters’ demands into account?

    MariCarmen Abascal had lived in her apartment since the 1950s, having inherited the lease from her parents. But the property was bought by an investment fund, which then challenged the validity of her lease and quadrupled her rent.

    Last week, MariCarmen was evicted from her home. The eviction sparked widespread outrage and led hundreds of protesters to camp in central Madrid, calling for action.

    Yesterday, she was finally allowed to return home after reaching an agreement with the owners.

    Aside from MariCarmen’s case, the demonstrations are largely driven by young people who are fed up with rising rents and property prices, especially in major cities such as Madrid and Barcelona.

    In Madrid, property prices have risen by around 87 percent over the past ten years. That’s less than in Portugal or the Netherlands, where prices have increased even more. But it’s still a significant rise, especially as wages have grown much more slowly over the same period.

    Rents are taking up a huge share of people’s incomes. In Madrid, they account for almost half of tenants’ net income on average. So, how did the Spanish government respond?

    Yesterday, it adopted two housing decree-laws. The first decree would suspend evictions until 2030 and automatically extend existing rental contracts by two years.

    It would also introduce tighter rules on seasonal rentals and prevent speculative investment funds from acquiring housing until 2028.

    The second decree is more ambitious. It would allow tenants to extend their future rental contracts indefinitely. This is what the tenants’ union has been calling for.

    Landlords would no longer be able to end a lease simply because it had reached its expiry date. Tenants who pay their rent and respect their legal obligations could remain in their homes for as long as they wish.

    This would also limit rent increases, since rents can only be raised moderately during an existing contract.

    So, the government has taken the protesters’ demands into account. But there is still a major obstacle: as our Spanish partner El Salto reports, the tenants’ union fears that this second measure may not pass through Parliament.

    Read more

    Even if prices stop rising, they are already so high that many workers can no longer afford to live in major cities.

    More social housing is needed, as well as more renovation. Increasing the supply of decent, affordable homes could help ease pressure on rents and property prices.

    ]]>         MEPs vote for €47bn in new Erasmus+ funds, as frugal states seek cuts to EU budget https://euobserver.com/240375/meps-vote-for-e47bn-in-new-erasmus-funds-as-frugal-states-seek-cuts-to-eu-budget/ Tue, 29 Sep 2026 15:54:11 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240375 With 24 votes in favour and one abstention, MEPs proposed to increase the European Commission's original proposal from €40bn to €47bn on Tuesday. ]]> The European Parliament’s culture committee on Tuesday (29 September) agreed to boost the flagship Erasmus+ student exchange programme by €7bn in 2028-2034 linked to rule-of-law conditions, even as so-called frugal countries seek to cut overall funding.

    The vague statements by Magnus Brunner, the EU home affairs commissioner, in Brussels on Tuesday (29 September), followed an equally vague proposal announced by commission president Ursula von der Leyen in her State of the Union speech on 11 September, who pledged to create a “European emergency response framework”.

    Read more

    Poland’s pushback drive and EU asylum ‘emergency’ plan put rights ‘on a cliff edge’, warns Europe’s top rights chief

    When asked if her new framework would include the possibility to suspend asylum at the EU’s external border in cases that mirrored this summer’s Ceuta crisis, when tens of thousands of people entered the Spanish enclave in north Africa, Brunner said: “I can’t go into details, because it’s a discussion which is going on at the moment”.

    His non-committal take on the hot button issue also came after a resolution adopted by the centre-right European People’s Party (EPP) in Brussels on Tuesday, which is demanding that member countries, in some cases, be given the option to temporarily suspend asylum applications.

    Specifically, it calls on the EU “to adopt legislative measures authorising refusal of entry or returns without individual asylum procedures for illegal migrants used in a hybrid attack”.

    Meanwhile, Brunner and von der Leyen come from the same conservative party in the EPP, posing questions to what extent political pressure has influenced the latest commission initiative.

    Greece’s prime minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis (also EPP) in early August had already gone public with demands for new EU rules allowing for asylum to be suspended for newly arrived people.

    The Polish government (EPP) also weighed in, claiming credit for getting von der Leyen to cite the idea in her big speech.

    Warsaw had earlier this month extended its asylum ban on people entering from Belarus, in what rights groups say involves pushbacks that cause loss of life.

    Read more

    ‘Hidden zone of violence’: investigators trace over 100 migrant deaths to Poland–Belarus border regime

    But for Brunner, the issue had already been broached in a commission asylum strategy report that was published back in January.

    That report references “weaponisation of migration” by hostile countries, such as Belarus and Russia, and links it back to another commission document from December 2024 that argues there are certain exceptional situations in which the ban on pushbacks cannot apply.

    For Michael O’Flaherty, who is the human rights commissioner at the Council of Europe, a rights watchdog based in Strasbourg, any effort to extend the existing EU ban criteria risked unraveling decades of human rights law.

    The issue will be discussed by EU interior ministers on Thursday and Friday in Luxembourg, where migration weighs heavily on the agenda.

    And those talks, in turn, will lean into and continue among heads of state and government at an EU summit on 15 October.

      <title>UK 30-year borrowing costs hit 6%, highest since 1998, as government bond sell-off intensifies – business live</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/live/2026/oct/01/uk-house-prices-september-mortgage-rates-bonds-stock-markets-manufacturing-latest-news-updates</link>
      <description><p>Global bond rout kicks off again, with US 10-year Treasury yields hitting highest since 2002</p><p><strong>Worryingly for Paris, <a href="https://www.borsaitaliana.it/obbligazioni/spread/francia/oat-bund.en.htm">the difference between French and German borrowing costs</a> has widened to a 14-year high this morning.</strong></p><p>The gap between French and German government bond yields – a market gauge of the risk premium investors demand to hold French debt - was at 127.51 bps, after reaching 128.80 bps, its highest level since June 2012, <em>Reuters reports</em>.</p><p>Inflation, deficit and issuance concerns continue to weigh on the bond market.</p><p>There is also a buyers strike on the street as investors do not want to step in till we get some form of stability. Hedge Funds have suffered in the latest round of sell-off and do not have the risk appetite to fade the move. Real money, potentially has the risk appetite, but won’t step in till we get some stability.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/live/2026/oct/01/uk-house-prices-september-mortgage-rates-bonds-stock-markets-manufacturing-latest-news-updates">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Federal Reserve watchdog finds no criminal violations for building renovation cost overruns</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/sep/30/federal-reserve-watchdog-building-renovation</link>
      <description><p>Trump criticized $2.4bn rehab amid attempts to pressure then Fed chair Jerome Powell into lowering interest rates</p><p>An internal watchdog said the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/federal-reserve">Federal Reserve</a> mismanaged costs associated with a $2.4bn renovation of its Washington DC headquarters, but noted that no criminal violations occurred, according to a report released on Wednesday.</p><p>For over a year, <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a> has centered his attacks against the Fed and former chair <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/jerome-powell">Jerome Powell</a> around the renovations, including a months-long Department of Justice criminal investigation that was <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/apr/24/doj-drops-criminal-probe-jerome-powell-fed">dropped</a> in April.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/sep/30/federal-reserve-watchdog-building-renovation">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>A ‘freaked out’ US food industry is hitting back at Maha – with social media influencers</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/sep/30/us-food-industry-maga-social-media-influencers</link>
      <description><p>Cross-partisan support in Washington on issues like pesticides and food additives pose a threat to the industry’s bottom line </p><p>Some of the biggest food and agriculture corporations in the US are funding a campaign that pays social media influencers to combat elements of Robert F Kennedy Jr’s Make America Healthy Again platform, according to an investigation by the Guardian and Documented, an investigative watchdog and journalism project.</p><p>The ascension of RFK Jr to secretary of health and human services has boosted his putative campaign to end chronic illness in the US, which he believes is primarily caused by processed foods and dyes, exposure to certain chemicals, and poor farming practices, along with an overuse of what he falsely claims are dangerous vaccines. The “Maha” movement blends long-running mainstream concerns about food and farm safety with conspiracy theories about everything from medicine to milk. A Maha “<a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/28/vance-rfk-tyson-hines-maha-summit-01095218">summit</a>” in Washington this week will feature JD Vance and several members of Trump’s cabinet.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/sep/30/us-food-industry-maga-social-media-influencers">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/29/ban-canada-imports</link>
      <description><p>It marks another ratcheting up of Trump’s trade war and affects nearly $1bn in imports of a $880bn trade relationship</p><p>US-<a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/canada">Canada</a> relations, already tense, are likely to deteriorate further after the United States went ahead early on Tuesday with a decision to ban nearly $1bn worth of Canadian imports, including alcoholic beverages, dairy products and motorcycles.</p><p>The ban amounts to barely a ripple in $880bn worth of annual two-way trade between the two northern neighbors.       <description><p>Trump’s tariffs and his war against Iran caused prices to rise, but the US president continues to claim it’s ‘the greatest economy in history’</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/04/sign-up-to-the-stakes-2026-your-weekly-guide-to-the-us-midterms">Sign up for The Stakes 2026: your weekly guide to the US midterms</a></p></li></ul><p>Donald Trump has taken to repeating a familiar boast: “<a href="https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/pool-reports-september-16-2026">We have the greatest economy</a> in history,” Trump said recently at a White House press gaggle. The boast comes even though inflation is higher and economic growth lower than when Joe Biden left office, even though <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/business/energy/gas-prices-trump-midterms-iran-rcna598523">gas prices have jumped about 50%</a> since the war against Iran started, and even though <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/09/15/polls/times-siena-poll-likely-voter-crosstabs.html">73% of Americans think the economy</a> is in fair or poor shape (48% say it’s in poor shape). What’s more, the Federal Reserve is so worried about inflation that it just raised interest rates.</p><p>“It’s bluster, it’s gaslighting for him to say the economy is the greatest ever,” said Darrick Hamilton, chief economist for the AFL-CIO, the nation’s main union federation. “The economy is trending down by many measures. A lot of that has been caused by Trump’s unforced errors.”</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/sep/28/trump-us-economy-midterm-elections">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Demand for Scotland’s most famous export has slumped, with industry facing job cuts and closures</p><p>Obscured by the Scottish countryside on the outskirts of Kirkcaldy, Cluny bond is, in effect, a small town built to store whisky.
