]]>Feodora Chiosea<![CDATA[Still paying bank fees? It may be time to switch]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/09/30/still-paying-bank-fees-it-may-be-time-to-switch/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/09/30/still-paying-bank-fees-it-may-be-time-to-switch/Wed, 30 Sep 2026 05:00:00 +0000Is it time to break up with your bank? If you’re still paying current account fees in an era of free banking, it might be time to have the talk.

Once upon a time, a relationship with a bank was exclusive. Maybe you got together when you were younger, you trusted them with your salary and your savings, maybe you even took out a mortgage together. Your current account did the basics, such as paying the bills, receiving and dispensing cash, and offering access to a bit of foreign currency for your holidays.

But when a new generation of digital banks comes along offering current accounts that are free and full of snazzy features, what do you do? Do you stay loyal to your old fee-charging current account provider or do you ditch them for mostly free banking? Or is polyamorous personal banking the way to go, where you hang on to your “just in case” old branch bank while taking on a neobank too?

Fees

A number of new digital banks are now offering Irish customers current accounts with no monthly fees. Monzo, Revolut, Bunq and N26 do not charge a fixed maintenance charge for their basic accounts.

These are financial technology or “fintech” companies so there are no branches; you bank exclusively through an app.

Revolut, Bunq and N26 are licensed by the Lithuanian, Dutch and German central banks respectively. Monzo is the first digital bank to secure a full European banking licence through the Central Bank of Ireland.

Monzo, Revolut and Bunq customers will have an Irish Iban. Deposits, as with all the neobanks here, are protected up to €100,000.

The absence of fixed current account maintenance charges are a big part of the neobank sales pitch. AIB-owned EBS is the only “bricks and mortar” bank here that doesn’t charge a fixed maintenance fee for its current account.

From Revolut to Money Jar: What are your options among new digital banking players?

PTSB Explore current account customers pay an account maintenance fee of €96 a year – or €8 a month. Bank of Ireland, AIB and An Post customers pay €72 a year. Fees vary by credit union but can amount to between €48 and €60 a year.

If all your current account does is receive your salary and pay direct debits, it is likely time to question why you are shelling out the equivalent of six months of a streaming subscription for something that isn’t half as entertaining.

Cash is king?

The digital banks might offer free current account banking but there can be some limitations, depending on how you bank.

If you need physical cash regularly, the ease and cost of getting it is something to consider before ditching your old bank. The no branch/cash thing is one of the main reasons people who sign up to a neobank still keep some connection with a pillar bank on the side.

With the neobanks, you can use your physical or virtual debit card to pay at the till but, unlike AIB, Bank of Ireland, PTSB, EBS and a credit union current account, you can’t generally get cash back.

If you need a regular stream of fivers for birthday cards, bake sales and the tuck shop, that can be a pain.

You can take your neobank card to an ATM but withdrawals may come at a cost.

With a Revolut standard free account, you can withdraw up to €200 per rolling month, or five withdrawals, whichever comes first. Thereafter, you will be charged a fee of 2 per cent of anything withdrawn over those limits.

Monzo allows you withdraw up to €300 fee-free per rolling 30 days, with a 2.5 per cent charge on amounts withdrawn after that.

With a Bunq Free account, there is no monthly fee but ATM withdrawals will cost you €2.99 each. As physical cards are not included with this account, you’ll need to use an ATM supporting Apple Pay or Google Pay to withdraw cash.

An N26 standard account grants you two free euro withdrawals per month with a €2 per withdrawal fee after that.

Traditional Irish current account providers have long moved away from charging “per transaction” ATM fees for euro withdrawals, instead charging the flat monthly or quarterly account maintenance fee mentioned earlier.

Free banking and edgy banter: Monzo raises the stakes for traditional bank customers

The outlier is the An Post Money current account, where you’ll pay 60 cent for an ATM transaction.

Credit union current accounts offer five free ATM withdrawals per month within the euro zone, after which a 50 cent fee applies.

Cash and cheque deposits vary between neobanks. Monzo does not currently accept cash deposits, while Bunq supports cash deposits in Ireland through PaysafeCash, which entails generating a barcode in your app and scanning it at a participating local store.

Cheque handling remains much more limited than with traditional Irish banks.

So if you are opening a neobank current account, there is an argument for hanging on to your traditional current account too. But if that is your thinking, it makes sense to choose a traditional bank with low monthly fees, or none, such as EBS.

However, if you can’t remember the last time you handled cash or cheques, it seems time to question why you are paying daily banking fees with a traditional bank when a neobank could do the job for free.

Other fees to compare when assessing traditional and neobank current accounts are payment transaction fees and charges for non-euro transactions.

With a Revolut Standard account, for example, foreign currency exchange is fee-free within the plan’s €1,000 monthly exchange allowance on weekdays. A 1 per cent weekend exchange fee applies, and a 1 per cent fair-usage fee applies to amounts above the monthly allowance.

Revolut’s plan: a global bank with ‘effectively zero risk’

Taking your Bank of Ireland or AIB debit card on holiday can be far more expensive.

Bank of Ireland charges 3.5 per cent, or a minimum of €3.17, for non-euro ATM withdrawals up to a maximum of €11.43, and 2 per cent on foreign currency purchases.

Withdrawing cash outside the euro zone using an AIB debit card incurs a 2.5 per cent currency conversion fee plus a 1 per cent cash withdrawal commission with a minimum of €2, and a maximum of €6.

Use your debit card to pay in foreign currency and you’ll pay 1.75 per cent of the euro value on purchases, or a minimum of 45 cent on the transaction and a maximum of €11.43.

Bells and whistles

Who knew your current account was not just a place for your salary to land and bills to leave? The neobanks offer more features than you can shake a stick at. Whether some of these are simply gimmicky or genuinely valuable is another story.

The neobanks can help you get more granular with your budgeting and saving. You can do things like track and analyse your spending, or automatically divide your income into different budget lines or pots. You can set spending limits on these budget lines and even split bills with friends.

The ‘two good salaries but still broke’ problem: What’s behind it and what can you do?

Monzo’s “pots”, like Revolut’s “pockets”, Bunq’s “money pockets” and N26’s “spaces”, allow you separate your money into discrete subsections within your main account earmarked for specific expenses such as rent, bills or holidays.

This enables you to, in effect, hide a portion of your money from your current account balance so you don’t accidentally spend it with your debit card.

You can create multiple spending and savings pots, name them, stick a photo on each one if you like and instantly move money between them and your main balance.

You could have a pot for Christmas, summer holidays or car repairs for instance, so that when those bills hit, you will have squirrelled enough money into the respective pot over time to cover them.

When you have a current account with a bank, it’s handy to have some sort of instant access savings option alongside it. Some neobanks also offer an interest-earning savings feature in their current accounts.

Take the Instant Access Savings Pot available with Monzo’s free current account for example. On the money you keep in this pot, separated from your main current account balance, you can earn 2 per cent annual equivalent rate (AER) variable interest. Interest is applied monthly and tax is automatically deducted.

Bank of Ireland offers an Instant Access Demand account, which it says can be used as a money pot but is actually a separate demand deposit account linked to your profile, with its own separate bank account number, rather than just a virtual sub-balance inside your main current account.

It will earn a variable interest rate of just 0.1 per cent AER a year, with deposit interest retention tax (Dirt) at 33 per cent handled by the bank.

Which banks and fintechs have the best rates for Irish savers right now?

Monzo’s app can split your salary automatically into your savings and spending pots. You can set savings goals and targets too and track your progress. You can even use a “lock pot” feature to stop yourself from withdrawing money until a specific date.

If you were to use all of the features available in some of these neobanks, it could turn managing the money in your current account into a second job.

Using the various pots could also see you stockpiling too much money in subsections of your current account when it could be earning a bit more interest elsewhere. Financial advisers might say it would be better and easier to put your money in one all-inclusive short-term savings account where it can earn the best interest available.

Rounding

Revolut, Bunq, N26 and Monzo current accounts also offer a feature called rounding. This allows you opt in to automatically save the change from every purchase. Do this and the next time you spend €4.50 on a coffee, the 50 cent spare change will automatically be added to your savings.

Bank of Ireland, AIB, PTSB and EBS do not currently offer any similar feature, though An Post does.

Again, is this a dinky feature that enables you to save effortlessly, or a bit of a pain? If you are watching the pennies and hoping you will have enough in the account to honour your direct debits, watching your current account balance whittle down even faster than your spending can be unsettling – even if those cents are being siphoned into your savings.

Instant payments

Instant payments were the entry point to neobanking for most Irish people. Revolut has amassed millions of customers here on the back of this feature.

Monzo offers instant transfers too, though the usefulness of this feature will be limited by how many Monzo customers there are in your network.

Why now is the time to review your mortgage

There’s now Zippay too. That’s the instant payments system launched recently by the pillar banks – AIB, Bank of Ireland and PTSB.

The one big advantage for Zippay is that it’s in the app of these three banks, so it has potential to reach more than five million customers. And using it will spare them having to keep toggling to Revolut. Monzo will struggle to compete with Revolut and Zippay on instant payments.

Joint accounts

Being in a couple is where all these new current account options can get a bit messy.

If you have an account with a pillar bank and a neobank, and your partner has an account with a pillar bank and neobank, that’s four different current accounts.

If you are both maintaining a current account with a traditional bank, you could be paying up to €96 each a year each in account maintenance fees, or €192 between you. That’s a Netflix subscription right there.

Biggest difference to your pension pot is not how much money you put in

If you feel you need to hang on to a traditional bank current account for the sake of the odd cash withdrawal or lodgement, you’ll save some money by opting for a joint account here.

Like the main banks, all the neobanks offer free joint current accounts too.

If you do decide to change current account providers, there’s the matter of switching all your direct debits from one current account to another. Ask your new bank if they provide a switching service.

The mismatch reflects the significant value-add attached to certain multinational products and the high level of spending on R&D by these companies.

The foreign-dominated manufacturing sector, which contains the State’s pharma sector, recorded the highest labour productivity in 2025 at €524.8 per hour, while labour productivity in the information and communication sector stood at €415.9 per hour.

Irish productivity metrics are flattered by the presence of multinationals. When the multinational element is removed, labour productivity here is similar to rates seen elsewhere in Europe.

Despite the current era being defined by technological advancement, productivity growth across the world, in both advanced and developing economies, has been sluggish in recent decades. Flagging productivity has been at the core of the UK’s stumbling economic performance since the 2008 financial crisis.

The so-called “productivity puzzle” in the UK and other countries has perplexed economists. Many believe the new jobs created since the crash are predominantly in low-skilled, low-paid sectors where productivity is low anyway.

The stock is now down 48 per cent from a peak in June 2025.

Even well-received Netflix shows have struggled to maintain their audiences past their first seasons, Bloomberg News reported in July. The company’s attempt to buy Warner Bros Discovery, which it abandoned earlier this year, was seen by some investors as a lack of confidence in its ability to grow organically.

A Netflix spokesperson declined to comment.

Ads coming to Netflix in Ireland next March, company confirms

The dearth of Netflix blockbusters stands in contrast with smaller streaming services like Apple’s, which dominated this year’s Emmy Awards, or to the resurgence of theatrical moviegoing, fuelled by big hits such as Obsession, Spider-Man: Brand New Day and The Odyssey. Cinema companies such as AMC Entertainment Holdings, Cinemark Holdings and IMAX have seen their shares rally more than 50 per cent this year, far outperforming the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100’s gains of 12 per cent and 20 per cent, respectively.

However, Netflix’s biggest rival for viewers is Alphabet’s YouTube, whose share of the US TV market reached an all-time high of 14.2 per cent in July, according to Bloomberg Intelligence, which used the most recent monthly data from Nielsen. Netflix’s share dropped below 8 per cent.

YouTube’s gains are “increasingly coming at the direct expense of Netflix,” HSBC analyst Mohammed Khallouf wrote in his September 22nd downgrade. He blamed the trend on “a declining reception to NFLX’s original content,” adding that a “near-term recovery in engagement looks unlikely”.

Of course, Netflix has a long track record of popular titles and some of its biggest hits seemed to come out of nowhere, such as KPop Demon Hunters, Adolescence and Squid Game. It also has some high-profile releases on the horizon. The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, a sequel to Once Upon a Time ... in Hollywood, starring Brad Pitt, will be available to subscribers in December.

The next read on Netflix’s financial performance will come on October 20th when the Los Gatos, California-based company reports third-quarter earnings.

Wall Street is anticipating revenue growth of nearly 12 per cent, which would be the slowest expansion since 2023, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Net income is expected to rise 36 per cent, up from growth of 8 per cent a year ago.

Even with Netflix’s expansion expected to slow, many investors remain positive on the stock’s long-term potential. Part of the reason is its beaten-down valuation. At roughly 19 times estimated earnings, Netflix shares are trading at a more than 60 per cent discount to their 10-year average of almost 50 times.

“I don’t think the concerns about competition are overdone, since everyone is fighting for the next bit of market share, but Netflix has a proven record of finding hits and moving into new growth areas like sports, podcasts and gaming,” said Gerald Sparrow, chief investment officer of the Sparrow Growth Fund, which owns the stock.

“The growth and valuation continue to look attractive, and the management team has been able to get out from overhangs like this in the past. It may not be this quarter, but I think in a year, we’ll look back on these prices as an opportunity.”

– Bloomberg

]]><![CDATA[Australian firm to take 35% stake in Daft.ie owner]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/09/29/australian-firm-to-take-35-stake-in-daftie-owner/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/09/29/australian-firm-to-take-35-stake-in-daftie-owner/Tue, 29 Sep 2026 08:47:51 +0000Australian property group REA is to buy a 35 per cent stake in Daft.ie owner Distilled in a deal worth an estimated €248 million.

The company said the purchase of the minority stake would be funded from debt and existing cash reserves.

Distilled Media, which was founded by brothers Eamonn and Brian Fallon, includes property portals Daft.ie and PropertyPal, classified ads site Adverts.ie, and car marketplaces Used Cars NI and DoneDeal.ie.

Irish-based investment manager Blacksheep Fund Management led an acquisition of the listings group in 2024.

Who are the Fallon brothers behind Daft and DoneDeal?

“This is an exciting opportunity to extend our core property strategy into an attractive, profitable, high-growth market, with increasing adoption of vendor-paid advertising and where our intellectual property and technology is directly relevant,” said REA chief executive, Cameron McIntyre.

“The investment provides immediate exposure to an exceptional business with a strong growth trajectory and a portfolio of high-growth assets.”

The deal, which must clear regulatory hurdles, is expected to close before the end of the year.

Chief executive Eamonn Fallon will continue to lead the business and will retain, along with Brian Fallon, a “meaningful” holding following the deal. Asked for details, the company said it does not comment on individual shareholdings.

“REA is a natural partner for Distilled, combining leadership in digital marketplaces with capabilities that can support our growth,” he said. “There are clear opportunities for collaboration, and we look forward to tapping into REA’s experience to create new value for customers, consumers and partners.”

Recent Companies Registration Office filings revealed that Blacksheep’s deal for Distilled was valued at €627.4 million.

The transaction consisted of almost €450 million in cash, with €312 million of that sum paid to European online classifieds group Adevinta, which had owned 50 per cent of Distilled. Adevinta was a spin-off of Norwegian classified group, Schibsted, which acquired a 50 per cent stake in Distilled in 2015, merging it with its DoneDeal.ie platform.

The Fallons shared almost €240 million from the Blacksheep deal, which was “settled in part by cash consideration and part in exchange for shares”, according to the filings.

The deal also reduced the brothers’ combined stake in the group from around 38 per cent to 16.66 per cent.

In response to questions from The Irish Times last week, the Fallons said: “We love building this business, and we’re focused on continuing to grow it over the long term. With the support of our strategic partners, we see plenty of runway ahead, and we’ll keep investing in the platforms and the people behind them.”

Distilled also owns around 13 per cent of the shares in Journal Media, the online news platform the brothers established in 2010, according to its most recent annual return.

The Fallons continue to hold a controlling stake in that business through their company, DML Capital.

The Irish Times reported in 2024 that the Fallons were in talks to sell The Journal and the42.ie to Irish Independent publisher, Mediahuis. It was understood at the time that the Business Post, then controlled by Galway businessman Enda O’Coineen’s Kilcullen Kapital Partners, was an underbidder for the business in a sales process being run in-house by Journal Media, the parent of the news brands.

However, the deal, said to be valued in the low single-digit millions, was later called off.

]]><![CDATA[Central Bank to slash crash-era levy on insurance policies to 0%]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/09/29/central-bank-to-slash-crash-era-levy-on-insurance-policies-to-0/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/09/29/central-bank-to-slash-crash-era-levy-on-insurance-policies-to-0/Tue, 29 Sep 2026 12:36:44 +0000The Central Bank has said it will cut the financial crash-era levy on general insurance policies to zero from January, a move that could save car insurance policyholders around €6.50 on their annual premiums.

Introduced in 2011 in the wake of the collapse of Quinn Insurance, the Insurance Compensation Fund levy was created after the Government paid €1 billion into the vehicle that is used to pay compensation to consumers for claims on failed insurance firms.

It was designed to ensure that policyholders could be compensated in the event of the liquidation of a regulated firm.

The levy was initially set at 2 per cent but was reduced to 1 per cent last year.

From January, the levy will be cut to 0 per cent, the Central Bank said on Tuesday. The changes will affect holders of non-life insurance policies, such as home and motor insurance.

“The changes announced today reflect the financial position of the fund and follows the full repayment of the outstanding loan balance to the exchequer,” Central Bank deputy governor, Mary-Elizabeth McMunn said. “The reduction of the levy will positively impact a large cohort of policyholders in Ireland.

“The Central Bank will continue to conduct annual reviews of the fund and, should circumstances change, the levy may change in the future.”

The reduction is estimated to eliminate around €60 million that is currently collected under the levy across the whole sector.

Policyholder savings will vary depending on policies and premiums. However, given that the average motor insurance premium was €655 in the first half of 2025 according to the most recent data, a 1 per cent reduction would result in savings of €6.50.

Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris welcomed the reduction.

“At a time when households are experiencing cost of living pressures, the reduction will have a direct and positive impact on the cost of insurance for approximately 2.35 million private motor insurance policies and 1.3 million home insurance policies on renewal next year,” he said.

Minister of State for Financial Services, Credit Unions and Insurance Robert Troy said the Government had done “significant work” to reduce motor insurance premiums since 2016.

“It is further evidence of progress being made in the insurance market, and it is now on insurers to act responsibly and pass on this reduction to their customers,” he said.

Insurance Ireland, the representative body for the industry, also welcomed the move.

“At a time when increasing costs are an important consideration for households and businesses, this is tangible proof of the ongoing stability of the Irish non-life insurance market,” a spokeswoman said.

The reduction comes against a backdrop of a sharp rise in motor insurance premiums last year despite an ongoing decline in the costs incurred by insurers from injury claims.

Central Bank data published earlier this year revealed that motor premiums increased by an average of 4 per cent in the first six months of 2025, more than double the rate of consumer price inflation over the same period.

At the time, Insurance Ireland blamed the increase on rising volumes and the costs of damage-related claims, rather than injury claims. The total cost of damage claims jumped by 8 per cent in the first six months of 2025 compared to the same period in 2024.

]]>Aleksandr Fedosov

   <description>Nach Angaben von Bürgermeister Witali Klitschko haben am Donnerstag zwei russische Drohnen eine wichtige Brücke in der ukrainischen Hauptstadt Kiew getroffen. Activists in Poland have launched what they say is the world’s first delivery locker that provides women with abortion pills, access to which is normally tightly restricted.

They have placed the device opposite parliament in Warsaw, a location intended to send a message to the politicians who have made Poland’s abortion laws among the strictest in the world.

The locker (called an “abortomat” in Polish, combining the words aborcja, meaning abortion, and automat, meaning an automatic machine) has been launched by Women Help Women (WHW), a global organisation that provides “self-managed abortion”, and Abortion Dream Team (ADT), a Polish activist group.

They emphasise that the installation “is completely real [and] not an artistic performance”. It consists of 22 numbered lockers and a numeric keypad. Women who have contacted WHM seeking an abortion are given a six-digit PIN code that opens one of the doors, inside which is a package containing the pills.

Recipients can either take the pills at home or do so in a specially prepared space opened last year by ADT and where the locker is located.

 

The activists emphasise that such delivery mechanisms for abortion pills are particularly important in Poland because of the country’s highly restrictive laws.

Abortions are only allowed in two circumstances: if pregnancy is the result of a crime (such as rape or incest) or if it threatens the mother’s life or health. As a result, only 851 legal terminations took place in Poland last year.

However, activist groups such as WHW, ADT and Women on Web (WOW) say that they help tens of thousands of women in Poland obtain abortions each year through other means, in particular by providing pills.

But they face legal risks for doing so: assisting someone in obtaining an unlawful abortion is a crime punishable by up to three years in prison. In 2023, ABW activist Justyna Wydrzyńska was convicted of that offence. Two years later, the sentence was annulled on a technicality and a new trial was ordered.

Polish activist Justyna Wydrzyńska, who was convicted for providing abortion pills to a pregnant woman, has succeeded in having the conviction overturned on appeal.

However, the case will now return to the lower court, where it will be heard again https://t.co/U3J5FmXdMw

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 14, 2025

“The abortomat transforms a closely guarded, criminalised procedure into something as simple as picking up a package,” wrote ADT. “A door that opens when all others have slammed shut.”

They say that the machine is intended for women who have an urgent medical need that means they cannot wait for the several days it takes to deliver pills by post, or who are in abusive, controlling relationships that make postal delivery unsafe.

Wydrzyńska’s conviction came after the husband of a woman she helped obtain abortion pills found them and reported the case to the police. However, although assisting a woman in obtaining an unlawful abortion is an offence, the woman who had the abortion is not criminally liable.

“The abortomat is not a human being, and the person collecting the pills, in accordance with the regulations, is not breaking the law,” said Wydrzyńska, quoted by news website Wirtualna Polska. WHW and ADT do not collect any personal information from women using the service.

The European Court of Human Rights has ruled that Poland violated the rights of a pregnant woman who had to travel abroad to obtain an abortion after her foetus was diagnosed with a birth defect https://t.co/TgckusMxmJ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 13, 2025

Under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which ruled from 2015 to 2023, the abortion law was tightened and was strictly enforced.

In December 2023, a new, more liberal coalition led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk came to power, promising to liberalise the abortion law. However, it has so far failed to pass any such legislation.

In 2024, a move to decriminalise abortion assistance up to the 12th week of pregnancy was rejected by parliament, after the most conservative element of Tusk’s coalition joined the right-wing opposition in voting against it.

Tusk subsequently admitted that it would be impossible during the current parliament to soften abortion laws. Instead, his government issued guidelines on when and how abortions can be carried out, with the aim of ensuring that doctors and prosecutors “take the women’s side” when making decisions on the issue.

]]> Fugitive opposition politician granted safe passage to return to Poland against prosecutors’ wishes https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/09/30/fugitive-opposition-politician-granted-safe-passage-to-return-to-poland-against-prosecutors-wishes/ Wed, 30 Sep 2026 19:08:37 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=104835

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

A Warsaw court has approved a request from Marcin Romanowski, a fugitive former government minister who has been on the run for almost two years, to receive safe passage back to Poland. Romanowski is believed to currently be in the pro-Russian Moldovan breakaway region of Transnistria.

Although Polish prosecutors have long been seeking Romanowski’s return, they opposed his request for safe conduct, arguing that he cannot be trusted to comply with its terms given that he has repeatedly sought to evade the law.

Waldemar Żurek, the justice minister and prosecutor general, has already announced that prosecutors will appeal the court’s decision, which he claims was issued by an illegitimately appointed judge and in violation of regulations.

Nie ma i nie będzie bezkarności dla ludzi Zbigniewa Ziobry.

Prokuratura złoży ZAŻALENIE na decyzję o wydaniu listu żelaznego dla Marcina Romanowskiego.

Spójrzmy prawdzie w oczy: kto jednoosobowo próbuje zapewnić nietykalność człowiekowi podejrzanemu o gigantyczne nadużycia w…

— Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) September 30, 2026

Romanowski served as deputy justice minister in the former Law and Justice (PiS) government between 2019 and 2023. After PiS lost power, prosecutors sought to bring charges against him for 11 alleged crimes committed while he served in government, including participating in an organised criminal group.

However, Romanowski fled Poland in December 2024 and was granted asylum by Hungary, which was then ruled by Viktor Orbán, a conservative ally of PiS. When Orbán lost power earlier this year, Romanowski went on the run, and for months his location was unknown.

In August, it emerged that Romanowski had sent a letter to Poland requesting safe passage to return. The document indicated that he was in Tiraspol, the capital of Transnistria, a region that sought to break away from Moldova in the 1990s and is now effectively under Russian control.

Prime Minister @donaldtusk says that, based on intelligence sources, Poland is now “99% certain” that fugitive opposition politician Marcin Romanowski is in Transnistria, a breakaway region of Moldova that has close links to Russia https://t.co/mdvmJpkFf7

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 18, 2026

At the time, the spokesman for Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office, Przemysław Nowak, said that there were “no grounds whatsoever” to approve Romanowski’s request for safe passage to Poland.

He noted that “the suspect has evaded legal proceedings, questioned the legality of the authorities’ actions, left Poland and then Hungary to avoid arrest, and publicly declared his lack of intention to return to the country due to the ongoing criminal proceedings against him”.

However, on Wednesday, Warsaw’s district court approved Romanowski’s request. A spokeswoman for the court said that the decision had been made as “previous methods used [to secure Romanowski’s return] were ineffective” and safe passage would “allow the case to be clarified”.

The politician’s lawyer, Bartosz Lewandowski, said that safe passage meant his client could not be detained in Poland and that a European Arrest Warrant against him, which applies in other EU countries, would no longer be valid.

❗️Sąd Okręgowy Warszawie wydał @RomanowskiPL list żelazny, uchylając środek zapobiegawczy w postaci tymczasowego aresztowania od momentu uprawomocnienia się orzeczenia❗️

Mój Klient na terytorium Polski nie będzie mógł być zatrzymany i tymczasowo aresztowany, a ENA „upada”, jeśli…

— Bartosz Lewandowski (@BartoszLewand20) September 30, 2026

In a subsequent justification for the ruling, quoted by the Rzeczpospolita daily, judge Konrad Mielcarek wrote that Romanowski had pledged to “voluntarily return to the country”.

Conditions for his safe passage include Romanowski reporting to the court and prosecutors at designated times and places, not leaving his declared place of residence, and not seeking to obstruct the criminal proceedings against him.

The judge said that prosecutors had failed to provide adequate arguments as to why Romanowski’s request should be denied. He also found that Romanowski had not obstructed proceedings against him, but had merely exercised available legal remedies.

The fact that Romanowski had fled Poland does not count against him, argued the judge. In fact, “the very nature of safe passage is to provide a person residing abroad with a legal guarantee…in exchange for voluntarily submitting to the jurisdiction of Polish authorities”.

The judge also clarified that safe passage is neither a “reward” nor a “privilege” and that, given that evidence in the case is already secured and Romanowski no longer has influence over justice ministry officials, the risk of tampering is low.

 

The National Prosecutor’s Office immediately issued a statement declaring its opposition to the ruling and its intention to appeal. It noted that there had been no confirmation that Romanowski really is in Tiraspol and that the suspect had repeatedly sought to evade the law.

“These circumstances do not provide assurance that the suspect will comply with the conditions of the letter of safe conduct,” wrote the prosecutors, who also pointed to the fact that Romanowski had admitted to using travel documents issued under a false identity.

Żurek, meanwhile, noted that Mielcarek is one of the so-called “neo-judges”, appointed by a judicial body rendered illegitimate by PiS’s reforms. There are legal doubts about the status of such judges and the rulings issued by them, some of which have been overturned on that basis.

In his statement, the justice minister also argued that, under the law, safe passage cannot be issued without a prosecutor’s consent. Lewandowski, however, cited examples of case law that he said disproved this. He also noted that prosecutors had not filed any motion to recuse Mielcarek from the case.

Prokurator ocenia dzisiejsze postanowienie Sądu o wydaniu podejrzanemu Marcinowi Romanowskiemu listu żelaznego jako niezasadne.

Na postanowienie to prokurator złoży zażalenie.

Sąd może wydać list żelazny, jeżeli podejrzany przebywający za granicą złoży oświadczenie, że stawi…

— Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) September 30, 2026

Romanowski served in the justice ministry when it was led by Zbigniew Ziobro, a deputy leader of PiS, who is also wanted by the Polish authorities on suspicion of 26 crimes relating to his time in office.

Like his deputy, Ziobro also obtained asylum in Hungary. When Orbán lost power, Ziobro fled to the United States, reportedly with help from a senior Trump administration official. Poland has requested that Ziobro be extradited, though that process could take years.

Both Ziobro and Romanowski deny committing the crimes they are accused of and claim that they are being pursued as an act of “political revenge” by the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

After eight years of service, Cobra, one of the first dogs to serve in the security force of Poland’s parliament, has retired. To mark the occasion, the speaker of the lower-house Sejm, Włodzimierz Czarzasty, personally informed Cobra of the decision.

“An application for transfer to retirement?” said Czarzasty, sitting opposite the extremely well-behaved Cobra in a video published by the Sejm.

“Impeccable reputation. No disciplinary punishments. You’ve never barked in the Sejm,” he read from her files. “OK, signed. As of tomorrow, you are free.”

Cobra idzie na emeryturę! 🐕‍🦺
Decyzję o przejściu w stan spoczynku przypieczętował podpisem Marszałek Sejmu @wlodekczarzasty. 😉
Psy Straży Marszałkowskiej to ważny element systemu ochrony Sejmu. Czuwają nad bezpieczeństwem wszystkich osób w gmachach pozostających w zarządzie… pic.twitter.com/dKRvHOlKxe

— Sejm RP🇵🇱 (@KancelariaSejmu) September 30, 2026

On a more serious note, the Sejm pointed to the vital role played by dogs in the so-called Speaker’s Guard (Straż Marszałkowska), which is responsible for security in parliament.

“They watch over the safety of all people in the buildings managed by the chancellery of the Sejm,” they wrote, thanking Cobra for eight years of “exemplary” service and wishing her well on her “well-deserved retirement”.

Two weeks ago, the Sejm announced the arrival of a new dog, Otik, who would serve as part of the Speaker’s Guard. He has worked alongside Cobra and another canine colleague, Hela, until now.

State broadcaster TVP reports that Cobra was one of the first dogs to enter service in the Speaker’s Guard. It notes that dogs serving in the force are eligible for retirement after reaching the age of nine.

Their handler has the option of taking in the dog after it retires, or they can nominate another person to care for the animal. The chancellery of the Sejm then continues to cover the costs of any veterinary care that the dog requires. It has not been revealed where and with whom Cobra will spend her retirement.

In 2021, Poland’s government moved to introduce retirement benefits for dogs and horses who had served in the police force, border guard and fire service, providing them with support after they finished working. The following year, that was extended to the prison service.

The development means that inflation has now risen above the upper bound of 3.5% set by the National Bank of Poland (NBP), which aims to keep the figure at 2.5%, plus or minus one percentage point. Analysts say that an interest rate hike by the NBP is now more likely.

The new preliminary inflation figures from Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, show that prices in September were 4% higher than a year earlier, the fastest rise since June 2025. On a monthly basis, prices in September were up 0.7% from August.

The rise was caused in particular by the price of fuel for private transport, which was up 36.1% on a year earlier and 9.2% from the previous month. Energy prices also rose, with electricity, gas and other fuels up 4.9% year-on-year and 0.9% month-on-month.

The government has been under pressure from the opposition and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki to reintroduce the subsidies. However, it argues that Nawrocki’s decision to block a proposed windfall tax on fuel companies makes the measures harder to fund

 

Food and non-alcoholic beverage prices provided some offset, falling 0.5% from a year earlier, although they edged up 0.1% from August. Analysts, however, expect food prices to rise later in the year to reflect lower agricultural yields.

According to GUS’s own estimates, also published on Wednesday, the grain harvest came in 5% lower compared to the last season. This will, in turn, “push the CPI index higher in the coming months”, wrote Erste Bank.

A Polish painting looted by Nazi Germany during World War Two, and which once hung in an SS officers’ club, has been returned by its owner, who donated it to the National Museum in Warsaw.

Her ministry is responsible for seeking the return of tens of thousands of artworks and other cultural items that were looted during the war and remain missing.

— Ministerstwo Kultury i Dziedzictwa Narodowego (@kultura_gov_pl) September 28, 2026

Wierusz-Kowalski, who was active in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, was a renowned realist painter whose work often featured animals alongside people. His Winter – Napoleon’s Retreat from Moscow had, by the 1930s, become part of the collection of Andrzej Rotwand, a wealthy banker and industrialist.

In June 1939, it was featured in an exhibition organised by the Society for the Encouragement of Fine Arts in Warsaw, which occupied the building that is now the famous Zachęta National Gallery of Art.

However, the exhibition was brought to an abrupt end when Nazi Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939. The works on display, along with other items from the gallery, were seized by the occupiers, with many used to decorate the offices and apartments of German officials.

Winter – Napoleon’s Retreat from Moscow was displayed in a club for high-ranking SS and police officers located in Warsaw’s Blanka Palace. The same building also housed Warsaw’s German-installed commissioner, Helmut Otto, and mayor, Ludwig Leist.

 

No information has been released as to the fate of the painting in the immediate aftermath of the war. However, it eventually came into the possession of Ewa Tsonis, who has now handed it back.

Speaking at a ceremony in the National Museum in Warsaw, Tsonis said that her late father, Michał Stefan Koryzna, had purchased the painting in the 1960s from Desa, a major gallery and auction house, in the city of Kraków.

“I grew up with this painting. It was greatly appreciated and loved in our family,” she said. However, after recently conducting research into the painting’s history, she became aware of its provenance and notified the culture ministry.

Ewa Tsonis (right) alongside the painting with culture minister Marta Cienkowska (centre) and the director of the national museum in Warsaw, Agnieszka Lajus

Experts from the National Museum in Warsaw confirmed the identity of the painting, which remains in good condition and in its original frame. Tsonis then donated the work to the museum.

“Restitution is not possible without the cooperation of many people and institutions – both on the side of the state and on the part of the owners of the works,” said Cienkowska, who thanked Tsonis for her “incredibly responsible and civic-minded attitude”.

“Such attitudes are still rare but, because we constantly talk about restitution – we search for lost works and strive to recover them – we are increasingly approached by people who own lost objects and feel a sense of responsibility for cultural heritage.”

Cienkowska noted that the culture ministry has so far secured the return of over 920 works, with around 200 more restitution cases currently underway in 18 countries.

Germany has agreed to return to Poland a collection of 73 medieval documents that were looted during WWII.

However, that is still just a small fraction of the over 60,000 missing items listed in the ministry’s database of missing works, which includes seven further paintings by Wierusz-Kowalski.

Two other works from Rotwand’s collection – Italian Woman by Anna Bilińska and Mother with Children by Kazimierz Alchimowicz – were also hung in the SS officers’ club during the war and today remain missing.

Several early medieval Arabic silver coins have been found in a forest near Elbląg in northern Poland. Experts believe they may have belonged to merchants travelling to or from the Viking Age port of Truso, which was situated nearby.

The silver dirhams date back around 1,200 years, to the first half of the ninth century, before the founding of the Polish state. They may have remained in circulation until the turn of the 10th/11th century, the time of the settlement’s collapse.

The discovery of the “new treasure” was announced last week by the Archaeological and Historical Museum in Elbląg. It did not reveal who had unearthed them, but said that the find had taken place during a legal search in a forest near the town of Młynary, just east of Elbląg.

After conservation and processing work, the coins will be included in the collection of the museum, whose archaeologists will also visit the site hoping for further finds.

The museum’s Jakub Jagodziński told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that the find consists of “six early medieval Arabic dirhams and two fragments of these silver coins”. He said that they are provisionally dated to the first half of the 9th century, but a more precise estimate will be possible after they are processed.

 

The coins could have belonged to merchants travelling along the routes leading to or from Truso or to Prussian guards who later collected tolls on these routes, Jagodziński explained.

Truso was a Viking Age port of trade set up by the Scandinavians on the shores of lake Druzno near the Vistula river delta. Established by the late 7th century and active until the early 11th century, its location enabled trade extending towards Kyivan Rus, Byzantium and the Islamic world.

Historians knew of Truso’s existence because of the account of the Anglo-Saxon traveller Wulfstan of Hedeby. Centuries-long efforts to find the precise site proved fruitless until it was finally discovered in the early 1980s by the young archaeologist Marek Jagodziński, Jakub’s father.

Finds of Arab coins in Poland are not unprecedented. A silver deposit was discovered in 1986 on the site of Truso itself, consisting of 11 complete coins and five fragments. Coins found there were minted in places including Baghdad and Damascus, according to the Medievalists.net website.

More recently, in 2024, a fragment of an early medieval Arabic dirham was found during renovations of an old manor house on the Baltic coast in northwestern Poland.

In transactions involving dirhams, it was the value of the silver that mattered, so the coins were often broken into pieces, archaeologist Grzegorz Kurka told PAP.

“Therefore, when hoards of Arab coins are discovered in Poland, they are divided into several pieces. Whole coins are also found, but much less frequently,” he explained.

Poland has proposed that, if the United States grants Ukraine permission to produce its own missiles for Patriot air-defence systems, the factory could be located on Polish territory to ensure its security.

The news was revealed by deputy defence minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, who also confirmed that Poland would seek to establish a Patriot servicing and production facility even if it does not host Ukraine’s.

Poland wants to host Patriot production

Poland has proposed that the US and Ukraine launch joint production of Patriot missiles. Warsaw is citing security concerns and is proposing to host the facility in Poland instead of Ukraine:

“If such a factory is planned to be built in… pic.twitter.com/syCkNt0o0V

— Belsat in English (@Belsat_Eng) September 27, 2026

Patriot missile systems have been a key part of Ukraine’s defence against Russian aerial attacks. However, Kyiv has suffered from a shortage of missiles used in the system, prompting President Volodymyr Zelensky to appeal to allies to transfer their interceptors as well as to allow Ukraine to produce them itself.

US President Donald Trump initially told Zelensky at a meeting in July that “we are gonna give you a licence to make Patriots”. However, he then backtracked on that offer later the same month.

But, following weeks of uncertainty, on Friday last week Zelensky claimed that Trump had personally told him he had made a “final decision” to approve a licence for Ukraine to produce Patriot missiles. Washington has not confirmed that development.

 

Asked about the issue on Saturday, Sobkowiak-Czarnecka told broadcaster TVN, “let’s see if it happens”. However, she added that, “we proposed that, if such a factory is planned to be built in Ukraine, we propose building it in Poland, so that it would be in the so-called safe territory”.

Poland is already the primary hub for military equipment, goods and people being transported in and out of its eastern neighbour.

Sobkowiak-Czarnecka added that, regardless of where the plant serving Ukraine is located, Poland would also still seek to establish a facility for servicing and, eventually, production of Patriots.

“What my interlocutors in Washington confirmed is that, even if such a decision is made regarding Ukraine, it does not change our efforts and does not rule out consent for Poland,” she said. Sobkowiak-Czarnecka was in Washington last week for talks with US officials.

In May this year, another deputy defence minister, Cezary Tomczyk, told TVN that Poland had “received preliminary approval from the US State Department to produce missiles for Patriot systems”.

The Polish government has confirmed that it has transferred Patriot missiles to Ukraine following opposition criticism

It also released a list of all military donations to Ukraine since 2022, showing that the former PiS government gave much more equipment https://t.co/8BmDy5BjiB

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 7, 2026

In 2018, as part of its Wisła air defence programme, Poland signed a $4.75bn contract to purchase Patriot launchers and missiles from the US.

In October 2023, the first Patriot systems procured from the US were deployed at Warsaw Babice airport. In December 2025, Poland announced full operational readiness of its US-supplied Integrated Battle Command System (IBCS), an air-defence network that includes Patriot missile batteries.

Poland also has an agreement to domestically produce launchers for Patriot systems through cooperation between Polish state-owned defence contractor Huta Stalowa Wola SA and US defence giant Raytheon.

Poland has announced a $1.2bn deal that will see a Polish state-owned defence firm manufacture 48 launchers for Patriot missile systems domestically in cooperation with US defence giant Raytheon https://t.co/PQOjKvhqYM

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2024

The issue of Ukraine’s need for more Patriot missiles caused domestic political controversy in Poland earlier this year, when the right-wing opposition reacted angrily to reports that the government had handed over some interceptors to Ukraine.

In July, the government confirmed that it had done so. However, Prime Minister Donald Tusk later revealed that only five missiles had been transferred to Ukraine.

In late July, the Center for Strategic and International Studies reported that the Iran war had depleted America’s stockpile of Patriot missiles to 800 interceptors from roughly 2,300 before the war began.

Last week, Germany’s defence minister, Boris Pistorius, confirmed that his country has also proposed that it could manufacture interceptors and perhaps even entire Patriot systems.

One of the priests injured in a knife attack by a Ukrainian man at a Catholic abbey in Poland last week – which left one of his colleagues dead and another fighting for his life in hospital – has delivered a homily calling for people to forgive the attacker and not to blame Ukrainians as a whole for his actions.

“I ask you not to repay evil with evil, but with love, support, understanding and care,” said a visibly injured Father Adrian Mantykiewicz. “I ask you to respect and support each other as two brotherly nations.”

🙏 Poruszające słowa ks. Adriana po ataku nożownika w Opactwie w Jarosławiu. W swojej pierwszej homilii po napaści duchowny mówił o przebaczeniu, miłości do bliźniego i odpowiadaniu dobrem nawet na doznaną krzywdę. pic.twitter.com/zGEGvC5meB

On Thursday last week, a 31-year-old Ukrainian man, who can be named only as Ihor H. under Polish privacy law, entered the grounds of the Benedictine abbey in the town of Jarosław.

Using a knife he took from a kitchen, he attacked five people before he was stopped. One priest, Stanisław Zbojnowicz, died from his injuries shortly afterwards. Another, Marek Pieńkowski, is still being treated in hospital.

Ihor H. was arrested at the scene and, on Saturday, a court approved a request from prosecutors for him to be placed in detention for three months. For now, he is being held in a psychiatric facility, with prosecutors saying that he “displayed symptoms of mental illness”.

President @Zelensky has condemned an "evil" knife attack by a Ukrainian man at a Catholic abbey in Poland today, which left a priest dead and others injured

Polish Prime Minister @donaldtusk says the perpetrator will face the “full severity of Polish law” https://t.co/SIonlR4JpJ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 24, 2026

On Saturday, in a church that is part of the Benedictine abbey complex, Mantykiewicz celebrated the Eucharist for Zbojnowicz. With bruising under his left eye and bandages on his head and hand, he delivered a homily in which he addressed the attack, its victims, and the perpetrator.

“I am a disciple of my master, a disciple of my lord, and Christ teaches me love,” he said. “And from this place, as a disciple of Jesus Christ, I wish to say very clearly in my name, in the name of Father Marek, and in the name of Father Stanisław, that we forgive.”

“I ask you to pray for our tormentor,” he continued. “He needs this prayer most of all. Because no matter what happened, we must overcome the evil that occurred here in our abbey with goodness, love, and forgiveness.”

 

Mantykiewicz also appealed for people not to blame Ukrainians more broadly for the incident. There have been fears that the attack could prompt a backlash against Ukrainians, Poland’s largest immigrant group, who have already been experiencing a growing number of hate crimes this year.

“I also want to ask you not to blame the nation from which the perpetrator came,” said the priest. “The evil was committed by a specific person…responsible for their own actions. It was not done by other people. It was one person, one person alone.”

“Let us be disciples of Christ. Disciples who help others with love, care, respect, help and kindness,” he continued. “It does not matter who they are, what nation they come from, what religion they are, or what colour their skin is; they are human beings…and we must not deprive anyone of their dignity.”

On Friday, the head of the Polish Catholic church’s council for migrants and refugees, Bishop Krzysztof Zadarko, gave a press conference at which he condemned the “outpouring of aggression and artificially stoked hatred towards Ukrainians that this event [in Jarosław] has fuelled”.

“The church can only appeal to the consciences, primarily of Catholics and Christians, but also of all people, that this is not the right response; it is downright reprehensible, and incompatible with the Gospel,” he added, quoted by broadcaster RMF.

“We are dealing with a tremendous tragedy, but shifting the blame of one person onto an entire society, ethnic group, or nationality is wrong,” he added.

Thursday’s attack caused widespread shock and mourning in Poland, and also prompted condolences from Ukraine, including President Volodymyr Zelensky, who said that “we are shocked by this evil”.

On Saturday, Ukraine’s ambassador to Poland, Vasyl Bodnar, told broadcaster TVN that he had spoken with Ihor M.’s mother and was able to provide more information about him.

He confirmed that the man had left Ukraine in 2022 and lived in Germany. Bodnar, however, said that media reports claiming Ihor M. had served in the Ukrainian military were false.

Regarding the motive, Bodnar said that it appears Ihor M. “had some kind of mental illness”. He pledged that the Ukrainian authorities would cooperate and were “working on all the information we can provide to the Polish side”.

City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Thu, 01 Oct 2026 13:33:33 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.0.6 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 Chef’s Table: Victor Garvey interviews top Japanese actress Yoh Yoshida https://www.cityam.com/mater1a-chef-victor-garvey-interviews-japanese-actor-yoh-yoshida/ Thu, 01 Oct 2026 13:30:48 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2462455

Dine with Yoh Yoshida and Victor Garvey at MATER1A as they discuss Shakespeare, Japan and Michelin-starred cuisine—read the full conversation.]]>

Japanese actor Yoh Yoshida  is interviewed by her friend Victor Garvey, the restaurateur behind two Michelin-starred Notting Hill restaurants. They tuck into a tasting menu at his MATER1A to talk careers, inspiration and paying respects to Richard III

The Meal:

  • Tomato jelly noodles
  • Amuse bouches
  • Tuna sashimi
  • Roasted scallop 
  • Wagyu with miso and morels
  • Cherry with almonds and chocolate

Yoh Yoshida:  Hi Victor, it’s so nice to see you again. It must be six months since we last caught up!

Victor Garvey:  Yeah, this will be your first time in MATER1A. You’re in for a treat. What brings you to London?

YY:  It’s a funny story – I have been playing a series of Shakespeare characters on the stage in Japan: Hamlet, Brutus and Richard III. After that I wanted to come here to pay tribute to the real Richard III, so I have been in Leicester to visit his grave at the cathedral.

VG:  Oh wow, that’s so cool. I don’t know many people that would travel so far to pay their respects like that. I’ve never gone and paid my respects at Paul Bocuse’s grave. Is it normal in Japan, to go to all that effort?

YY:  Not really, it’s quite unusual but it’s something I really wanted to do. I felt a real connection to the character, an empathy for him, which is strange because I’m known in Japan for playing more honourable people, and Richard is one of the great villains!

VG:  It must be a really different experience to do Shakespeare in Japanese. I can’t imagine being able to keep the rhythm that Shakespeare originally intended in a language that takes longer to speak. If I say a sentence in English, it might be five words and take two seconds but the same sentence in Japanese is 12 words and takes six seconds. Japanese sentences are very descriptive, and they always have to have a place and a time – that’s just the way it works, right? So when you’re doing something as classical as Shakespeare, is it difficult to get the timing right?

YY:  Yes, it’s different. The translation I was working on was quite modern, similar to the way we speak now. Sometimes it can work in your favour though. Take the famous line: “A horse! A horse! My kingdom for a horse!” – in Japanese the word for horse is “uma” which leaves you with an open mouth shape, which makes it easier to convey the feeling to the audience.

VG:  So Yoshida-san, do you remember where we met?

YY:  Of course! I was in London for the Film Festival, promoting A Pale View of Hills, an adaptation of the novel by Kazuo Ishiguro. I was in a Japanese izakaya with the director Ishikawa-san for the after-party and we got talking. I remember being a bit scared because of all your tattoos. They are becoming a little more normal in Japan but for a long time they were associated with criminals.

VG:  Yeah, the first time I visited Japan about 20 years ago I only had one tattoo but they still wouldn’t let me go in the onsen! The restaurant where we met is called Jugemu and it’s the best izakaya-style place in London. My good friend Kikuchi-san owns it. I used to go there once a week and I still go when I have some spare time. I was just sitting there minding my own business drinking beer when suddenly 15 or 20 Japanese people came in. I moved to the back of the bar, almost in the kitchen, and you came and sat beside me. I was just drunk enough to introduce myself. My daughter lives and breathes Harajuku style and anime so we got talking about that. I had no idea that you were famous until the manager at Jugemu came over and said you’re like the Jennifer Lawrence of Japan.

YY: And I had no idea you were a Michelin starred chef – it’s a nice way to start a friendship, we just bonded as people. We must have chatted for about three hours. 

VG:  Our schedules actually work when you’re back in Japan, too – as a chef I work late so we usually chat at one o’clock in the morning here, which is early in the morning in Japan. There’s a chance we might end up seeing a lot more of each other soon: my daughter wants to go to culinary school in Japan. She’s 14 and she wants to leave school when she’s 17 to learn the trade. I said, ‘No problem, just show me good grades’. If everything works out I’ll probably move back for six months and stay with her – you can take me around Japan like I’ve taken you around London. Because visiting Japan as a normal gaijin and visiting Japan with Yoshida-san is very different, I imagine.

YY:  We will make a strange pair wandering around Tokyo together but there are some restaurants I’d love to take you to. I have so much love for sushi.

VG:  I love sushi too. When my daughter and I are together, it’s all sushi all the time. I love everything about it, but I’m a bit bored of tuna and hamachi. So if I’m eating sushi in Japan, I want something exciting and different.

YY: I know some places you would like…

VG:  Of course you do, you eat at the best restaurants in Japan, right? It makes cooking for you here at MATER1A quite daunting. My cuisine is very modern, very fusion, so I was worried that someone like you who’s very knowledgeable might think I was going to shit all over Japanese cuisine! It’s a relief to see you enjoying it.

YY:  I knew I would enjoy it. I knew from when we first met that you were an open-minded person and you can see that in your food. You can see your cooking comes with a great love and respect for Japanese cuisine. 

Often Japanese-Western fusion feels contrived but this is something else entirely. It’s also funny you say you might spend some time in Tokyo – one of my ambitions is to study acting in London. I’d love to study at LAMDA. 

VG:  Is there a role you’d love to play?

YY:  There is – I’d love to play Carol, the title character in the movie starring Cate Blanchett. One day I would like to star in a Japanese version of that film. I have so much admiration for Cate Blanchett and she is amazing in that film. On the surface she plays this strong, intelligent woman but inside she is very fragile, vulnerable even. That’s the kind of role I love to play. What about your career – tell me what you have been up to.

VG:  I’ve been so busy Yoshida-san. Since we met last October I opened MATER1A, which has been doing really well and getting great reviews. Then we relocated my other restaurant Sola from Soho to Notting Hill. That’s all up and running and it’s really great, very different from the original – it’s smaller and more intimate but it’s the best food I’ve ever made. I’m feeling so creative at the moment, just spending hours in the kitchen, coming up with new dishes.

YY:  Remind me what brought you to Japan…

VG:  I was there from 2011 to 2012 on an exchange programme. I was working at the Bellagio hotel in Las Vegas and they sent me and a small cohort to the Park Hyatt in Tokyo. I was a young, broke chef but I had a bit of pocket money to go out and the restaurants there changed the way I thought about food. 

The culture in Japan is to hyper-specialise. Even at a neighbourhood counter restaurant you’ll find someone who does something at a level you can’t get your head around. There was one place we went that specialised in Spanish mackerel and I’m not kidding it was the best Spanish mackerel I’ve ever had. Everything was just absolutely perfect. There’s a reason Japan has so many Michelin stars and it’s all about quality of ingredients and consistency.

At some point I’d love to open a restaurant in Japan. It calls me. I wake up in the middle of the night thinking I need to go back. I have six beers and I look on my phone to see when the next flight leaves for Tokyo. I wouldn’t open a sushi restaurant – I’ll leave that to the masters. Maybe something Spanish. Don’t worry, you’ll be invited to the opening!

• For more information on MATER1A visit the website here; For Sola go to the website here; Yoshida-san’s latest film Ha-Chan, Shake Your Booty! directed by Josef Kubota Wladyka is out now in the US

The chemical group owned by billionaire Jim Ratcliffe has urged the government to reopen the North Sea for drilling as it lashes out at its latest energy cost scheme for businesses.

INEOS, which was founded by Ratcliffe in 1998, said Labour’s British Industrial Competitiveness scheme (BICS) fails to address UK industries relying “far more heavily on gas than electricity”.

BICS is an initiative which allows manufacturing companies to apply for a cut of up to 25 per cent on their electricity costs. The government first announced the scheme, which opened for applications on Thursday, in June 2025 as part of its modern industrial strategy to unlock economic growth and give businesses “breathing space”.

Business secretary Jonathan Reynolds said the scheme will “help companies spend less on energy and more on growing their business”.

But INEOS said this was a “fundamental misunderstanding” from the government over what companies truly need amid rising gas and oil prices.

UK natural gas prices have climbed eight times higher than those in the US over the past two weeks. Domestic prices have hovered at £18 per unit, compared to just £2.19 in North America.

“This is destroying our manufacturing base, threatening skilled jobs and increasing the UK’s dependency on carbon-intensive imports,” said an INEOS spokesperson.

“Unless this imbalance is addressed, we will only see further decline.”

Domestic gas projects

CV

  • Name: Suresh Balaji
  • Job title: Chief marketing and experience officer at Lloyds Banking Group
  • Previous roles: Global head of marketing and communications at Standard Chartered; CMO Asia and global head of media and marketing innovation at HSBC; NED of a Blackstone-invested marketing technology firm, other roles in banking and pharma.

What was your first job?

Selling vaccines to medical practitioners, long before vaccines became a dinner party topic. Turns out the hardest sell in the world is prevention, because nobody ever thanks you for the disease they didn’t get. Everything I know about marketing intangible value, I learned in a GP’s waiting room.

What was your first role in the City?

This one, strictly speaking. Although if you’ll grant me Canary Wharf as the City’s younger, taller cousin, I was global head of media and marketing innovation in a previous life.

When did you know you wanted to build a career in the City/banking?

I studied chemistry, which is essentially the study of what happens when two things that shouldn’t work together do. Then vaccines, then a stint in advertising, then a chow-mein of a career in banking across Asia-Pacific, Middle East and London. I’m not sure I ever decided on a career so much as kept following the more interesting.

What’s one thing you love about the City of London?

The density of unimaginable juxtaposition. You can walk five minutes and pass a Roman wall, a Wren church and three people building AI agents in a basement. Two thousand years of continuous reinvention inside a single square mile.

And one thing you would change?

The majority of the City runs almost entirely on league tables, titles and promotions, and almost not at all on whether the work was any good. I’d also retire the belief that seriousness and imagination are opposites. The city still dresses its best ideas in the dullest jargon. What’s been your most memorable business lunch?

Meeting Tim Berners-Lee. He gave the web away rather than monetising it, which is arguably the most consequential marketing decision in history and the precise opposite of what any of us would have advised him to do.

I did a short stint in advertising in the days of proofs and bromides. We published a full sale advert with the client’s logo missing. Fallen clean off. Successfully refreshing a 250-year-old brand in Lloyds and a 350-year-old brand in Scottish Widows in the same year. Making them ready for the app and AI economies and everything that follows.

Uncertainty is the price of an interesting career. The certain jobs are rarely the interesting ones, and certainty is usually what a role feels like just before it becomes irrelevant.

“Stay in your lane.” Everything worthwhile I’ve done has happened in the gap between two lanes. Or an interesting never-trodden lane.

A neighbourhood boot camp, or a protein shake at Joe & the Juice. I don’t drink, so I’ve quietly swapped the pub round for burpees. Aspirational or antisocial, depending who you ask.

South-west London, deep in nappy valley.

Family, and Luna the dog, who is entirely non-negotiable. Which means the New Forest or Cornwall rather than anywhere requiring a passport and a kennel.

Britain’s AI minister has ordered changes to government guidance that urged civil servants to limit their use of AI, saying it failed to reflect ministers’ ambitions to ramp up adoption across Whitehall.

Kanishka Narayan said guidance published last week had now been updated after it advised government workers to use AI only when necessary, choose smaller models and keep prompts to a minimum to cut energy use and costs.

“Being environmentally conscious and keeping an eye on running costs is, of course, important – but so is encouraging AI adoption and scaling up its use across the public sector”, Narayan said on X.

“This advice has been updated and we are reviewing similar pages to reflect the fullness of our ambition for the UK”.

It comes just days after government guidance attracted attention for telling civil servants there was no need to thank AI chatbots, alongside recommendations to use lighter models such as Gemini Flash rather than Gemini Pro and GPT Instant instead of GPT Thinking.

The guidance said AI uses more energy and resources than conventional software and told staff to consider whether a spreadsheet or search engine could do the job instead.

Civil servants were also advised to keep prompts “short, clear and direct”, use as few prompts as possible and only turn to AI when needed,

The latest version instead puts greater emphasis on responsible use rather than discouraging unnecessary use.

It tells civil servants they remain responsible for their work when using AI and must check its output for inaccuracies, bias or unfairness.

Staff are also warned to protect sensitive information and use systems provided by their departments for government work.

“You are responsible for any content or decisions you make using AI”, the new advice says, telling officials to use their own judgement and be prepared to explain decisions made with the technology.

The change highlights the balancing act facing ministers as they push AI deeper into government while trying to control the risks and costs that come with it.

Whitehall’s AI push

The change in direction comes as the government looks to accelerate AI adoption across the public sector, an area that now falls directly within his ministerial responsibilities. Minister Narayan’s brief covers both the government’s AI strategy and public sector adoption.

Existing government guidance already encourages civil servants to explore how generative AI could improve their work, while warning them not to enter sensitive or personal information and to check outputs for misinformation and bias.

A government AI playbook published last year similarly set out ten principles for the use of the technology across Whitehall, covering how officials should select, buy and deploy AI safely.

But the push to accelerate adoption has come alongside concerns over how quickly AI is being introduced into public services and whether sufficient human oversight remains in place.

The government’s Responsible AI Advisory Panel discussed the need for effective coordination across Whitehall at its latest meeting in September as departments expand their use of the technology.

Narayan has nevertheless made expanding adoption a central part of his brief, arguing that Britain should develop and deploy advanced AI rather than allow the next technological shift to happen elsewhere.

The findings highlight a “continuing lack of confidence in the current administration’s long-term fiscal framework”, authors of the study wrote, despite the UK boasting the most ambitious deficit reduction path of any G7 economy.

Last year, Rachel Reeves announced a surcharge of £2,500 to £7,500 a year on homes worth more than £2m. Outside of London, £1.5m might buy you something resembling a mansion. Inside London, it will often only get you a terraced house with a small garden.

Of the London homes sold between £1.5m and £2m last year, one in six were flats. Most of the rest were terraced houses. Nobody in Lewisham, where I was born, thinks that’s a mansion. Hamptons found that 60 per cent of the homeowners who would pay the tax bought their home for less than £1.5m. House price inflation dragged them in. At £2,500 a year, the charge is over £200 a month on top of council tax, for a family whose only crime was buying a house in London a long time ago.

Even Sadiq Khan has felt the pressure and now says he opposes it. He is right to. But the Mayor’s objection means little if his colleagues in Downing Street don’t listen.

That is a double whammy for London. Young Londoners can’t afford a home, because it has been made harder and more expensive to build them. And those who have worked hard to buy their own home are now taxed for it. Labour is punishing both the people trying to get on the housing ladder and the people who climbed it.

It’s also unlikely any of the tax revenue raised from this hike would stay in London. Wandsworth, Kensington and Chelsea, Westminster and Richmond say their residents alone would pay over £270m a year, but not a penny would fund a local service. It goes straight to the Treasury. 

At the same time, Labour’s funding formula is stripping money out of those same boroughs, with Wandsworth alone losing £84m. Londoners pay more, London keeps less, and the money leaves the capital.

London needs a Mayor who will say no to this tax and back Londoners instead of treating them as a cash cow. That is the Mayor I intend to be.

James Cleverly is prospective Conservative candidate for Mayor of London

Prices fell 0.2 per cent during September, faster than economists had expected and reversing August’s 0.2 per cent increase, according to data from Nationwide. The average UK home was valued at £274,251 in September.

Prices were 0.8 per cent higher in September than a year earlier, half the 1.6 per cent year-on-year rise recorded in August, according to Nationwide.

The figures add to signs of a sluggish property market ahead of John Healey’s first Budget on 28 October, when further measures affecting the housing market are expected.

Separate HMRC figures published on Thursday showed home sales also fell in August, down one per cent on July and two per cent from a year earlier.

Robert Gardner, Nationwide’s chief economist, said: “Market activity and house prices have remained subdued in recent months, in part reflecting the uncertain economic backdrop”.

Higher energy prices have fuelled inflation concerns and expectations that interest rates could rise, putting further pressure on mortgage costs.

Gardner said higher borrowing costs had partly offset an improvement in affordability as wages continued to rise faster than house prices.

But he said there were “encouraging signs” that higher energy prices were not feeding through to underlying price pressures.

“Underlying affordability is improving, as house price growth has been well below earnings growth for some time”, Gardner said.

He added that activity could regain momentum if the energy shock fades, confidence returns and market interest rates fall.

The property industry is now looking to the Budget for further clarity. The government has already confirmed Healey will set out details of its new Your First Home scheme, which will offer government-backed equity loans to some first-time buyers purchasing new-build homes.

North pulls further ahead

The national slowdown masked a sharp divide across Britain, with northern regions continuing to outperform the South.

Northern Ireland remained the strongest-performing part of the UK in the third quarter, with prices up 5.9 per cent from a year earlier, although that slowed from 8.6 per cent in the previous quarter.

The North West led England with a 3.9 per cent rise, while prices increased 3.3 per cent in both Scotland and the North.

Southern England went in the opposite direction, with prices falling 0.1 per cent overall.

London was the only southern region to record an annual rise, although prices edged up just 0.4 per cent compared with 1.6 per cent in the previous quarter.

Eight of Nationwide’s 13 regions recorded annual rises of less than one per cent, while four posted outright falls.

There was also a growing gap between different types of homes. Terraced houses performed best, with prices up 1.8 per cent from a year earlier, while flats were virtually unchanged.
