    Robert De Niro talks to City AM The Magazine about his enduring love for Nobu, and how aged 83, he is fiercely protective of his businesses

    In an intimidatingly futuristic building made almost entirely of glass, I pass through a marble-clad lobby, up a flight of stairs and into an expensive-looking hotel suite. Here a handful of serious-looking people sit around a brightly lit boardroom table. Most of them are hospitality professionals: a general manager, a chief executive, a gaggle of publicists. One of them is the most famous actor in the world.

    Robert De Niro looks at the ground, channelling all of his energy into standing up to shake my hand. He lifts slowly out of his chair but I ask him to, please, sit down, don’t get up on my account. He’s shrunk a little from his heyday, his shoulders more rounded, but that’s all that reveals his 83 years. And if he’s a little less formidable, it’s only physically. His vibe is still deadly: De Niro would rather spit than say a single word more than is necessary, or, worse, a word he didn’t mean.

    We’re at Nobu Portman Square hotel in Marylebone, part of the group the actor co-founded in the 1990s, a fact that still carries a sheen of unbelievability even after three decades. De Niro isn’t even the only octogenarian around this table. Also joining us is Nobu co-founder Meir Teper, the 83-year-old film producer who, like De Niro, side-hustles as a lifestyle tycoon.

    Robert De Niro and the Nobu story

    De Niro is here to discuss the three Nobu Hotel & Residences opening in Egypt, including a restaurant on the north coast that’s already started plating up sushi, and the phased launches over the next five years of resorts in Cairo and the coastline. Residences are also soon-to-launch in Manchester, as is Nobu’s first wellness club and countryside retreat, Nobu Woolfox, which will open next year on an estate near Rutland in the Midlands, rivalling luxury offerings in the Cotswolds. De Niro is coming for the wellness industry, too.

    Nobu is an incredible success story. There are now 19 Nobu hotels and 55 restaurants serving namesake chef Nobu Matsuhisa’s Japanese-Peruvian cuisine. International openings are green-lit by De Niro himself, who is a kind of vibe checker for the brand. As Teper puts it: “We follow his vision.” The story goes that De Niro convinced chef Nobu to open a restaurant in Tribeca in New York in 1994; that flagship, still thriving, was the beginning of a global empire now estimated to be worth $1.3 billion (De Niro, Teper and Matsuhisa are understood to own 80 per cent; with the other 20 per cent held by private equity firm Blackstone).

    He’ll say, ‘I don’t think we belong here’

    By all accounts, De Niro has an instinct for destinations that will – and crucially, will not – work. Sometimes that instinct seems to border on the preternatural: when our sister publication spoke to him in 2025, he admitted he’d never been to Manchester and knew nothing about the city, despite having commissioned a Nobu Residences there. So how on earth does a man regarded as one of the best actors of his generation know what makes a good location for a Japanese restaurant? “I just say, ‘Where do I wanna go?’” De Niro tells me. He really does speak in that smash-em-up, gravelly, menacing tone. “Would I like to walk into that restaurant in that particular place?” He scrunches his face to make an impression of a first-time visitor. “That first sight, where it is, what part of the world… it’s important.”

    His strategy clearly works: only five Nobu restaurants have closed in 30 years, which is especially impressive when you consider the hardships faced by the hospitality industry (in London alone half of restaurants shut within two years of their first service). Madonna once said you could tell if a city was going to be fun by whether it had a Nobu in it. In keeping with De Niro’s reputation for speaking his mind, he’ll happily draw a red line through potential new locations. “He’ll say: ‘I don’t think we belong here,’” says Teper. “I don’t want to name names, but it’s not like when somebody approaches us we just say ‘Okay let’s do it.’”

    De Niro inspired by eating on location

    When I ask De Niro what’s unique about the brand, he says it’s simple: the quality of the food and the location. There is no pandering to trends, no evolving ‘concept’. It’s just good sushi. It was British film director Roland Joffé who first introduced De Niro to the cooking of Nobu Matsuhisa in the late 1980s and it was love at first bite. At that point, chef Nobu had only one restaurant in Los Angeles. “Roland said, ‘Come to this restaurant, you’ll like it,’” remembers De Niro. “I was maybe an hour into eating and meeting Nobu and I said ‘If you ever want to open a restaurant in New York just let me know.’

    “For me it was a no-brainer. It would work in New York. And here [in London], too. The Japanese restaurants I’d been to were all the same. Very good, but conservative, staid, nothing exciting. They didn’t pretend to be. But Nobu had another thing, the Latin from his time in Peru, that made it special. So that was it: I said: ‘This will work’. I’d opened a grill with Drew Nieporent, a local restaurateur in Tribeca, a year or two before I met Nobu and I put him and Drew together. It took a while to get it going, Nobu was apprehensive. I can’t remember all the details but finally it happened.”

    The question is, why?

    The partnership makes sense. While Nobu, 76, was brought up slicing fish and thinking about flavour, De Niro spent years travelling the world filming, developing an eagle eye for what makes a restaurant people want to hang out in.

    The bigger question, though, is… why? Why does one of the most lauded actors in the world spend his time promoting expensive condos in Egypt when he’s already worth an estimated $500m? Especially when he might not even live to see them completed? And how does an 83-year-old factor business into his life when he has a three-year-old daughter, who in a recent interview, through tears, he described as the “pure joy” in his life? “She has a very sweet kind of way of looking at you,” De Niro told AARP. “And just taking you in… They just look at you and take it in. I want to be around for as long as I can, to enjoy it, to enjoy her.” He lives with his girlfriend, 46-year-old martial arts instructor and dancer Tiffany Chen, and his youngest daughter in a 100 acre Hudson Valley property that boasts its own ski slope. He has seven children altogether with four women; the oldest, Drena, is 55.

    Maintain the quality. Period. It’s that simple.

    I suggest it’s unusual for someone of his age to be working at all, let alone as the co-founder of an international hospitality empire. De Niro nods deeply and puts up no defence. Does he find something here he can’t in Hollywood? Like, is the public-facing world of film sets and red carpets passé compared to the rigour of the luxury restaurant world? Just for a second, I experience old-school De Niro: He tenses his facial muscles to pull that characteristically strained expression, as if he’s just sucked on a lemon. “No, that’s different,” he says, in combat mode. “It’s just a different thing. I enjoy it and feel very protective of it because I’m part of the creative… We all want to make sure we maintain the quality and everything. That’s it. That’s the key. You’ve got to be careful with that stuff.”

    What happens if the quality isn’t maintained? “We were talking about this the other day – someone was saying, ‘Why have you got to spend that?’. But somebody will visit and notice that’s something a little… off. And then maybe they notice something else and then something else, and all of a sudden it’s not the same restaurant. Then people start to say, ‘Nah I don’t wanna go there.’ The only thing you can do is maintain the quality. Period. It’s that simple.”

    Nobu offers a sense of control

    His acting roles have, of course, changed with age: he’s unlikely to play a character as iconic as Travis Bickle today. Perhaps the Nobu empire offers De Niro a sense of control, speculates PR guru Mark Borkowski, who has worked with Michael Jackson, Prince and Macaulay Culkin. “The parts inevitably narrow: patriarch, mob elder, grandfather. Nobu reverses the power relationship,” he says. “Here, De Niro says ‘Yes’. He chooses where to appear, when to appear and what bears his name. The business makes acting optional, and perhaps at his age optional is the only kind of work worth doing. In a curious way, it is still the same job he has always done: turn up somewhere beautifully lit, hit the mark, say very little and allow everyone else to project meaning onto him. The difference is that now he owns a piece of the room.”

    Nobu has undoubtedly had a good run, but it isn’t what it once was. In the noughties, the Park Lane restaurant – the second in the world to open after Tribeca – was a celeb magnet, the number one destination for actors on the junket circuit. It’s part of the same building that housed the Met Bar, once the city’s coolest watering hole; 20 years ago, that 50 metre stretch of real estate was the most coveted in London. But the creatives have moved on: now the majority of the visitors to Nobu’s London restaurants appear to be international.

    Robert De Niro: movies not to miss

    Today the brand is courted not by the coolest cities in the world, but the ones that wish to replicate the aura of the coolest cities in the world. It is a brand synonymous with ‘placemaking’, helping to establish burgeoning destinations like the Egyptian coast that are keen to welcome moneyed Western visitors. “People are constantly asking us to be in their place to give them a certain cachet or credibility,” De Niro says in a press conference following our interview.

    You could, at a stretch, liken the trajectory of Nobu to De Niro’s film career. He was an unstoppable heavyweight during the 1980s and 1990s, when his collaborations with Martin Scorsese on Goodfellas, Taxi Driver, Raging Bull and Casino made him the most in-demand actor in Hollywood. But his post-2000s career has been more hit-and-miss: his latest straight-to-Netflix thriller The Whisper Man was slated by critics (the Guardian accused him of “sleepwalking” through the movie). His 2025 mob film The Alto Knights also landed badly. His first TV lead, in Netflix thriller Zero Day, in which he played a former US president, received mixed reviews. The last clear hit was 2023’s Killers of the Flower Moon, in which De Niro played an ageing cattle rancher orchestrating a series of murders of Osage tribe members; it is no coincidence the project reunited him with Scorsese for the first time since The Irishman in 2019.

    Early 70s breakout

    Born in Manhattan in 1943 and raised in Greenwich Village, De Niro’s parents Virginia Admiral and Robert De Niro Senior were prominent abstract expressionist painters and poets (they separated when De Niro was two and his dad came out as gay). Initially a shy child, he starred in a school production of The Wizard of Oz aged 10, which helped develop his confidence. He dropped out of high school aged 16 to study acting and took his first paid role that same year in a production of Chekhov’s The Bear. Delivering food and doing extra work to bring in money while auditioning and landing bit part roles, he secured his breakout in Mean Streets in 1973, the first of ten films he made with Scorsese, who grew up in the same New York neighbourhood as De Niro. His role as ‘Johnny Boy’ Civello was a meteoric success, both critically and at the box office, establishing De Niro’s reputation for depicting violent men.

    The year Robert De Niro met Nobu

    His method acting style would go on to be filtered through a raft of intense, highly physical roles before he softened a little in the late-1990s, shifting towards more comedic parts, such as retired CIA counterintelligence officer Jacky Byrnes in Meet the Parents.

    Two significant turning points happened in 1988: De Niro met chef Nobu, and that same year the actor first pushed away from action and into light comedy with the release of Midnight Run (Nobu took six years to come around to opening a restaurant called ‘Nobu’, which eventually launched in 1994).

    Two weeks after my interview, I book into the restaurant at Nobu Portman Square. It feels slightly less exciting entering the imposing glass building this time, but only a bit: it really is a stunning place. I order chef Nobu’s signature omakase menu, on which many of the dishes haven’t changed since the 1990s, including the superlative black cod miso that he popularised during the restaurant’s heyday. House music plays as I eat my way through salmon tartare with caviar and a tiny Japanese wakamomo peach. The glamorous, moody interior is softened by floor-to-ceiling views of the trees outside. If there’s anything to criticise, it is the service, which is not at the level you’d expect.

    Can I remind you he is 83?

    The brand’s impending push into the wellness space feels on-the-nose, given the age of the men behind it. What does wellness look like to a man like De Niro, especially given conversations surrounding longevity? He’s explaining that he’s keen to visit the site in Rutland but hasn’t been yet, when an agitated PR runs in from the other room to close down this topic of conversation. My questions have been heavily vetted and I’ve been instructed to speak only about the Egyptian hotel launches. Time for my final question, she says, despite there still being a quarter of my interview left. The question doesn’t appear to bother De Niro, though. After I finish recording, instead of bolting, he walks past the publicists to shake my hand and tell me to “take care”.

    Unlike stars half his age, who tend to disappear into waiting Mercs to the airport, De Niro goes from our interview to a conference to talk about the Nobu projects in Egypt. Then he had a cocktail reception. Then, in the evening, he has dinner with 30 or 40 journalists and industry figures. In the foyer before the conference, property writers more used to penning dry business-to-business stories could barely contain their excitement at a chance to spot such a huge star. When it comes to promoting a brand, this level of commitment is practically unheard of. Can I remind you that he is 83?

    Staying active into old age embodies a Japanese concept called ‘ikigai’, which chef Nobu himself practices. At 77, some years he still travels for 10 months out of the twelve. Perhaps De Niro’s dedication to Nobu – meeting journalists, architects and business people, scoping out new developments – is his way of keeping the lights on.

Most people protect their digital lives with a handful of passwords they've memorized—a security practice so common it's become catastrophic.]]>

For about five months, a browser extension sat quietly on the home computers of 154 people and watched them log in.

The researchers never saw a password. Everything was hashed on the machine before it went anywhere, leaving them with the shape of each one: its length, its mix of characters, the site it was typed into, and whether the same string had appeared before.

Very often, it had.

What 154 people actually typed

Sarah Pearman and her co-authors at Carnegie Mellon University presented the results at a 2017 computer security conference, having followed each participant for an average of 147 days. Those people logged in across 26 web domains apiece and covered the lot with fewer than 10 distinct passwords.

Roughly 60 per cent of those distinct passwords were recycled, either typed identically on another site or built around a chunk of four or more characters lifted from one the same person used elsewhere.

Banking got no special treatment. Around 85 per cent of the passwords on financial sites appeared elsewhere too, and nearly all of that crossover ran into unrelated categories, so the login for a savings account was also the login for a shoe shop.

What partial reuse looks like up close

Mostly it looks like adding a character.

Among passwords that shared a substring with another, the most common gap between the two was a single character. Digits were the strongest predictor in the Carnegie Mellon model, multiplying the odds of reuse by more than twelve. The authors’ own explanation is that a password with a number in it satisfies more websites’ fussy signup rules, so it travels further.

The tidy minority had barely any accounts

Ten participants mostly built something new for each site, which sounds like a win for good habits until you look at what they were doing online. With one exception, every one of them entered passwords on eight domains or fewer, and they were active on their computers on only 17 per cent of the days they spent enrolled.

The heavy users went the other way. Ninety-four participants, the largest cluster by far, both copied passwords outright and modified them, and they averaged 32 online accounts each. Discipline held up fine at eight accounts and collapsed at thirty.

The password manager result, with a handbrake

Only 19 of the 154 participants had a password manager installed, and the study found no measurable effect on either reuse or strength.

That result deserves caution. One paper is one paper, the subgroup is tiny, and the software could not tell whether people were generating random strings or merely parking passwords they had invented themselves. Rick Wash and colleagues at Michigan State University, who watched 134 participants over six weeks, found each password being reused on 1.7 to 3.4 websites. Their study did not measure partial reuse at all, so the higher figure out of Pittsburgh partly reflects counting a habit nobody had counted before.

Why a recycled password is worth money

Somewhere there is a text file with an old forum password in it, sitting in a folder alongside a few hundred million others. Troy Hunt, the Australian security researcher behind the breach notification service Have I Been Pwned, has documented the trade in combo lists, which are exactly that: vast dumps of email and password pairs scraped out of past breaches. A camera that stayed switched off cost a Florida software company about 75,000 euros.

It belonged to a telemarketer working from the small Dutch town of Diessen, employed since January 2019 by Chetu, an American software firm that at the time ran a Dutch office in Rijswijk. On 23 August 2022 he was told to join something called the Corrective Action Program, which meant staying logged in for his whole shift, sharing his screen and leaving his laptop camera on. He shared the screen. The camera stayed dark.

His objection was brief and entirely unlegalistic. Court filings quoted by The Register record him saying he was not comfortable being monitored for nine hours a day, calling it “an invasion of my privacy” and noting that his laptop activity was already visible to management.

Two more instructions followed, each firmer than the last. On 26 August he was dismissed on the spot, the stated reasons being refusal to work and insubordination.

Three days from the first instruction to the sack.

What the company argued

Chetu’s case, set out in the published judgment of the Court of Zeeland-West-Brabant, was that watching a remote worker through a webcam is no different from a manager walking past a desk. Performance software already sat on the man’s laptop, and that was not considered enough. Chetu wanted to see him working.

Nobody from the company turned up to make the argument in person, as TechCrunch noted, so it went undefended.

What the judge decided

Ruling on 28 September 2022, the subdistrict judge in Tilburg found that ordering an employee to keep a camera running for a full shift conflicted with his right to respect for private life, and that nothing had been offered to justify it. An unreasonable instruction cannot be unreasonably refused, so there had been no refusal to work and no grounds for summary dismissal.

Data protection law dropped out early. On the understanding that no footage would be recorded, stored or used for anything, the judge treated the monitoring as falling outside data processing altogether, and tested it directly against Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alongside Strasbourg case law holding that filming staff at work, covert or not, is a serious intrusion into private life. Had the images been kept, the analysis would have looked quite different.

One much-quoted line deserves care. Coverage including a report in Fortune presented the claim that all-day camera tracking is disproportionate and not allowed in the Netherlands as a finding of the court. In the Dutch record it sits among the employee’s own submissions. What the judge actually held was narrower, and sufficient: this instruction, to this man, in his own home, breached Article 8 with no justification advanced.

Why the sum was so large

Almost none of the money was a penalty for the privacy breach. The largest slice, 50,000 euros, was a billijke vergoeding, an equitable award Dutch judges reserve for employers whose conduct in ending a job has been seriously culpable, with a wrongful summary dismissal among the standard triggers, as the Amsterdam employment firm Workx Advocaten explains. Privacy is why the sacking failed. The sacking is what got billed.

Around that sat roughly 8,375 euros for ignoring the notice period, close to 9,500 euros in statutory transition payment, more than 2,700 euros in unpaid wages, 23 days of untaken leave, the 8 per cent holiday allowance and some 585 euros in costs, all itemised by NL Times. His non-compete clause was lifted as well, leaving him free to walk to a competitor.

How common all-day camera rules are

Is this a bizarre one-off or a policy plenty of people are quietly living with? A survey of 1,000 business leaders at mostly remote companies, commissioned by ResumeBuilder in March 2023, found 37 per cent required staff to sit on a live video feed, and that 93 per cent of those firms had somebody monitoring it, usually for four hours or more a day.

The same survey found 73 per cent had dismissed workers on the strength of monitoring data, and 69 per cent had lost staff who would not accept it.

One survey is one survey. It polled American executives, it relied on self-reporting, and executives describing their own management habits are not a neutral instrument. Treat it as a temperature reading rather than a census.

Where the line actually falls

Whatever this settles, it settles in one jurisdiction, on one set of facts, at the lowest rung of the court system. Article 8 offers nothing in Florida, where employment is generally at will and can end without a stated reason, subject to the usual exceptions for discrimination, retaliation and whatever a contract says.

What the case supplies is a price tag on a boundary that remote-work policy has been drifting across without much thought: supervising the work is one thing, keeping a lens open in somebody’s house for the length of a shift is another. A Dutch judge has now looked at that question once, and the employer left lighter.

Markus Villig was 19 in 2013, fresh out of high school in Tallinn, and frustrated with how hard it was to get a reliable taxi in his own city. He borrowed €5,000 from his family to build a first version of an app, then did the unglamorous part himself: walking up to taxi drivers on the street in Tallinn and persuading them, one at a time, to sign up. What Bolt actually is today looks very different from what Villig built in 2013. Ride-hailing still accounts for the large majority of its revenue, 82 percent in 2024, according to figures reported in public company profiles of Bolt, but the company has spent the years since methodically bolting on new verticals, largely by copying its own playbook of arriving in a category cheaper and faster than the incumbent. Bolt Food launched in Tallinn in August 2019 and now operates in more than 80 cities across 20 countries with over 30,000 partner restaurants. None of that expansion was cheap, and for most of Bolt’s history it wasn’t profitable either. The company pushed early and aggressively into markets Uber had mostly ignored or arrived in late, establishing itself in South Africa, Kenya and Nigeria as early as 2016, and it now operates in more than 850 cities across over 50 countries spanning Europe, Africa, Asia and Latin America, with more recent entries into Dubai (December 2024) and the Toronto area (February 2025).

Villig’s own €5,000 loan covered exactly one prototype. Everything after that came from investors willing to bet that Bolt’s low-cost, fast-mover approach would eventually outlast better-funded rivals in the markets it entered. Operating profit told a similar story of a company just crossing the line, at €19.5 million, reversed from the prior year’s €87.7 million loss. A margin that thin is not really a statement about profitability so much as a statement about intent. Estonia’s population stood at 1,360,745 at the start of 2026, according to Statistics Estonia. That is smaller than many single cities. Out of it has come ten companies that reached a billion-dollar valuation at some point in their history, among them Skype, Wise, Bolt, Pipedrive, Playtech and Veriff, according to Invest in Estonia’s own tally.

Using CB Insights’ underlying company data alongside that population figure, a figure Invest in Estonia and outlets including Fintech Baltic put at roughly 7.1 unicorns per million residents, based on Invest in Estonia’s cumulative count of companies that have ever reached $1B — not a live ranking CB Insights itself publishes, second only to Liechtenstein and more than three times the United States’ rate of about 2.2 per million.

The tiger leap that came before the unicorns

This density didn’t happen by accident, and it didn’t start with a startup. In 1996, five years after regaining independence from the Soviet Union, Estonia launched a state programme called Tiigrihüpe, or Tiger Leap, championed by future president Toomas Hendrik Ilves and education minister Jaak Aaviksoo. Its goal was blunt: wire the country’s schools for computers and the internet as a deliberate act of catching up. It worked faster than almost anyone expected.

The rollout was rapid but not instantaneous. Education Estonia says all schools had computers by 2000 and all were connected to the internet by 2001. It wasn’t only talent that recirculated. Toivo Annus, one of Skype’s founding engineers who led its engineering team until the eBay sale, went on to co-found Ambient Sound Investments with three other early Skype engineers in 2003, a private investment firm that has since backed more than 50 early-stage ventures, according to documented accounts of his career. The ecosystem underneath those ten companies is larger and more active than the unicorn count alone suggests. A per-capita unicorn count says nothing about how many of those companies are still worth a billion dollars today, still headquartered in Estonia, or profitable. Playtech moved its primary listing to London years ago. Skype no longer trades as an independent business at all. What the figure does capture, reliably, is how much outsized technology output a small population has produced relative to its size, whatever has happened to any individual company since, and how much of that output traces back to a single, now-defunct voice-calling app and the state’s own earlier bet on wiring its classrooms. For a country with fewer people than a mid-sized American county, that is the more durable claim.

What the 2025 numbers actually show

Vinted’s first profitable year, by its own account, was 2023, when it reported revenue of €596.3 million and a net profit of €17.8 million, a milestone The Next Web covered as the company’s first since founding. Two years later, the picture is bigger but less straightforwardly better. Vinted moved €10.8 billion in gross merchandise value in 2025, up 47 percent on the year before, and took €1.1 billion of that as revenue, up 38 percent, almost double the 2023 figure. But net profit, which had grown substantially in the years after 2023, fell 19 percent in 2025 to €62 million, and adjusted EBITDA slipped 5 percent to €151 million. CEO Thomas Plantenga framed the trade-off plainly in the release: the company is spending on expansion, including a push into Germany, category diversification beyond clothing, and the launch of a payments wallet called Vinted Pay, rather than banking the growth as profit this year.

That is a company reinvesting in expansion while remaining profitable, not a company in trouble. It is worth naming the distinction because the two can look similar on a spreadsheet, and a 19 percent drop in profit reads very differently once it’s clear the company was profitable at all only two years earlier, and is still profitable now, just less so by design.

A platform built on other people’s closets

What the €10.8 billion figure represents is how far secondhand clothing has moved from a hobby into ordinary consumer behaviour across Europe. The company has said it intends to bring the same model to the United States next, according to Dealroom’s coverage of the 2025 results. Whether Vinted’s European logistics playbook, built over seventeen years and hundreds of thousands of parcel points, transfers to a market with a completely different postal and returns infrastructure is the open question the 2025 numbers don’t answer.

Rapidly changing feed content may increase task switching and decision-making, which can make scrolling feel mentally tiring.]]>

An hour disappears into the phone and the honest inventory afterwards runs to three items: a man cutting marble, somebody’s strong opinion about interest rates, a dog on a skateboard.

None of it is retained in any way worth having. The hour still lands like work.

That mismatch, between the feeling of effort and the absence of anything learned, has a reasonable research explanation behind it, and willpower barely features in it.

A feed is a run of cold starts

Reading a book is one long continuous job. The brain loads a setting, a cast, an argument, and then keeps using that same setup for as long as the reading lasts.

A feed offers nothing of the kind.

Each post arrives with its own subject, tone, format and rules, which means the machinery of attention has to reconfigure itself before any of the content can be processed.

A feed adds another recurring job: a verdict. Each item has to be sized up for whether it is true, whether it is funny, whether it is aimed at anyone in particular. That call gets made before the thing can be dismissed, and then made again at the next one, and the one after that.

Psychologists have taken that reconfiguration apart. In a paper published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, Joshua Rubinstein, David Meyer and Jeffrey Evans described two stages: goal shifting, meaning the decision to do this now instead of that, and rule activation, meaning the swap of mental instructions from the old job to the new one. Both stages take time. A single switch might cost only a few tenths of a second. That sounds trivial until you count the switches inside an hour of scrolling.

Their experiments used arithmetic and shape-sorting rather than phones, so applying the finding to a feed is an inference, not a measurement.

The part that stays behind

Switching also leaves something on the floor. Sophie Leroy, now a professor at the University of Washington Bothell, coined the term attention residue in a 2009 paper in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, after experiments in which people were pulled off one task and pushed onto another. Performance on the second task dropped, because a slice of their attention was still parked on the first, and the effect was sharpest when the first task had been left unfinished.

Scrolling has the shape of that setup. Post after post is dropped mid-thought and replaced by the next one, which looks a great deal like the unfinished condition Leroy identified as the costly one. Her participants were working through lab tasks, though. The parallel to a phone is drawn by analogy, and nobody has run the experiment there.

Forty-seven seconds

Gloria Mark, a professor of informatics at the University of California, Irvine, has been logging how long people stay on a single screen since 2004. Back then the average was about two and a half minutes. In an interview with the University of California, she put the recent figure at roughly 47 seconds, with a median of 40, meaning half of all observed stretches were shorter than that.

That number needs handling with care. It is assembled from separate studies across two decades, not one group of people followed the whole way, and what it measures is screen behaviour. People still read long books. They just do it somewhere other than a browser tab.

Why a book behaves differently

Does the medium itself change how much gets understood? Pablo Delgado of the University of Valencia and three co-authors pooled 54 studies covering more than 171,000 participants in a meta-analysis for Educational Research Review, and found a consistent, modest advantage for paper. The gap widened when reading was timed instead of self-paced, held for informational texts but not narrative ones, and grew across the years studied, an unhelpful trend for anyone expecting digital natives to close it.

Pooling dozens of experiments makes that result sturdier than any single study, though the effect itself stays small.

Maryanne Wolf, who studies the reading brain at UCLA, argues in an op-ed for the Guardian that skimming squeezes out the slower processes that make reading useful: drawing inferences, making analogies, testing whether a claim is true, stepping into another person’s point of view. Move the eye fast enough and there is no room left for any of it.

Where the tiredness comes from

Fatigue needs its own explanation, and it comes from a separate strand of Mark’s research.

In a study presented at the 2008 CHI conference, Mark, working with Daniela Gudith and Ulrich Klocke, interrupted people mid-task and measured what happened. The interrupted group finished faster, with no drop in quality, which was the surprise. They also reported more stress, more frustration, more time pressure and more effort.

Compensation, in other words.

The brain appears to cover the cost of fragmentation by spending harder. Mark’s participants were working rather than scrolling, and the equivalent test has not been run on a feed, so the link is suggestive rather than established. Even so, the flatness and irritability at the end of a long scroll, the vague sense of having been mugged, match what those participants described.

Which puts the whole exercise in a different light. An hour on a feed involves several hundred small decisions made at speed, each one demanding a quick ruling on what the thing is and whether it matters. The content was the least of it. The deciding was the job.

Nobody sends an invoice for that. The tiredness is the receipt.

Across five studies of secondhand-market haggling, sellers were often more candid than buyers expected. Three minutes of small talk before the haggling narrowed the gap, and so did asking buyers to think about the seller's conscience first.]]>

A pair of speakers, two years old, is up for sale online. When no music is playing, they give off an annoying static noise, and the listing does not say so.

A buyer’s message ends with a pointed question: “The speakers don’t have any problems, do they?” In one of the experiments built around that exact question, 85 percent of sellers mentioned the noise, and fewer buyers than that expected their seller to mention a problem.

Shira Garber and three colleagues staged a string of these secondhand sales online across five main studies and a pilot, added a second pilot that surveyed people about what drives negotiators, and reported the results in an open-access paper in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin this July. Buyers, they found, often underestimated how honest sellers would be. Sellers also reported more concern with being honest, fair and kind, and less concern with the money, than buyers credited them with.

How often did sellers come clean?

In each of the five main studies, some participants played sellers of a secondhand device with a defect they had been told about: an iPod whose battery drained fast, an electric scooter with a faulty battery, the speakers with the static. The rest played buyers, who could earn bonuses for accurately predicting how honest sellers would be.

In the first four studies, a seller counted as honest only if a reply named the defect. Staying quiet counted as dishonest, and so did a dodge like a battery that “isn’t brand new.”

The first pilot set the pattern. Of 76 online workers playing sellers, 63.2 percent picked a truthful opening message over one describing the iPod as being in excellent condition. Of 85 observers given the same information, 43.5 percent predicted the truthful one.

In Study 1, the 176 sellers wrote their own replies to “What can you tell me about it?” and “Anything else?” Of those sellers, 51.7 percent disclosed the battery problem, while the 270 buyers guessed, on average, that 43.2 percent would. With the scooter and a direct question in Study 2, three quarters of sellers disclosed the fault.

The rate swung with the setup. One cause, a direct question, got its own test; other swings the researchers could not fully explain. Until the last study, the exchanges were also largely scripted, with sellers answering pre-written buyer messages rather than a live counterpart.

The way the question is asked

Study 3, with 483 participants, gave half the sellers the pointed “The speakers don’t have any problems, do they?” and half the open “What can you tell me about them?” Buyers here were not told about the static, which is closer to how a real listing works.

The direct question made sellers more likely to mention the noise. Buyers’ predictions did not move with it.

The gap between expected and actual honesty was statistically significant under the direct question and not under the open one, so even inside this paper it did not show up everywhere. Of several possible reasons Study 1 still found a gap with open questions, the authors single out one: sellers there had two chances to come clean, and concealing twice may weigh more on a seller’s conscience than concealing once.

A few minutes of small talk

Study 5 was the only one that paired people live. It matched 422 participants into 211 buyer-seller pairs on an online platform, and some pairs first spent three minutes chatting about something they had enjoyed recently or how they unwind after a busy day.

Across the study, buyers rated their seller’s likely honesty at 6.56 on a ten-point scale, while coders scored the sellers’ actual replies at 7.51. Among pairs who chatted first, that difference was no longer statistically significant. Sellers’ scores did not differ significantly between the two conditions. The chat raised buyers’ expectations of honesty instead.

Study 4 tried a different nudge on 358 participants. Some buyers were asked about the seller’s moral concerns before predicting, others afterward. Thinking about the seller’s conscience first raised buyers’ expectations, and the gap was nearly halved.

It did not close. The authors suggest one reason: 85 percent of sellers in that study disclosed, a rate higher than in the matching condition of Study 3 for reasons they say are not readily apparent.

Where the suspicion comes from

Study 2 measured three motives, adding the pull of money to the two that Study 1 had tracked. The 214 management undergraduates who took part rated, on a seven-point scale, how much the seller had been weighing being decent, feeling guilty, and getting the best price. Sellers put their concern with being a decent person at 4.99, and buyers guessed 3.78. Buyers put the seller’s interest in money at 6.03; sellers reported 5.06.

The sellers still cared about the money. They cared about it less, and about their own decency more, than the buyers pictured.

The paper’s explanation leans on moral typecasting, the idea that people tend to see others as either doers or feelers, rarely both. A seller holds the object and the information, so, the authors argue, a buyer casts them as a doer, and the competitive setting makes that doer look like someone chasing an advantage rather than guarding a clean conscience. In the abstract’s words: “While sellers tended to be honest because of moral identity concerns, buyers expected them to be driven primarily by self-interest.”

Two duller explanations get a hearing too, and the authors say their own mechanism is not the only one. Poor forecasting in general, they point out, gives no reason to expect guesses to run low rather than high. Plain caution, a buyer bracing for the worst to avoid a loss, gets mixed treatment: the Study 4 discussion offers it as a possible added force, while the general discussion says it cannot explain the results, because in the first pilot observers with nothing at stake still underestimated the sellers.

Their mediation analyses deserve a lighter touch than the abstract’s sentence suggests. Buyers and sellers answered parallel versions of the motive questions rather than the same ones, and the authors say the results should be “cautiously interpreted” for that reason. Sellers rated their motives after choosing whether to disclose, which leaves room for a flattering story told afterward, though the authors argue buyers’ parallel ratings may reduce that concern. And in Study 1, the measure of anticipated guilt and related feelings showed no significant difference between buyers and sellers.

Small stakes, narrow scope

The stakes stayed small. Most bonuses were paid by lottery, and a seller in Study 1 had a five percent chance of earning at most $7. The authors grant that low stakes may keep self-interest from fully switching on, while citing earlier work that finds self-interest at work even when stakes are small.

The honesty studied was one kind: telling a buyer about a defect the seller knew. Misrepresenting a bottom price or inventing urgency, both named by the authors, were outside the design. They describe the findings as “based primarily on Western participant samples,” and the sales were one-off exchanges between strangers, chosen to keep reputation largely out of play. Ongoing work relationships and repeat customers sit outside what was measured.

Suspicion is sometimes the sensible response, and the paper says so. A buyer facing a salesperson expected to use persuasion tactics, or shopping where one side knows far more than the other, as with used cars, has good reason for care. The paper does not argue for trusting everyone. It asks for work on when doubting a counterpart’s honesty hurts a negotiator and when it protects one.

Every finding in this piece comes from the published text and tables of one paper, read by an editorial desk that reports on research and does not train negotiators; the supplementary files the paper points to could not be opened. The studies compared predictions with replies across hundreds of people, which says something about buyers and sellers like the ones studied, taken as groups, and cannot tell anyone whether the particular seller in their inbox is being straight with them. For a purchase that matters, sensible safeguards include an independent inspection, a written description of the item’s condition, and the buyer protection some platforms offer.

This paper did not measure what the gap costs. The authors’ illustration is a used car that looks too good to be true, and a buyer who distrusts the seller, walks away, and settles for something worse. Examining what the honesty gap does to the outcomes of negotiations is what they call an important next step; they also call for testing the idea where far more money is at stake.

]]> Research suggests if you say ‘please’ and ‘thank you’ without thinking twice, you may have grown up learning that kindness is not a performance for important people — it is simply how you treat anyone in front of you https://siliconcanals.com/d-research-suggests-if-you-say-please-and-thank-you-without-thinking-twice-you-may-have-grown-up-learning-that-kindness-is-not-a-performance-for-important-people/ Thu, 17 Sep 2026 11:15:57 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109428

The difference between performing politeness for authority and treating service workers as fully human often comes down to lessons learned before you could remember them.]]>

Every restaurant service contains a half-second that gives the whole game away. A plate lands. The customer looks up at whoever carried it and says thanks, or looks straight through them and carries on talking.

Nobody is scoring it. Nobody remembers it an hour later. And yet the reflex tends to have a long history behind it, much of it laid down years earlier by an adult asking one small, maddening question at exactly the wrong moment.

The magic word was never magic

Spend an afternoon near a toddler and the routine is unmissable. Someone offers a biscuit, the kid grabs it and turns to leave, and a parent says: what do you say?

Linguists have sat down and measured this. A 1980 study in the journal Language in Society watched 22 children and their parents at play, then sent an assistant in with a gift. Unprompted, the children rarely produced these little courtesies, and thank you was the scarcest of the three. What did happen was prompting. Parents nudged, the children almost always complied, and they parroted the adult’s phrasing exactly.

One detail is easy to skip past. Parents used the routines themselves, in front of the child. Mothers more than fathers. The study measured that behaviour without testing its effects, but it is hard to watch a parent thank a stranger a thousand times and come away with nothing.

So that reflexive thanks nobody thinks about? This is one place it can begin. Hundreds of tiny repetitions, every one long forgotten, are the sort of thing that builds a habit able to fire before conscious thought does.

Who actually says thank you

This is where the usual class assumptions wobble. A 1986 study of 250 preschoolers tested what children did with no parent in the room. Around 37 per cent said thank you spontaneously when handed a reward. Children from low-income families did so more often than those from middle-income families.

Worth holding that one loosely. It is a single study, forty years old, run in one country, and income is a crude proxy for a great deal else. Still, it dents the comfortable assumption that manners arrive bundled with money.

The people who can do nothing for you

Anyone who has run a dining room knows the tell. How a guest talks to the owner reveals almost nothing, because that exchange is a performance. The reading comes later, when the seventeen-year-old arrives to clear the plates and nobody important is watching.

Some people adjust their voice. It goes flatter, clipped, faintly impatient, then swings back up the moment a manager appears. Others do not change at all. Same warmth for the kid with the tray as for the owner, because nobody told them there were two settings.

Where does that second group come from? No research trails those adults back to their childhoods, so this next bit is a hunch rather than a finding.

The hunch: they grew up in houses where courtesy went to everyone who came through the door. The plumber got offered a drink. The delivery driver got thanked by name. Nobody sat the children down and explained a value system. They watched it happen a few thousand times.

Does it matter who gets it?

A reasonable objection: surely kindness shown to people you love matters more than kindness shown to whoever hands over your coffee.

Researchers put that to the test. A 2019 experiment with 683 participants had people spend a week performing deliberate acts of kindness. One group directed them at close friends and family, one at weak ties and strangers, one at themselves, and a fourth just watched for kindness around them. A control group did nothing.

Every kindness group got happier than the controls, and the more acts people performed, the bigger the lift. No group pulled ahead of the others.

Two things to flag before anyone runs with that. It was a short study measuring self-reported happiness. And an act of kindness performed because a researcher asked for it is a long way from an unthinking thank you at a coffee counter. The study was not built to measure everyday courtesy and cannot settle anything about it.

What it does suggest is that closeness to the recipient mattered far less than most people would guess. Whether that holds for the small automatic stuff is an open question.

Small things that shift it

None of this requires a personality transplant. Four places to start:

  • Get names. Baristas, security guards, cleaners, the guy at the corner shop. Ask once, use it forever.
  • Thank people for work, not just favours. Someone doing the job they are paid for still did something for you.
  • Watch for the voice switch. Most people who have one are unaware of it.
  • If there are kids around, demonstrate instead of explaining. They are reading the room, not the lecture.

An unthinking please earns its owner remarkably little credit. It costs nothing and takes no effort, which is rather the point. Someone put the work in years ago so that it would not have to be a decision.

]]> Quote of the day: “Sometimes you find yourself in the middle of nowhere, and sometimes, in the middle of nowhere, you find yourself” https://siliconcanals.com/d-quote-of-the-day-sometimes-you-find-yourself-in-the-middle-of-nowhere-and-sometimes-in-the-middle-of-nowhere-you-find-yourself/ Thu, 17 Sep 2026 10:45:39 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109380

What happens when your plans collapse, your phone dies, and you're stranded at a gas station thousands of miles from home—and it's the best thing that could've happened.]]>

The last time I was properly lost, I was standing at a petrol station somewhere north of Chiang Rai with a dead phone, a warm bottle of water and a dog who clearly ran the place. My bus had left without me. I had four hours to wait, nothing to do and no way to tell anyone about it.

It was the calmest I had been in about eighteen months.

Sometimes you find yourself in the middle of nowhere, and sometimes, in the middle of nowhere, you find yourself.

Yes, it is the sort of line that ends up engraved on a bracelet and screwed to somebody’s kitchen wall. Both of which have happened, it turns out. I went looking for whoever wrote it and found nothing, only evidence that it has been circulating since at least 2014 with no author attached. Anonymous, then. It holds up better than most things sold at a craft market.

Nowhere is mostly an absence of audience

Here is what I think the line is really about. Nowhere has very little to do with distance. It is any situation where nobody knows your job title.

In a city you are surrounded by people who already have a version of you loaded. The neighbour who thinks you are the loud one. The old colleague who still introduces you by the thing you did in 2019. You end up performing that version without noticing, because it is easier than correcting everybody.

Take the audience away and something odd happens. For a day or two you feel faintly useless, because nobody needs anything from you. Then the noise drops. You start hearing your own opinions, which are less impressive and a good deal more honest than the ones you say out loud.

That is the whole mechanism. No mysticism required.

The year my diary went blank

I lost my business, restaurants, during the pandemic. The deal was agreed over a phone call while I sat on a plastic chair in a dining room with the lights off, and it was the least bad option available to me at the time.

For years my day had been decided for me by suppliers, staff rotas and the seven o’clock rush. Then it was not. I woke up on a Tuesday with an empty calendar and genuinely no idea what a Tuesday was for.

I would love to tell you this was peaceful. I reorganised the same cupboard twice. I developed strong opinions about a neighbour’s parking. I rang people I had not spoken to in five years and could hear them wondering what I wanted.

The useful part arrived about three months in, once I had run out of things to tidy. With no restaurant to point at, I had to work out what I would actually do with a day if nobody was paying me for it. The answer was writing, which was inconvenient, as it pays considerably worse than a burger.

You can get lost for the price of a bus ticket

You do not need to sell a business or fly to Patagonia. Nowhere comes in small doses and most of them are free.

Pick a district of your own city you have no reason to visit and spend three hours there on foot. Not a famous one. A dull one, with hardware shops and a wet market and nothing on sale to anyone carrying a suitcase. I do this in Bangkok about once a month and I have never regretted it, though I have frequently regretted the shoes.

Go somewhere your phone cannot help you. Not switched off, just outgunned: the lanes are not on the map and the only language on offer is one you do not speak.

Be a beginner at something in public. Take a class where you are visibly the worst person in the room. It is physically uncomfortable for about twenty minutes. After that it stops mattering, and what is left is quite close to fun.

And if you do travel, leave one day entirely unplanned. No booking, no list, no reservation you have to walk fast to reach. Most people schedule a trip so tightly that they never get further than a warmer version of their normal week.

What actually turns up

Let me manage expectations. You do not come back from a petrol station with a revelation.

What you come back with is a shorter list. Two or three things you thought you cared about turn out to belong to somebody else. One or two things you have never mentioned to anyone are suddenly all you think about when there is nothing else to think about. That is it. It looks like very little on paper. It does not feel that way at thirty-eight, when you are still doing a job you picked at twenty-two to impress someone who stopped watching years ago.

There is a trap in this, though. Some people use the middle of nowhere as somewhere to hide, and the giveaway is that they keep having to go back. If every trip is an escape from the same unaddressed thing at home, the scenery is doing the work of a conversation you have been avoiding. Distance is excellent for seeing a problem clearly. It has never once solved one for me.

The dog at the petrol station, for the record, took no interest in any of this. He sat under the ice cabinet, moved twice in four hours, and had evidently worked something out about Wednesdays that I am still catching up on.

The Robot Report https://www.therobotreport.com/ Robotics news, research and analysis Wed, 30 Sep 2026 23:29:42 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.2 https://www.therobotreport.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/cropped-robot-report-site-32x32.png The Robot Report https://www.therobotreport.com/ 32 32 How Maven Robotics plans to automate industrial work, one task at a time https://www.therobotreport.com/how-maven-robotics-plans-automate-industrial-work-one-task-at-a-time/ https://www.therobotreport.com/how-maven-robotics-plans-automate-industrial-work-one-task-at-a-time/#respond Thu, 01 Oct 2026 12:30:39 +0000 https://www.therobotreport.com/?p=589743 With the $100 million it raised earlier this month, Maven Robotics is looking towards mass producing its mobile manipulator robot.

The post How Maven Robotics plans to automate industrial work, one task at a time appeared first on The Robot Report.

]]>

Maven founders, CFO Khalid Derbas and CEO Hamza Derbas with the company’s robot. | Source: Maven Robotics

Since it was founded in 2024, Maven Robotics has created four iterations of its mobile manipulator, raised $100 million, and gone from early pilots to a production contract with its first customer. It currently has robots running 16 hours a day, five days a week, with up to 99% uptime, according to Hamza Derbas, co-founder and CEO of Maven Robotics. 

Maven has moved fast, raising Series A funding last month, but the Santa Clara, Calif.-based company started its journey by focusing on which problems it wanted to solve.

“Maven started with a small group of people, and we together started looking deeply at industrial labor, and realized that it’s facing a grim reality,” Derbas told The Robot Report. “The world needs more and more industrial output every day, but the workforce available to do this work is dwindling.”

Currently, there are over half a million unfilled manufacturing jobs just in the U.S., and market analysts expect this number to grow to millions over the next few years, Derbas said.

“At the same time, we noticed that the humanoid robotics companies, the ones with legs, were starting with the human form factor and trying to work backwards into a problem to be solved,” he added. “That’s when it became very clear to us that there’s a massive opportunity for the right kind of team, carrying all the battle scars of building hard technologies, to come tackle this problem with a completely different approach, specifically geared towards activating autonomous labor at scale in these environments.”

Use case informs morphology, says Derbas

Right now, humanoids dominate conversations in the robotics industry. But legs aren’t the only way to create a general-purpose robot, noted Derbas.

“Instead of starting from a robot or specific morphology or even a model, we started from the jobs to be done, down to the dust, the dirt, and the grease on the factory floor,” he recalled. “Then we work up to the robot, asking the question: What does our robot need to do? How far does it need to be able to reach?”

One downside of a robot with a wheeled base is its footprint. A big, heavy base creates a very stable robot, but it’s not realistic in all manufacturing or logistics facilities.

“We found a way to make the footprint super small so that it can fit through doors, really go anywhere, while maintaining very large dynamic reach,” Derbas said. “We can reach to the back of a 48-in. [121.9 cm] pallet or deep into a storage shelf up to 3 m [9.8 ft.] high while carrying 30 kg [66.1 lb.] payloads.”

The Maven System as a whole is more than just the robots, which can collaborate autonomously with human workers or in robot fleets. It also includes the ability to communicate with customers’ infrastructure, so it can exchange crucial information, as well as the Maven Network.

“[The Maven Network] is a global fabric of shared learning,” said Derbas. “If a robot makes a mistake somewhere in California, a robot in Japan can learn how to deal with that mistake the next day.”

Maven Robotics worked with customers early on

Early on, Derbas said Maven started working with a few partners to co-develop a general-purpose robot. These customers were willing to offer their deep operations insights to inform system design.

“We didn’t ask them to just come see our robots in our lab,” said Derbas. “We insisted that we go out to the field on the factory floor or in the warehouse to watch people do the work and see where the friction lies, and we zeroed in very fast on a couple of workflows that we thought we could master quickly and scale up fast.”

Maven’s first two workflows were mixed-case palletizing and tote handling. “These became the seed of our journey to generalization, because we started deploying these and creating value for our customers, it opened up a bigger conversation,” Derbas said. “What if our robots could acquire more and more skills faster and faster?”

Maven worked with its customers to create a roadmap of use cases and a progressive approach to rolling out automation. The company deploys its robots to automate a task and improves operations as it learns from that deployment. When the mobile manipulator masters the skill, the customer scales up that deployment. Then, Maven starts working on the next task.

“By doing this iteration, we earn customer trust to deploy fast and learn from the real world as opposed to from the lab, and we unlock this data flywheel so that we can train more and more general models to compound the intelligence and in the long run,” Derbas said.

Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

The road to generalization

Looking ahead, Maven Robotics plans to tackle assembly and fabrication of durable goods. This would allow its robots to build cars, ships, planes, and even other robots in the future.

“Industrial work is not for the faint of heart,” said Derbas. “The bar for reliability is very high. There’s less demand on wanting a robot to be perfectly generalizable in its intelligence on Day 1. Generalization is a journey; reliability is not. It’s required from Day 1.”

To handle a variety of tasks, Maven equipped its robots with a modular end-of-arm interface so it can adapt different grippers to the job at hand. Derbas said the company landed on two kinds of grippers, a vacuum suction gripper, and a parallel gripper with two fingers.

“We started with off-the-shelf grippers, they didn’t work well,” he said. “We ended up designing our own gripper, then we iterated on that. We’ve landed now on an extremely capable and miniaturized vacuum gripper.”

The team experimented a lot when it came to multi-fingered tooling. Derbas said Maven looked at grippers with five, four, and three fingers with different sensing and actuation methods.

“We realized that the hand itself doesn’t need to have that much actuation or degrees of freedom, because if you leverage the fact that the hands are sitting on seven degree-of-freedom arms, and we have two seven degree-of-freedom arms, the extra articulation and maneuverability you get can help you simplify the gripper,” he said. “Combined with the right intelligence, you can accomplish a lot.”

Maven Robotics looks to scale up deployments

Maven Robotics is working to scale up its deployments and get its robots working for more hours. Derbas said the company plans to run its fleets 24 hours a day, seven days a week before the end of the year. The company is offering its robots as a service (RaaS).

“We went from zero to production contracts with long-term recurring revenue contracts in about two years,” Derbas said. “We’re going to have a couple hundred robots on production contracts over the next year, and then hopefully in the thousands by 2028 as we gear up for mass production.”

For mass production, Derbas said there are three major areas the company will focus on: streamlining how it manufactures the mechanical and structural components of the robot, working with suppliers to bring down the cost of actuators, and eliminating redundancy in the robot’s electronic systems.

The post How Maven Robotics plans to automate industrial work, one task at a time appeared first on The Robot Report.

]]>

The ANYmal quadruped now works with ANYbotics Shift for autonomous inspections. Source: ANYbotics

Undetected failures cost the world’s 500 largest companies an estimated $1.4 trillion each year in downtime, with a single hour of outage averaging $250,000, according to ANYbotics AG. The company today launched ANYbotics Shift, a platform intended to simplify asset health assessments and enable preventive maintenance.

“The new platform empowers businesses to harness the full potential of autonomous inspection by planning and running multi-robot missions, while organizing captured field data directly around existing asset management infrastructure,” explained ANYbotics.

“Robotic inspection delivers the most value when field data flows directly into maintenance action,” stated Péter Fankhauser, co-founder and CEO of ANYbotics. “Shift makes that seamless. It unifies plant mapping, robot fleet coordination, inspection AI analytics, and systems integrations into one platform. At its core, Shift AI powers the intelligence that transforms field findings into work orders, saving millions in avoiding unplanned downtime.”

Founded in 2016, ANYbotics said its ANYmal quadruped robots are suitable for tasks including routine inspections and real-time data collection, addressing labor shortages and improving worker safety. The Zurich-based company serves the global energy, power, metals, mining, and chemicals industries.

Shift includes four modules

ANYbotics said its cloud-based platform delivers visibility, action, and measurable impact through four interconnected modules:

    • Shift Fleet unifies scheduling, monitoring, and control for an entire fleet of inspection robots. A distributed control system (DCS) can trigger missions directly. The system ensures that critical assets are inspected repeatedly and consistently, freeing reliability engineers to review findings and prioritize repairs.
    • Shift Insight combines thermal, acoustic, visual, and gas readings with operating conditions such as motor speed, load, and ambient temperature. A reading only counts as an anomaly when the context says it should, reporting overheating, partial discharge, leaks, and misalignments while they are still relatively harmless, said ANYbotics.
    • Shift Connect turns confirmed anomalies directly into work orders inside operations software. Through productized connectors and standard REST APIs, Connect integrates across five categories:
      1. Distributed control systems (DCS) such as Yokogawa
      2. Computerized maintenance management systems (CMMS)
      3. Enterprise resource planning (ERP) tools like SAP and IBM Maximo
      4. Asset performance management (APM) platforms such as GE Vernova APM
      5. Digital twin or contextualization layers like Cognite and Oracle

      This bi-directional integration allows process thresholds to automatically trigger new robot inspection rounds, while an integrated notification center delivers real-time alerts through tools such as email and Microsoft Teams. ANYbotics plans to add SMS and WhatsApp support.

    • Shift Maps provides a live digital twin of a manufacturing plant. It maps inspection targets into APM and enterprise asset management (EAM) infrastructures. Structures are imported by asset ID, so every reading is tied to the right piece of equipment.

ANYbotics said the transition from its Data Navigator asset management product to Shift will be automatic with an upcoming update. Shift AI learns from every connected module, which operates from the same plant model.

Shift includes modules for fleet management, maps and deployments, workflow integration, and asset intelligence. Source: ANYbotics

ANYbotics answers questions about Shift

Jacob Euler-Rolle, head of product management and workflow integration at ANYbotics, replied to the following questions from The Robot Report:

How much integration work with enterprise systems is required for a first-time customer?

Euler-Rolle: Very little. Shift is designed to work with the systems your plant already runs, so a first-time deployment requires no enterprise integration at all, it operates the fleet and delivers findings independently right out of the box.

When users are ready to connect their ANYmal or ANYmals to their software stack, we offer pre-built integrations through our partnerships with SAP, GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, Cognite, SLB, and Yokogawa.

For any other system, the Shift REST API (documented with OpenAPI) links its data and findings to their CMMS or APM and enables their existing platforms to trigger inspections. Our team can also build custom connectors during onboarding, if required.

So for users, the effort is very minimal and largely limited to granting network access, securing approvals, and mapping asset IDs to align with their plant’s existing asset hierarchy.

The Shift API connects the ANYbot fleet to digital twins, asset performance management platforms, enterprise software, and facility systems. Source: ANYbotics

How much training do customers need?

Euler-Rolle: Training takes just a few days rather than weeks, and users require no prior robotics expertise. The entire onboarding process is organized by job role through our ANYbotics Academy, which has already trained over 1,000 users.

Because Shift uses role-based access, each user sees an interface tailored to their specific responsibilities. So, whether they are operators scheduling and monitoring the fleet, reliability engineers reviewing inspection findings, or maintenance teams receiving work orders directly within their existing systems, the UI is tailored to their role. That role-based access means the interface adapts to each persona, so nobody gets lost in functions they don’t need or sees data they shouldn’t.

What other robots could Shift work with?

Euler-Rolle: Today, Shift supports landing or incoming inspection data from third-party robots and sensors. Full fleet management for non-ANYmal hardware will start to roll out next year, as Shift advances towards being a single operations hub for mixed-robot fleets.

Will Shift enable interoperability among robots from different vendors and comply with VDA 5050 or U.S. standards?

Euler-Rolle: Interoperability sits at the heart of our Shift roadmap. While standards like VDA 5050 were designed for AGVs and AMRs navigating fixed nodes in intralogistics, inspection robots in process facilities operate differently. Their core focus is capturing asset inspection data rather than executing transport orders.

The Shift API delivers an interoperability layer centered directly on inspection tasks and asset management, while integrating established fleet standards wherever they’re relevant. Because no unified inspection-robot standard currently exists in either the U.S. or Europe, we plan to help shape one.

Shift unifies management of autonomous inspection fleets, keeping people out of harm’s way. Source: ANYbotics

What provisions have you made for cybersecurity?

Euler-Rolle: Data security is fundamental to physical AI. Industrial users require a verified, secure end-to-end data flow before deploying autonomous systems. ANYbotics enforces strict digital boundaries to maintain the integrity of ANYmal’s decision-making, prevent external manipulation, and ensure safe deployment in sensitive industrial environments.

Shift operates under ISO 27001 standards and provides end-to-end encryption for data in transit and at rest, strict tenant isolation, and detailed role-based access control to protect information and ensure secure operations.

Hosted in the ANYbotics Cloud, Shift supports regional data residency to keep information within specified geographic areas and offers an on-premises deployment option for organizations with strict local regulatory requirements.

Is Shift available immediately in North America and Europe? What about Asia?

Euler-Rolle: Shift will be available globally with the 1.0 release, including North America, Europe, Asia, and all regions where we currently operate.

Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

Users already report benefits

Shift is already deployed across more than 200 robot deployments and runs hundreds of thousands of inspections every month, noted ANYbotics.

“Shift makes it easy for SAP to integrate robot inspections into business processes,” said Adelya Fatykhova, global lead architect for embodied AI agents, physical AI, and robotics at SAP. “Physical AI on SAP Business AI Platform translates a business need into a Shift mission, with results stored back in SAP for follow-ups like maintenance order creation. Robot inspection missions through Shift enhance SAP’s Autonomous Supply Chain for asset and field service with robot execution.”

At Sacramento Municipal Utility District (SMUD), the platform saved more than $3.5 million in its first months of operation on critical substation assets. It flagged overheating conductors, partial discharge, and gas leaks that manual rounds had missed, ANYbotics said.

“ANYbotics Shift’s API gives our APM platform consistent, valuable equipment-level inspection data from across the plant floor,” said Neha Joshi, product leader at GE Vernova APM.

“Combining field insights with our analytics creates a more complete picture of asset health, helping teams identify, validate, and address issues more effectively,” she added. “When our models flag a potential issue, we can use the same API to send robots to verify it and capture additional context.”

At a Vigier Cement plant running 24/7, Shift executed more than 33,000 autonomous inspections in 16 months, said ANYbotics. The platform structured every reading against the plant’s asset hierarchy so the maintenance team could compare condition trends over time and prioritize repairs.

]]>

Innodata has opened a new lab to capture motion for accurate data to train AI for robotics. Source: Innodata

While humanoid robots can be agile, the artificial intelligence driving them needs more data to be able to conduct useful tasks. Innodata Inc. today said it has opened a laboratory to generate the data for training the next generation of human-like robots. The facility will also independently validate the performance data that robots generate internally.

“Physical AI is growing faster than any other segment in AI, but every robotics team hits the same wall: There isn’t enough real-world interaction data, and what exists is expensive and slow to produce,” stated Rahul Singhal, CEO of Innodata. “This facility removes that wall. We now offer physical AI companies a complete end-to-end capability — from data collection through model evaluation — that compresses development cycles and gets more capable, safer robots into the world sooner.”

Founded in 1988, Innodata asserted that data and AI “are inextricably linked.” The Ridgefield Park, N.J.-based data engineering company said it provides the high-quality data, evaluation frameworks, and human expertise required to build AI systems that can builders and adopters can trust at scale.

Physical AI poses new data demands

While large language models (LLMs) benefitted from the vast amount of data on the Internet, robots do not have the same corpus of data on the physical world, noted Franklin Tanner, vice president of robotics and physical AI at Innodata. “Physical AI has to earn its tokens one interaction at a time, and they have to be deliberate,” he told The Robot Report.

The new research and development facility addresses an urgent need for high-quality training data for humanoids, industrial robots, and other forms of physical AI, according to Innodata. While other data providers infer 3D motion by analyzing 2D video, the company said it captures 3D data directly from bodies themselves — whether those bodies are human or mechanical.

“There’s just no substitute for direct 3D motion capture,” Tanner stated. “When a computer vision model tries to make sense of a 2D grid of pixels, mistakes inevitably creep in.”

“Our sensors are designed to register the tiniest motion of every joint, which makes training more accurate and efficient,” he added. “When you’re training a humanoid that weighs almost 200 lb. [90.7 kg], your readings can’t be in the ballpark. They need to be precise. And with this lab, they are.”

Tanner cited the example of telling a robot to pick up a mug.

“You want it to make sure that it’s picking it up in the right way. So most of us pick it up by the handle, but you can also pick it up from the base,” he said. “That’s not wrong, but if it is filled with hot liquid, you may end up burning your hand. So the context matters, and that’s not always encoded in even the data sets that are out there right now.”

Editor’s note: Physical AI and humanoids are among the session topic tracks at RoboBusiness 2026, which will be on Oct. 20 and 21 in Santa Clara, Calif. Register now to attend.

Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

Data from robots in the wild is the ‘gold standard’

Innodata said it captures real-world data and produces training data across humanoids, teleoperated hardware, wearable systems, sensor rigs, Universal Manipulator Interface (UMI) grippers, and other multimodal capture setups. The data can then help build digital twins to generate edge cases.

“There’s no substitute for real-world data,” said Tanner. “As much as possible, we collect data of an actor or a robot doing something in the wild. I think that’s the gold standard. However, that’s super expensive, and figuring out all the ways mugs can come down a conveyor with their handles facing different directions is not efficient.”

“The crux of it is how can we create enough real-world data and then seed a simulation with that?” he asked. “Simulators are getting pretty good with taking real-world data, doing the real-to-sim translation, and then permuting the environment to take care of some of these little combinatoric explosions of different parameters. NVIDIA‘s Cosmos environment is actually becoming really good at that.”

There are also limitations to real-world data. Tanner said that human responses for teleoperation or egocentric data capture can be incomplete. If a person in a data-collection scenario drops a knife, for instance, he or she might take a step back and turn off the device thinking they made a mistake, he said.

“We don’t have training data right now where humans and robots are interacting,” noted Tanner. “It’s one area we’re working on in the lab — instrumenting it so multiple agents can work together. We need larger and custom data sets.”

Vicon captures sub-millimeter motion for Innodata

Vicon says its cameras can capture data with submillimeter accuracy and millisecond latency. Source: Innodata

Innodata developed the lab with Vicon, a motion-capture leader that continues to provide technical consulting. The New Jersey lab is equipped with high-precision, low-latency infrared optical tracking cameras that measure movement down to the sub-millimeter level — a degree of accuracy that methods such as wearable inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors and single-camera (monocular) video analysis typically cannot match.

“Plenty of motion-capture companies have discovered humanoid robotics lately,” acknowledged Andrew Knox, managing director of Vicon. “But the teams building the most capable robots keep reaching the same conclusion: If the training data is approximate, the robot will be too.”

“Vicon sets the standard that motion data is measured against,” he said. “Our systems capture people, robots and the objects they handle in the same space, with sub-millimeter accuracy and millisecond latency.”

OpenShell provides a secure runtime boundary that traces all actions and enforces policy as AI agents run on NVIDIA Vera CPUs. It provides deterministic governance for agent execution, access, and where inference goes, according to NVIDIA.

As open-source software, OpenShell can be extended to work with third-party compute platforms, including those from Arm and Intel, added the Santa Clara, Calif.-based company.
