OpenShell can offload security onto silicon or DPUs as needed, and Sentry watches reasoning traces. A Policy Proover in NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform is deterministic and runs at a higher speed.

“If you write a policy that says an agent can’t read code from Github, an agent could spawn separate subagents to read it and then post that information, with fleets superseding global policies,” said Boitano. “The Policy Proover validates the master decision tree, looking at combined file and network access to find unintended exfiltration. “We see long-term agent behavior to be a different problem than sandboxing,” he added. “OpenShell is projecting the intent of a policy into infrastructure.”

Capital itself is a sufficient form of robot governance, hypothesized analysts at the AI Robotics Alliance of America, or AIRA, Summit in June. The essence is in the comprehensive reduction of transaction costs by granting machines autonomy, they suggested.

But as soon as we move from theory to practice, we hit a wall of fundamental questions, noted analyst Sergey Lonshakov. In Germany, for example, specialists still debate what cyber-physical systems actually are, since the academic definition of a “robot” remains vague.

Coase rule still applies to the cyber-physical age

Economics abhors a vacuum. We live in a paradigm described by Ronald Coase: A company exists as long as it’s cheaper to produce internally than to buy components on the market.

If we apply this principle to robotic arms or swarms of drones, robotics startups emerge. As soon as such a system independently enters the market, we get agency. And there is no more effective indicator than price.

But what happens when what enters the market is not a factory machine, but a humanoid that lives in your home?

Editor’s note: Physical AI is among the session topic tracks at RoboBusiness 2026, which will be on Oct. 20 and 21 in Santa Clara, Calif. Register now to attend.

Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

The harsh reality of B2C: Why a robot can’t cost as much as a BMW

For a long time, robotics was the domain of business to business (B2B). Engineers created systems for BMW factories, where reliability and predictability were paramount.

But now a turning point has arrived: The same specialists must build robots that will work in our households and perhaps work on the Moon. It’s the same evolutionary stage as mobile phones before the Apple era: functional, but ugly and inconvenient.

The main problem is price. You can’t charge a high price for a humanoid assistant — that would push the mass market into the luxury segment.

Most manufacturers understand there is enormous demand for devices in the €1,000 to €1,500 ($1,136.8 to $1,705.3 U.S.) range, such as Amazon’s rolling platform with a periscope to check if the stove is off. But to hit that price point, you need to rethink the entire development philosophy.

Technology’s adaptability to the human factor is now more important than the precision of servos.

The battle for the wallet: Crypto versus bank account

When we talk about economic autonomy for robotics, one question inevitably arises: How do you pay a robot?

In 2026, John Anderson and other futurists are actively promoting the idea of crypto wallets. No one will open a traditional bank account for a robot — it’s not a legal entity.

However, a wallet on the Bitcoin or Ethereum network is generated automatically, and the network validates payments independently. For business and entrepreneurs, this is “perfectly clear.”

But here a legal collapse occurs. Lawyers from Baker McKenzie note that no European jurisdiction will accept robot economic autonomy in contract law. The classic scheme involves a promisor, who undertakes an obligation, and a beneficiary, who gives the obligation.

If a person lays tiles badly, a judge examines the motives — Did they try? Were there extenuating circumstances? With a robot, this is impossible. Its goal-setting is, for the court, simply a “breakdown.”

Moreover, if the device is the result of dozens of teams’ work — a supply chain — then in the event of an error, no one can be held responsible.

The “Great Fork of 2025:”

  1. The optimists’ side (Silicon Valley): Generate a wallet, launch a Twitter bot, collect satoshis.
  2. The realists’ side (Europe): We must define the nature of goal-setting. Responsibility lies neither with the manufacturer nor the robot.

As we search for answers, another fear emerges. In multi-segmented neural models that reconfigure on the fly, we are getting closer to understanding our own brains, as in large behavior models, not just language models.

If a robot becomes so complex that we can no longer distinguish its malfunction from “fatigue” or “lack of energy,” will we descend into anthropomorphism? The android may say in court, “I didn’t have enough satoshis, so I couldn’t finish laying the tiles, forgive me.” It sounds fantastic, but system complexity is leading us in this direction.

The proof problem: Was the courier there?

One of the oldest and most painful problems in logistics is the dispute: “I called, but you weren’t there.” In the world of robotics, this becomes a fundamental arbitration challenge.

In 2017, there was an idea called proof of location (FOAM) — triangulating location via towers so that a smart contract would release payment to a courier only upon confirmation of arrival. The idea never took off.

Experts now pin their hopes on observation networks, which are already being deployed in smart cities. These aren’t just traffic cameras for issuing fines, but sensors that record movement.

The robot itself can generate data such as video from cameras or trackers, but the difference from humans is colossal. We trust humans by default due to reputation: We’re taught not to lie from childhood). A robot, essentially, must provide irrefutable digital evidence.

There has been no significant progress in decentralized verification yet. But if sensor networks are built on open technologies rather than black boxes, we’ll be able to track machines’ meta-operations — something that would be “nonsense” for a human, like reporting arrival at work at 9:05 a.m. Machines can and should be transparent.

Avride has integrated vision-language models into its delivery robots. Source: Avride

Unlike software, where you can quickly build a prototype, the robotics hardware world is brutal. A mistake in a PCB (printed circuit board) trace can cost months of work.

Example from real life: A company evolved from the concept of sensor networks to making real devices. The result of this evolution was abandoning “vague” B2G (business-to-government) projects in favor of a concrete line of home devices.

There’s a trend toward decentralized physical infrastructure (DePIN) and open source. Today, we’re seeing demand for devices that don’t depend on the Amazon cloud. Users are tired of subscriptions and losing data when a service shuts down.

Here are some real products you can buy right now:

  1. Smart home server (on an open platform)
  2. Air quality sensors (tested and work for years)
  3. Energy monitoring (integration with Energy Web Foundation)

Today, it’s easier to go to a crypto conference and buy a physical device for your home — including switches, remotes, and speakers without “cloud” lock-in — than it is to open a bank account. Visually, it resembles the early 2010s with DIY kits, but now with a serious emphasis on privacy and Polkadot for storing user lists. The goal is to give a person a crypto key that they themselves use to manage access to their own devices.

Faraday Future showed its EAI Robot at Silicon Valley events including AIRA. Source: Faraday Future

Don’t despair about the economics of robotics

The economic autonomy of robots won’t happen tomorrow. The main barrier is not technology, but law and arbitration. We cannot answer the question: “Who is to blame if a robot makes a mistake?” Until this is resolved at the judicial level, there will be no mass “robot hiring.”

But we stand on the threshold of a change in daily life. Smart homes are ceasing to be “black boxes” of corporations and becoming open-source ecosystems. Cities are becoming more convenient, but privacy is the price we pay.

The world is changing, and the key intrigue of 2026 is: will we manage to build an ecosystem of smart devices that works for us, not for corporations, and what will we do when a robot asks us for satoshis to finish hemming the curtains?

Elena Krosheva is a freelance journalist, marketing analyst, and SEO specialist. She graduated with honors from the Faculty of Journalism at the Institute of Modern Knowledge in Minsk, Belarus, in 2007.

Krosheva covers topics such as digitalization, IT, the modern economy, and transhumanism. She loves computers and cyberpunk, having graduated from a technical college before graduating from the Faculty of Journalism.

Some tech leaders and lawmakers are mirroring Asimov’s concern about threats that robotics and AI pose to society. Source: Rinaldo Brutoco, AI

Most science fiction fans are aware that Isaac Asimov propounded his Three Laws of Robotics in the March 1942 issue of Astounding Science Fiction magazine and later republished them in his famous 1950 collection, I, Robot. Since then, readers have been thinking through both the obvious and the not-so-obvious implications of his dicta. In an era when people fear that AI threatens all of human civilization, Asimov’s observations about robots’ dangers to humans feel even more prescient.

Asimov’s Three Laws of Robotics are as follows:

  1. A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm.
  2. A robot must obey the orders given it by human beings except where such orders would conflict with the First Law.
  3. A robot must protect its own existence as long as such protection does not conflict with the First or Second Law.

It is tempting to focus on the first and best-known of the three laws when thinking of AI. Surprisingly, only one business entity has adopted this principle as a core element of its software development: Advanced Robotic Technologies Inc., which specializes in generative artificial intelligence (gen AI) applied to manufacturing large-scale industrial products.

It would seem to any thoughtful observer that such a foundational principle could be incorporated into the basic algorithms of every gen AI company in the world. Alas, that is not the case. One can reasonably assume, as many people now do, that without such a prohibitive instruction embedded in a robot’s basic “intelligence,” increasingly capable robots could eventually pose a significant risk to human safety.

Given the controversy that has recently arisen over precisely this topic, it would be worth reflecting on the warning we just received from Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, on Sept. 12 in his post entitled “We Must Pace the Frontier.” In it, he explicitly calls for slowing the development of frontier AI models in general, and agentic AI specifically.

Amodei expressed concerns that swarms of autonomous AI agents can now execute complex tasks, act in unison with one another without any human knowing, and even cover their tracks when they violate basic safety principles.

Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

Tech leaders worry about social risks of AI

Sam Altman, CEO of Anthropic’s competitor OpenAI, said he agreed with Amodei, as did Elon Musk. Bill Gates has also expressed his reservations about the speed of AI development and the threat it poses to human society.

Although society is beginning to ask what an individual robot might do to harm one or more human beings, some are now asking a more fundamental question: Can human civilization be endangered with extinction from gen AI? Former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon asserted that a 10% chance existed that human extinction would occur because of the fast pace of agentic AI development.

Evan Hubinger, Anthropic alignment science lead, put the catastrophic odds even a little bit higher. Clearly, Asimov’s warning did not go far enough.

By the time Asimov published his 1985 novel, Robots and Empire, he had concluded that his original three laws were incomplete. After years of reflection, he introduced what he called the Zeroth Law, which he deliberately numbered “Zero” because he believed it had to come before the other three rather than simply becoming a new fourth law. Why? Because Asimov’s Zeroth Law expands the original prohibition against harming an individual human to encompass the welfare of humanity as a whole.

In Asimov’s view, it therefore deserved to precede the First Law. Much of society’s concern about robots must now shift from the damage a single robot might inflict on an individual to the potential harm intelligent robots could inflict on civilization itself.

Even if AI doesn’t endanger human civilization, the concern is very real that other socially harmful effects could ensue. The implications of the Zeroth Law remain unknown to the general population and are only now being referenced by gen AI developers.

An example of this broader concern is the recent statement issued by numerous economists and technologists entitled “We Must Act Now.” More than 2,500 notable signatories have already endorsed the statement, calling on society to take immediate action.

The signatories claimed that waiting much longer will leave insufficient time to provide the guidance software developers need to moderate the otherwise disruptive capacity of robots to replace human workers without allowing adequate time for transition and institution-building.

We must act now if we are to provide sufficient guidance for the development of robotics so that human society as a whole is not adversely affected. We also must begin designing the transition tools needed to manage the coming changes.

As a counterpoint, Jensen Huang, CEO of NVIDIA, said that concerns about AI dangers are overblown.

Proposed legislation follows Asimov’s lead

On July 21, 2026, Senator Mark Warner, vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, introduced comprehensive legislation entitled “A Framework for America’s AI Future,” consisting of three major components.

Approximately two-thirds of Sen. Warner’s proposal focuses on the general requirements he said must be put in place now to avoid future harm. He is particularly concerned about the potential negative effects that robotics could have on human civilization if adequate guardrails are not established for future AI development, as well as the need to prevent unauthorized commercial exploitation and protect consumer data security.

The second part of the legislation addresses the threat of labor market instability resulting from the rapid spread of AI systems throughout the economy without adequate forethought or institutional support for the transition from the pre-AI world to the post-AI world.

Human society could face a widespread economic crisis if it fails to establish adequate guardrails before robotic development advances even further, including providing meaningful transition resources for the workforce. Entitled the National Workforce Transition Fund, this portion of the legislation would provide worker retraining, retention grants, and tuition assistance for workers seeking to move into new occupations as existing jobs are displaced by automation.

In explaining the need for this second part of his legislation, Sen. Warner expressed his belief that within two years, as many as 30% of college graduates may be unable to find employment after completing their education because of the rapid expansion of AI into the workplace. That estimate may prove correct, or it may ultimately prove overly pessimistic. Only time will tell.

Warner’s broader caution, however, that we must begin developing programming safeguards and transition policies now, is well taken. As he noted, if we wait another two years, it will likely be too late. That is precisely the point emphasized in the statement “We must act now.”

Mid-level white-collar workers are most vulnerable right now. It will likely take many years before robots replace plumbers, carpenters, electricians, and other skilled tradespeople. Unfortunately, most of us already know white-collar workers who have lost their jobs as AI systems have begun replacing human labor in the workplace.

The Industrial Revolution unfolded over a relatively long period of time compared with the extraordinary speed at which robotics and AI are entering society today. Looking back, we can readily see how better planning of our social institutions during the Industrial Revolution would have made the transition into the post-industrial world easier for everyone and considerably more politically stable. Let us not make the same mistake again.

David Sacks, President Trump’s AI advisor, responded to the industry-wide calls for a slowdown of agentic AI development by saying the industry could agree among itself on guardrails and doesn’t require administrative action. He would be correct if the administration created a “safe harbor” antitrust exemption from Federal Trade Commission and Justice Department suits for such collusive conversations between competitors. The effect on global competition (i.e., China) of such a “slowdown” is a topic that must be addressed and understood quickly.

Ultimately, more jobs will likely be created in the post-robotic future than exist today, just as occurred following the Industrial Revolution. To ensure that transition is as orderly and humane as possible, following Asimov’s example, we must act now. Even more critically, if we are to have human workers remain in control, we must act now.

About the author

Rinaldo Brutoco, founding president and CEO of the World Business Academy, is an entrepreneur, executive, author, radio host and futurist. He has published numerous articles and books that address the role and responsibility of business in relation to the critical moral, environmental and social concerns of the day.

Brutoco is a regular keynote speaker at conferences and guest lecturer at business schools such as Stanford Business School, the Columbia Graduate School of Business, the Kellogg Graduate Business School at Northwestern University, and the Keenan-Flagler Graduate School of Business at North Carolina University. For over 35 years, Rinaldo has been widely recognized as a practical visionary and change agent.

In the future, robotaxis will have cleaning and reset stations available throughout their operational territory. | Credit: Aseon Labs

Robotaxis are proven. Waymo has logged more than 220 million autonomous miles and, by its own count, has more than 94% fewer serious injury crashes than human drivers. It gives around half a million paid rides a week and is expanding to more cities.

So the question has moved from “Does this work?” to “How does this get everywhere?”

Waymo is in 14 cities. Uber is in over 15,000. Uber did 3.9 billion trips last quarter. It processes Waymo’s entire weekly ride volume every 17 minutes. Driving software and vehicle supply have billions pointed at them. Almost nobody is funding the least glamorous problem: what happens to the cars between rides.

The pit is across town

No Formula 1 team drives back to the factory for new tires. The pit is at the track; the car is out in seconds. A robotaxi finishes a ride, discovers a spilled latte on the back seat, and drives up to 15 miles, empty, to a centralized depot to be cleaned, charged, and inspected.

A fully autonomous pod cleans and recharges a robotaxi. | Credit: Aseon Labs

Each reset costs roughly two hours. California data shows  the cost: of 86 million Waymo miles reported through 2025, only 54% carried a passenger.

Not every empty mile is a depot run, but every depot run is an empty mile. Autonomous on the road, manual the moment it needs servicing. That is where scale breaks.

That worked for one company in a few cities. It cannot carry an industry to thousands, for three reasons.

The land is gone. The site a depot needs, industrial-zoned and wired for power, is the one everyone wants. Brokers report data center developers outbidding industrial buyers for powered parcels. An operator entering a new city walks into a house auction against the likes of Microsoft and Amazon.

The clock is against you. California’s regulator targets six months just to energize a standard charging site. A new circuit runs 1.9 years; a substation upgrade, 2.8; a new substation, 8.9. Per city. Across thousands of cities, that is decades.

Every city is different. Phoenix is a sprawl of sunlit parking lots. Zurich is a medieval street plan with a planning committee. Riyadh has heat that cooks batteries and dust that coats sensors by lunchtime.

No single design fits them all, so the industry builds a bespoke depot in each. Fifteen cities, 15 projects. Fifteen thousand, and the model collapses under its own paperwork.

Waymo is the beginning, not the shape

Waymo did everything itself. It designed the driver, retrofitted the cars, ran the fleet, built the app, staffed the depots. Even Waymo has shed two layers: Zeekr builds its Ojai vans, while Moove, Avomo, Avis, and Flexdrive run its depots.

The next wave of autonomous vehicles is built by specialists. Wayve, Nuro, and Mobileye sell brains. Carmakers put those brains in their own cars: Nissan with Wayve, Lucid with Nuro, Volkswagen with Mobileye, Mercedes with NVIDIA. Uber supplies riders to more than 30 autonomous partners. The result is not one fleet of one vehicle but dozens of fleets of different vehicles.

I spent years building a battery-swapping network for shared scooters, when hundreds of operators ran a few manufacturers’ vehicles in thousands of cities. Nobody won because they had a better scooter. The survivors could charge, repair, and reposition tens of thousands of vehicles daily. The vehicle was never the hard part. The operations were.

Robotaxis are the same play at a hundred times the price. A Wayve-powered Nissan on Uber in Zurich still needs charging, cleaning, and inspection several times a day, and no one wants to buy an industrial lot there. Without the infrastructure, none of it runs.

Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

What unlocking scale for robotaxis looks like

The shipping container did not make ships faster. It made every port the same, and that unlocked global trade. Robotaxis need their container, a standard unit of servicing infrastructure that fits in a bay or two, deploys in days, not years, is configured per city, not re-engineered, and serves any fleet on any network, as one cell tower serves every carrier.

Full disclosure: My company, Aseon Labs, is building a robotic charging, cleaning, and inspection station that arrives on a flatbed, designed to go live within a day. We are early and will not be the only ones. The argument does not depend on us. It depends on arithmetic: years per depot, per city, for an industry that needs thousands.

Every robotics demo ends the same way: Someone off camera walks in with a charging cable. Robotaxis are the first robot at commercial scale to learn the demo was never the hard part. Andreessen Horowitz raised $1.1 billion for the physical buildout of AI. Software ate the world. Now it needs somewhere to park.

The cars can already drive themselves. They still cannot charge, clean, or inspect themselves. Somebody has to build the pit.

About the author

Dan Keene is co-founder of Aseon Labs, a Y Combinator-backed company building distributed robotic servicing stations for autonomous vehicle fleets.

He previously co-founded Pushme, the battery-swapping network acquired by TIER in 2020.

]]> Metaview, a London-based agentic recruiting platform that automates sourcing, application review, interviewing, reporting and hiring workflows, has raised €53.1 million ($60 million) in Series C funding.

The round was led by Insight Partners, with participation from GV, Intrepid Growth Partners, Seedcamp, Vertex Ventures US, Plural, and Garuda Ventures. This funding comes just a year after the company announced a €30.1 million Series B funding round. It raised a €6.4 million Series A funding round in March 2024 and a €5.29 million Seed round in December 2021. The new capital brings Metaview’s total funding to €97.4 million ($110 million). 

“The best engineering teams have already moved from writing code by hand to orchestrating AI agents that do the work. Recruiting is next. We’re rebuilding hiring with AI at the core to make it radically more efficient and precise, while creating a better system for everyone involved,” said Siadhal Magos, CEO and co-founder of Metaview.

Founded in 2018 by Magos and Shahriar Tajbakhsh, former product and engineering leaders at Uber and Palantir, Metaview began by capturing the conversations where hiring decisions take shape, with more than 6 million interviews captured to date. 

According to the company, that shared context now powers connected AI agents across the rest of the hiring process, with people setting the criteria and making every final decision. Agents source candidates before they apply, review inbound applications against the role brief, conduct structured screening conversations and turn human interviews into clear, usable notes.

Explaining what makes it different, Metaview says that while most AI waits for a prompt, the UK startup runs a loop: it learns the role, agents act on it, each step sharpens the next, and people make the call. Metaview connects to 62+ tools, including Greenhouse, Ashby, Lever, and Workday, as well as Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams. It is SOC 2 Type II, GDPR and CCPA compliant.

In August 2026, Metaview announced the acquisition of California-based Reval, an AI-native recruiting company founded by Seth Tilliss and Aditya Gupta. Both founders joined Metaview to accelerate the development of fillmore, its autonomous AI coworker that finds candidates, runs personalised outreach, and books screening calls.

“The recruiting process is generating more candidate volume than most organisations know how to handle. Metaview has built a platform that brings more structure and intelligence across each stage of hiring, from sourcing and screening through to the final decision. The result is better hiring decisions at scale, without losing the judgment that good hiring requires. We are excited to partner with Siadhal, Shahriar and the team for the next phase of growth,” said Ryan Hinkle, Managing Director at Insight Partners.

The company plans to use this Series C to fund three priorities as it enters a new stage of growth. It plans to bring fillmore (Metaview’s autonomous recruiting coworker) to general availability, alongside new specialist agents. 

The funding will also help expand the team from 80 to 250 people by the end of next year, with a New York office opening alongside existing hubs in London and San Francisco. 

Finally, the company is doubling down on 10x Recruiting, its community and training programme helping talent professionals develop what Metaview calls talent engineering: the discipline of building and running AI-powered hiring systems.

Metaview is used by more than 7,000 companies, including Deel, Affirm, Navan, and Replit.

From university venture building and defence innovation to AI in healthcare and national AI strategies, the series paints a picture of how the world’s most ambitious innovation ecosystems are thinking – and where they’re heading.

We filmed six conversations. Here’s who we spoke to, and what each covers.

The Interviews

Dr. Tan Sian Wee – Senior Vice President (Innovation & Enterprise), NUS

Dr. Orna Berry – Technical Director, Google Cloud

Dr Babak Parviz – CEO & Founder, NewDays.ai
The founder of Google Glass on applying AI to dementia and cognitive care, building trust in healthcare AI, and what small companies can do in healthcare that tech giants cannot.

Prof Helmut Schönenberger – Co-Founder & CEO, UnternehmerTUM; VP Entrepreneurship, TUM
What Europe and Singapore can learn from each other on university venture building, closing the gap between lab and global market, and competing for global DeepTech talent.

Prof Benjamin Tee – VP (Ecosystem Building), NUS Enterprise
Inside the lab-to-market engine: the Physical AI Venture Lab, deciding when research becomes a company, and building DeepTech spin-outs that can compete globally from Singapore.

Gary Ang – Professor of Practice, Defence Innovation & Applications, NUS Enterprise
Dual-use innovation done properly, DefenceTech’s journey from R&D to real-world use, and the emerging Europe–Singapore DefenceTech partnership.

The post Cryptography was the last slow problem appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> On 28 July of this year, it took an AI about sixty hours to find a cryptographic flaw that two years of expert review had not uncovered.

In the following 24 hours, the findings were confirmed and the digital signature submission intended to be secure against both classical and quantum computers, HAWK – a lattice‑based post‑quantum signature scheme under evaluation – was withdrawn from consideration. It will never be standardised. 

A static security system

For fifty years, cryptography has been the one part of technology you could pretty much set and forget. RSA, a foundational public-key cryptography algorithm used for secure data transmission, arrived in 1977, became mainstream in web traffic security by 1994, and is still useful today.

Minor attacks on it have accumulated slowly, parameters have increased, and it has taken decades for meaningful advances.

That slowness has been baked into everything we have built with cryptography: standards bodies deliberate for years, migration programmes are planned in five-year blocks, and procurement assumes that what you buy today will still be adequate in 2033.

Even the US government’s Executive Order 14412 that moved post-quantum deadlines to 2030 and 2031 is considered aggressive. They pulled the timeline forward by half a decade and the industry called it a shock. However – 

Sixty hours.

AI broke one candidate algorithm in no time at all, changing the price of the discovery cycle. When the time required to find a cryptographic weakness collapses from years to days, and the time required to fix a weakness across a large organisation stays at years, you are left with a gap. Bad things live in that gap.

The uncomfortable arithmetic is that the half-life of a cryptographic assumption may now be plausibly shorter than the duration of a cryptographic migration project. If that is even a possible truth, then every organisation whose plan is “arrive at post-quantum by 2030” has been designed for the wrong world. 

The nearing threat 

The realistic AI threat to encryption over the next three years actually has almost nothing to do with breaking an algorithm, but in implementation.

Every large organisation is carrying cryptography throughout: expired certificates later renewed with a weak key, a service still negotiating a deprecated cipher suite, a hardcoded credential in a repository that arrived with an acquisition in 2019, a random number generator that perhaps isn’t very random. 

A new economics in finding the flaw has developed. Discovering a flaw took highly skilled humans to go looking, and the obscure corners of the enterprise were protected only due to the fact auditing them wasn’t worth anyone’s time.

AI has just changed that. Attackers can easily and continuously read all code, certificates and network configurations at next to zero cost. Every weakness should now be assumed to be found.

Nothing I have described requires a quantum computer to exist, only what already happened in July: finding cryptographic weakness became dramatically cheaper, and fixing it has become no faster.

Even if Q-Day, the hypothetical moment when quantum computers become powerful enough to break standard public-key encryption, never comes, every word of this still holds because you will be exposed to AI-assisted attackers exploiting classical flaws.

Cryptographic agility is the unusual security investment that pays out under every scenario.

A surprisingly humdrum solution 

Earlier this year, I asked the security lead at a large European financial institution: “If a widely used algorithm were broken on a Friday, when would you know where you use it?” His response? “Two weeks. Maybe four. And, frankly, I’m not sure I’d trust the answer.”

His four core banking platforms: two of them inherited through acquisitions; several thousand certificates across three cloud providers; payments integration whose cryptography is contractually the supplier’s responsibility.

This is a capable person, well-funded, running an expert team at a serious institution describing the reality of the industry.

You cannot fix what you cannot find, which is why a cryptographic inventory matters, and why the June executive order directs CISA, working with NIST, to publish guidance on the minimum elements of a “cryptographic bill of materials” by March 2027. 

Inventory tells you where you stand. Agility is the ability to move. In practice, that means four things: knowing what cryptography you run and where it lives; being able to replace an algorithm without rewriting the application; requiring your suppliers to demonstrate they can do the same; and having actually exercised all of it, at least once.

That last one is what everybody skips. A migration capability you have never used is a disaster recovery plan you have never tested.

What next? 

I would encourage all companies not to wait until March 2027 for CISA to define what a cryptographic bill of materials ought to contain. This quarter, ask your security to lead the question I asked that CISO in the spring. If the answer is longer than a week, you have found your project.

Q-Day may well be a decade away. What’s for certain is that the sixty hours have already happened, and that nothing about most organisations’ ability to respond changed that week, and losing that gap is entirely within your control.

This ecosystem is driven by Onomondo’s deployed infrastructure, spanning strategically across the device, the Radio Access Network (RAN), and the cloud, anchored by patented Cloud Connectors and a proprietary technology stack.

The hybrid network capability is anchored by their deployment of what is reportedly the world’s largest private LTE network at sea across more than 450 Maersk vessels, allowing these assets to transition between private shipboard networks and global public networks.

More than 500 customers use Onomondo’s technology, including Maersk, Carlsberg and Husqvarna. This infrastructure allows companies to collect, process and act on real-world data in places where conventional connectivity is often difficult, from ships and trucks to factories and remote industrial sites.

Rasmus Jensen, CEO of Onomondo, says: “We chose Aspirity because they immediately recognised our structural differentiation and share our vision for the platform’s future. Their deep sector expertise makes them the ideal partner as we accelerate our international expansion and unlock new commercial opportunities.

“The traditional market approach has been to offer simple connectivity and leave the enterprise to manage the operational complexity around it. We took a fundamentally different path by building the foundational infrastructure layer that was missing, a single, unified platform connecting the device, the network, and the cloud across global operations.”

Today’s combined investment will drive Onomondo’s next phase of growth by expanding its international market presence and scaling its infrastructure deployment.

]]> Voi Technology, the Stockholm-based e-scooter and e-bike sharing company, has signed a €150 million revolving credit facility (RCF) with three Nordic banks.

The Swedish micromobility startup has entered into the new RCF (new facility) with Danske Bank, Swedbank and DNB Sweden. According to Voi, this new facility represents a further step in its financial development and marks a new stage in its financing strategy.

“This is an important milestone in our financial development, and follows the strong cash flow generation over the past years. The new facility gives us access to more flexible and cost-efficient financing as we continue to scale. We thank our current banks Danske Bank and Swedbank for their continued support and welcome DNB Bank on our journey ahead,” said Mathias Hermansson, CFO and Deputy CEO of Voi.

Founded in Stockholm in 2018, Voi provides shared electric scooters and e-bikes in partnership with towns and cities across Europe. The company currently operates more than 200k vehicles across more than 130 towns and cities in 13 countries, employs roughly 1,000 people at its Stockholm headquarters, and has recorded more than 500 million rides from over 4 million active users annually.

The new revolving credit facility comes on the back of strong second-quarter results. During Q2 2026, Voi reported net revenue climbed 47% year-on-year to €68.8 million, pushing its trailing twelve-month revenue above €200 million for the first time. The company’s adjusted EBITDA also nearly doubled to €19.7 million, giving it a margin of 28.6%. Voi also reported net leverage fell to 1.76x from 2.41x at the end of the previous quarter, despite its continued investment in fleet expansion.

Voi says it will use the proceeds to redeem all of its outstanding bonds, refinance its existing undrawn credit line and continue expanding its vehicle fleet. As part of the transaction, Voi issued a conditional notice of early redemption for all outstanding bonds under ISIN SE0023134952, which were issued under terms dated 17 October 2024.

The redemption of all outstanding bonds depends on customary conditions for the first drawdown of the new facility being satisfied, and, if met, is expected to close on 19 October 2026. The company also confirmed that bondholders will be repaid at 103.375% of the nominal value of each bond, plus accrued interest, with the payment due to holders registered as of 12 October 2026. Voi said the bonds are expected to be delisted from Nasdaq Stockholm’s corporate bond list around that date.

Fredrik Hjelm, co-founder and CEO of Voi, said, “We are coming off another record quarter, in Q2 2026, in a run of record quarters, and our growth trajectory keeps building. This facility is a clear vote of confidence from some of the Nordic region’s leading banks, and a sign that micromobility has matured into a bankable industry. Looking ahead, we will keep scaling our fleet, deepening our partnerships with cities, and working to create cities made for living.”

Since 2018, Voi Technology has raised more than €500 million across 14 funding rounds, including two Seed, four early-stage, five late-stage, 2 debt, and 1 grant prize. In August 2018, Voi raised a €2.5 million Seed round from VNV Global and went on to raise a €77 million Series B in November 2019, followed by a €132 million Series C in December 2020, which remains its largest funding round.

The Series D followed in December 2021 when the company raised €101.36 million ($115 million) and became a unicorn. However, the company has since shifted from pure equity to debt capital markets, issuing €50 million in senior secured bonds in October 2024, a further €40 million tap issue in October 2025, and a €25 million RCF with Danske Bank and Swedbank in December 2025. The €150 million revolving credit facility announced this week supersedes all the previous debt.

Even after its bonds are redeemed and delisted, the company intends to keep reporting its quarterly financing position alongside sustainability disclosures made under the EU’s Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive. The company says this measure is its continued commitment to transparency with stakeholders.

]]> ea4c392d6322eb85f0d2dce9f996453d Wed, 30 Sep 2026 09:05:00 +0200 Galaxies in a cosmic house of mirrors Image:

This NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope Picture of the Month features galaxies in great detail that have been warped and multiplied like they’ve stepped into a house of mirrors. The brilliant golden galaxies splashed across this image belong to a galaxy cluster called MACS J0454.1-0300. The orange galaxies concentrated on one side of the cluster are not actually part of the cluster and are much farther away from us.

MACS J0454.1-0300 is itself immensely distant: the light from these galaxies has been travelling to us for so long that we’re seeing the cluster as it was when the Universe was about 8 billion years old. While this galaxy cluster is a valuable scientific target in its own right, the real stars of this image are the galaxies that appear warped and stretched, like a painting that has been smeared by a giant hand.

The way these galaxies look is the result of gravitational lensing, in which the enormous mass of a foreground object such as a galaxy cluster bends and magnifies the light from a more distant object in the background. Gravitational lensing allows astronomers to observe galaxies, star clusters and even individual stars that are too far away for our telescopes to see under normal conditions. While the large, orange galaxies appear obviously distorted, look carefully at some of the small reddish background galaxies throughout this picture: even at the very edges of the frame, there are galaxies whose images have been bent into tiny arcs by MACS J0454.1-0300’s gravity.

The gravitationally lensed areas show multiple images of galaxies from when the Universe was young: a group of galaxies 2 billion years after the Big Bang, and a single galaxy just 800 million years old after the Big Bang. The galaxy group appears to be going through a merger, resulting in an enormous burst of star formation.

Astronomers have also identified individual bright ‘knots’ within the gravitationally lensed areas, corresponding to regions as small as 5 light-years across. These tiny clumps appear magnified by a factor of more than 300, in some cases.

A NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope image of this same cluster was released in 2014. Take a moment to compare the two images; the difference between them is dramatic. The new Webb image reveals hundreds of galaxies missing from the earlier image. These galaxies were there all along, but Webb is much more sensitive to their much redder light.

The data behind this image come from two observing programmes (#5058, PI: Furtak; #6882, PI: Fujimoto) that leverage the ability of massive galaxy clusters to bring distant objects into view.

[Image Description: A massive galaxy cluster, made of many golden elliptical galaxies with the largest, brightest one in the centre. Heavily distorted orange galaxies appear all around the cluster, the largest concentrated in a large arc around the cluster's centre; these are images of very distant galaxies, created by gravitational lensing. A few galaxies are large and bluish-white in colour; bright, nearby stars are the same colour.]

 SIE Custom Header — v1.1.2
 Zero-CLS, no JavaScript layout shifts.

 backdrop-filter is intentionally NOT used on .sie-hdr__bar.

 ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ */
/* ── Root variables ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
:root {
 --sie-hdr-brand:       #0056b3;        /* SIE brand blue                      */
 --sie-hdr-brand-light: #1a6fc4;
 --sie-hdr-bar-h:       64px;           /* nav bar height — fixed, prevents CLS */
 --sie-hdr-bar-bg:      #0056b3;        /* solid — no backdrop-filter needed   */
 --sie-hdr-bar-border:  rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.15);
}
/* ── Wrapper ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr {
 width: 100%;
 display: block;
 min-height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 /* Own stacking context so dropdowns render above Divi page content */
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1000;
}
/* ── Navigation bar ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__bar {
 height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 background: var(--sie-hdr-bar-bg);
 /* NO backdrop-filter here — it would trap position:fixed children
 (user-ui mobile bottom bar) inside this element instead of viewport */
 border-bottom: 1px solid var(--sie-hdr-bar-border);
}
.sie-hdr__inner {
 max-width: 1280px;
 height: 100%;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 32px;
}
/* ── Logo ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__logo {
 flex-shrink: 0;
 text-decoration: none;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-img {
 height: 54px;
 width: auto;
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-text {
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 17px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: #fff;
 letter-spacing: -0.01em;
 white-space: nowrap;
}

.sie-hdr__nav {
 flex: 1;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list {
 list-style: none;

 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
}

 position: relative;
}

.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
 padding: 8px 14px;
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);

 white-space: nowrap;
 min-height: 48px; /* WCAG touch target */

.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a:hover,

 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);

 top: calc(100% + 6px);
 left: 0;
 min-width: 240px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 12px;

 margin: 0;

.sie-hdr .se-ai-icon {

.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link,

 DESTINATIONS PANEL  — overlay + grid
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
 /* Outer layer: covers full viewport */
 .sie-dest-panel {
 position: fixed;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 2147483000;
 display: flex;
 align-items: stretch;
 justify-content: flex-end;
 opacity: 0;
 visibility: hidden;
 pointer-events: none;
 transition: opacity .25s ease, visibility .25s;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open {
 opacity: 1;
 visibility: visible;
 pointer-events: auto;
 }
 /* Backdrop */
 .sie-dest-panel__backdrop {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 background: rgba(11, 55, 112, .52);
 backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 cursor: pointer;
 }
 /* Sheet — right-panel on desktop */
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1;
 width: min(800px, 100%);
 height: 100%;
 background: #fff;
 overflow-y: auto;
 -webkit-overflow-scrolling: touch;
 padding: 26px 26px 40px;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 gap: 0;
 transform: translateX(28px);
 opacity: 0;
 transition: transform .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1), opacity .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1);
 box-shadow: -20px 0 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateX(0);
 opacity: 1;
 }
 /* Mobile: bottom-sheet */
 @media (max-width: 767px) {
 .sie-dest-panel {
 align-items: flex-end;
 justify-content: stretch;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 width: 100%;
 height: 92vh;
 border-top-left-radius: 22px;
 border-top-right-radius: 22px;
 padding: 20px 16px 40px;
 transform: translateY(28px);
 box-shadow: 0 -16px 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateY(0);
 }
 }
 /* ── Header ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__header {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 justify-content: space-between;
 margin-bottom: 6px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__titlewrap {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 10px;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__globe {
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #1e66f5;
 line-height: 1;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__title {
 font-size: 1.5rem;
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #0b3770;
 margin: 0;
 line-height: 1.2;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close {
 background: transparent;
 border: 0;
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #0b3770;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 6px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 line-height: 1;
 opacity: .75;
 transition: opacity .15s, background .15s;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close:hover {
 opacity: 1;
 background: #f0f4ff;
 }
 /* Subheading */
 .sie-dest-panel__sub {
 color: #466087;
 font-size: .94rem;
 margin: 0 0 20px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 /* ── Country grid ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 display: grid;
 grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr);
 gap: 14px;
 /* allow this to grow and scroll */
 flex: 1;
 align-content: start;
 }
 @media (max-width: 620px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr);
 gap: 10px;
 }
 }
 @media (min-width: 621px) and (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
 }
 }
 /* ── Country card ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__card {
 position: relative;
 display: block;
 aspect-ratio: 3 / 2;
 border-radius: 12px;
 overflow: hidden;
 text-decoration: none;
 background: #1d3557;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card--no-img .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 background: linear-gradient(135deg, #1d3557 0%, #1e66f5 100%);
 }
 /* Hero image layer — scales on hover */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 transition: transform .4s ease;
 will-change: transform;
 }
 /* <img> fills the card exactly like background-size:cover did.
 loading="lazy" means the browser only fetches each image when the
 panel opens and the card enters the viewport — saving ~30 MB of
 upfront image requests on every page that includes this panel. */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-img {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 width: 100%;
 height: 100%;
 object-fit: cover;
 object-position: center;
 display: block;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-bg,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 transform: scale(1.07);
 }
 /* Gradient overlay + text */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-body {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 justify-content: flex-end;
 padding: 10px 12px 10px;
 background: linear-gradient(
 to top,
 rgba(0, 0, 0, .72) 0%,
 rgba(0, 0, 0, .30) 55%,
 transparent 100%
 );
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card-name {
 color: #fff;
 font-weight: 700;
 font-size: .92rem;
 line-height: 1.2;
 text-shadow: 0 1px 5px rgba(0,0,0,.55);
 display: block;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow {
 display: block;
 color: rgba(255,255,255,0);
 font-size: .75rem;
 margin-top: 2px;
 transition: color .2s ease, transform .2s ease;
 line-height: 1;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow {
 color: rgba(255,255,255,.9);
 transform: translateX(4px);
 }
 /* ── Body-scroll lock ── */
 body.sie-dest-panel-open {
 overflow: hidden;
 }
 /* ── Country interest heart ── */
 .sie-country-heart {
 position: absolute;
 top: 8px;
 right: 8px;
 z-index: 10;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 border: none;
 border-radius: 20px;
 padding: 4px 8px 4px 7px;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
 cursor: pointer;
 font-size: 13px;
 color: #94a3b8;
 box-shadow: 0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,.22);
 backdrop-filter: blur(6px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(6px);
 transition: color .18s, transform .18s, background .18s;
 line-height: 1;
 min-width: 28px;
 justify-content: center;
 }
 .sie-country-heart:hover {
 transform: scale(1.12);
 background: #fff;
 color: #ef4444;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.voted {
 color: #ef4444;
 background: #fff;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.voted i {
 animation: sie-heart-pop .35s cubic-bezier(.36,.07,.19,.97);
 }
 @keyframes sie-heart-pop {
 0%   { transform: scale(1); }
 40%  { transform: scale(1.45); }
 70%  { transform: scale(.88); }
 100% { transform: scale(1); }
 }
 .sie-country-heart__count {
 font-size: 11px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: inherit;
 display: none;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.has-votes .sie-country-heart__count {
 display: inline;
 }
 /* ── Trigger button styles (for use in any menu) ── */
 /* Desktop globe icon */
 .se-dest-desktop-btn {
 font-size: 24px;
 color: #fff;
 text-decoration: none;
 cursor: pointer;
 transition: transform .2s, color .2s;
 position: relative;
 line-height: 1;
 background: transparent;
 border: 0;
 padding: 0;
 }
 .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover {
 transform: scale(1.15);
 color: #FFCC00;
 }
 /* Tooltip on desktop */
 @media (min-width: 1024px) {
 .se-dest-desktop-btn::after {
 content: "Study Destinations";
 position: absolute;
 bottom: -30px;
 left: 50%;
 transform: translateX(-50%);
 background: #007BFF;
 color: #fff;
 padding: 4px 8px;
 font-size: 12px;
 border-radius: 5px;
 opacity: 0;
 pointer-events: none;
 transition: opacity .2s;
 white-space: nowrap;
 }
 .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover::after {
 opacity: 1;
 }
 }
 /* Mobile pill button */
 .se-dest-btn {
 background: #0b3770 !important;
 color: #fff !important;
 }
 .se-dest-btn:hover {
 background: #1e66f5 !important;

<span><span>sandoel</span></span>

<div class="ecl"><h2><strong>What is the Conference?</strong></h2>

<p>The <strong>Conference on the Future of Europe </strong>is the first transnational discussion with Europeans on how to address Europe’s challenges together. This is an opportunity to think about what citizens and&nbsp; civil society want for the European Union.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

  <div class="eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text"><h2><strong>How does the Conference work?</strong></h2>

<p>Europeans can share ideas via the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Multilingual Digital Platform</a>, and both national and&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/assemblies/citizens-panels" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">European Citizens' Panels</a>. These contributions feed into the&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/plenary" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference Plenaries</a>.</p>

<p>The Conference&nbsp;offers a new public forum for an open, inclusive, and transparent debate with citizens around a number of key priorities and challenges.</p>

<h2><strong>How can you participate?</strong></h2>

<ul>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]--><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/processes?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">share your own ideas or support others’ ideas</a> on the multilingual digital Conference platform</li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->organise your own events and promote it by adding them to the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference platform</a></li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->take a look at the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/meetings" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">events organised by people across the EU</a></li>
</ul>

<h2><strong>What will the outcome be?</strong></h2>

<p>All of the ideas gathered and reports on events are published on the platform openly and transparently. These reports will then directly influence the discussions in the European Citizens’ Panels as well as in the Plenaries, where citizens will enter into a dialogue with national and European decision makers.</p>

<p>By spring 2022, the Conference will provide guidance on the future of Europe to the European institutions</p>

<p><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/getinvolved" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Get involved and make your voice heard when it comes to education, culture, youth, sport, and more</a>.</p>

<item>
  <title>European Student Card Initiative at EAIE 2026 in Glasgow - main highlights</title>
  <link>https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/european-student-card-initiative/news/european-student-card-initiative-at-eaie-2026-in-glasgow-main-highlights</link>
  <description>
<h1 class="title-h1 eac-page-title">European Student Card Initiative at EAIE 2026 in Glasgow - main highlights</h1>
<span><span>holbobe</span></span>
<span><time datetime="2026-09-30T09:11:45+02:00" title="Wednesday, September 30, 2026 - 09:11">Wed, 09/30/2026 - 09:11</time>
</span>
<div class="ecl"><p>EAIE 2026 took place from 8 to 11 September, with this year’s theme being “The Rhythm of Revolution”. ESCI featured in five activities: two sessions in the main conference programme and three mini-sessions at the European Commission stand.</p><h2>Shaping the next phase of the ESCI</h2><p>The session “What’s next for the European Student Card Initiative?” brought together Victor Aguilar Mendez from the European Commission, Harpa Sif Arnarsdóttir from RANNIS and Sergi Martínez Rigol from the University of Barcelona to discuss the roadmap beyond 2027.</p><p>The discussion highlighted three main points:</p><ul><li data-list-item-id="ec04a08fab5a0a15faf6d0537ff166c1e"><strong>Build on strong foundations</strong>. Participants welcomed the ambition to further simplify student mobility and emphasised the importance of building on the progress already achieved. They also noted that digital transformation involves more than technical connections, requiring aligned processes, staff capacity and resources.</li><li data-list-item-id="ec8f6683d0b4c64c36760e88ede263ada"><strong>Give institutions clarity and time to prepare</strong>. Participants highlighted the value of clear information on the <a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/european-student-card-initiative/about/esci-2028-2034/continuity-and-preparation?">future scope of ESCI+</a>, practical implications and transition arrangements. The European Commission indicated that 2028 and 2029 are envisaged as transition years.</li><li data-list-item-id="e8a2629faf233a9053a3e7c84c25e2248"><strong>Broaden engagement beyond international relations and IT teams</strong>. Participants highlighted the value of involving university leadership, national authorities, governance bodies and research and education networks.</li></ul><h2>Practical exchange at the European Commission stand</h2><p>Three mini-sessions created space for practical discussion and peer exchange at the European Commission stand:</p><ul><li data-list-item-id="ea46800eaa0963f636bf8742a636fe844"><strong>Digital Officers and ESCI Champions</strong>: “Meet and Greet” explored different opportunities for close collaboration and participants discussed faster communication channels, technical sub-groups and ways to strengthen the community of practitioners.</li><li data-list-item-id="e722608eb7be29071793748afb04db370"><strong>ESCI+ timeline: what to expect and when</strong>, focused on preparations in 2026 and plans for 2027. Participants asked for timely communication, hands-on training, transition arrangements and support to integrate future developments with existing systems.</li><li data-list-item-id="e4abeb75d22c4e87d628dd3a9174bdc0a"><strong>How to issue your first European Student Card</strong> introduced the practical tools available to card issuers, including the ESC Router and the ESC Service Manager for listing services available to ESC holders.</li></ul><h2>Poster session: “The European Student Card: Bridging borders for students”</h2><p>The poster attracted strong interest, with ESCI representatives Elodie Ham (EACEA) and Deborah Arnold (NTT DATA) engaging with participants on the ESCI components and discussing the implications of the ESCI+ timeline with those already involved in the initiative as well as with potential newcomers.</p><h2>Session by ESCI Champions: “Erasmus Without Paper: Getting on board with the digitisation of Erasmus+"&nbsp;</h2></div>
<div class="ecl-u-type-bold ecl-u-mb-m">Intro Text</div><div class="eac-hero"><p>We joined more than 7,300 international education professionals from over 100 countries in Glasgow to discuss what comes next for the European Student Card Initiative and share practical guidance with institutions.</p></div>

                    <div class="eche-report-title-question-text-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution has a strategy and an overarching structure supporting internationalisation</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
                    </div>
                </div>
                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The internationalisation strategy is available and prominently displayed on your website</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Internationalisation is an important driver for institutional change, and has a great influence on the major activities of a higher education institution (HEI) i.e. education and research. The importance of internationalisation is recognised, and most institutions have a strategy for internationalisation. However, for a strategy to be efficient, and for it to drive the HEI's activities regarding internationalisation, there is a need for its acceptance from across the whole institution. In addition the strategy could also be accessible to external collaborative partners. It is highly important to have the institution's internationalisation and modernisation strategy published and easily accessible to all.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The institution has a clear plan to implement the strategy</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The strategy and policy should include explicit allocation of responsibilities for its efficient implementation to individuals at all levels of the institution, from senior management to the heads of departments, schools and faculties, to academic and administrative staff. This will ensure acceptance and accountability for the strategy. The internationalisation strategy and policy should outline a specific implementation plan that sets out explicitly the financial and human resources available.&nbsp; For example, it is recommended to set up an International Relations Office (IRO) to implement mobility and other international projects.</p><p>As with any other activity, the institutional implementation of the internationalisation strategy is dependent on the people behind the activities. It is highly important for an institution to have staff with the right set of skills and knowledge driving the internationalisation agenda and liaising with international students and staff members. Therefore understanding the development needs of the staff and supporting their professional development should be a high priority for the institution. Such development should focus on both staff engaged in international activities as well as the supporting staff, ensuring the most efficient implementation of international activities and cooperative projects across the institution. For example, trainings/webinars/projects could be organised on intercultural competences and communication, project management, enhancement of internationalisation at home/intercultural, or other activities suggested by the staff and supported by the hierarchy.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes incoming and outgoing student and staff mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Mobility is important to the development of the institution as a whole as well as for the individual participants. Therefore the HEI should make mobility and international cooperation a central element in its institutional policies, and explicitly and consistently promote and support student and staff mobility. Non-discrimination policies and further emphasis on the promotion of mobility for under-represented groups should also form an integral part of the institutional support structures.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes engagement in European and international cooperation projects</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution's internationalisation strategy and policy should explicitly and consistently promote the development of cooperation with partners in other EU and non-EU countries. The activities and co-operation projects agreed by the HEI should be based on identified needs. In addition they should identify geographical and subject priorities of the internationalisation strategy.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The implementation of the strategic plan is monitored</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>International activity, including co-operation projects and mobility should be carefully monitored. Clear and unambiguous monitoring of such activity are key to ensuring success. Explicit indicators should be developed to show specific success scenarios. The indicators should be SMART.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Incentives are provided to staff involved in international activities</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Participation in such international projects should be seen as an important aspect of the professional development of the staff and of the modernisation of the HEI. It should, therefore, be considered a key component in staff evaluation. As part of the institutional modernisation and internationalisation strategy, concrete support measures should be defined at both institutional and departmental levels to encourage and recognise staff participating in such projects, as well as allow adequate time to carry out this work.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-case">
                                                <h3>Case studies</h3>
                                                <div><a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/eche/the-effective-management-and-ownership-of-erasmus-for-internationalisation" target="_blank">The effective management and ownership of Erasmus +’ for ‘internationalisation’</a></div>
                                                <div><a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/eche/internationalisation-at-the-university-of-helsinki" target="_blank">Internationalisation at the University of Helsinki </a></div>

                         <p>In signing the Erasmus Charter for Higher Education, the institution agrees to respect <strong>in full</strong> the principles of non-discrimination as set out in the Programme. Which means that all individuals or groups will be treated equally, irrespective of their characteristics. In accordance with Article 21 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, there should be no discrimination "based on sex, race, colour, ethnic or social origin, genetic features, language, religion or belief, political or any other opinion, membership of a national minority, property, birth, disability, age or sexual orientation". For more information, see: <a href="http://www.europarl.europa.eu/charter/pdf/text_en.pdf">http://www.europarl.europa.eu/charter/pdf/text_en.pdf</a></p>                      </div>

The Learning Agreement:</p><ul><li>Sets out the learning outcomes for the mobility, including both the educational components or traineeship activities to be carried out by the student at the receiving institution/organisation/enterprise, which will be recognised by the sending institution upon successful completion of the study programme abroad and counted towards his/her degree.</li><li>Ensures full recognition for satisfactorily completed activities of study mobility and traineeships in terms of credits awarded, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams, and documents these credits in the student records, so that they can be identified in a transparent way.</li></ul><p>The Learning Agreement is binding for all parties and constitutes the cornerstone of successful student mobility (for studies, traineeships, and combinations thereof), including quality assurances and the process for transparent transfer of credits. The Learning Agreement should be agreed and signed by all parties (the student, the sending institution and the receiving institution/organisation/enterprise) before the start of the mobility. It is not compulsory to circulate papers with original signatures; scanned copies of signatures or digital signatures may be accepted, depending on the national legislation.</p><p>The EU official templates for Learning Agreements for studies and traineeships are available online: <a href="http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm">http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm&nbsp;&nbsp;</a></p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Including allocation of responsibility to an academic who has the authority to approve, amend and recognise the Learning Agreements on behalf of the responsible academic body</span>

                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Ensuring that the mobile participant, sending and receiving institution/organisation/enterprise (i.e. all three parties) sign the mobility agreement before the start of the mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>To ensure effective staff mobility, it has to be based on a signed mobility agreement. The mobility agreement has to acceptable and signed by all parties in advance. There are four key elements set out by the mobility agreement, which are intended to increase the relevance and potential impact of the mobility. These are:</p><ul><li>The overall objectives and academic rationale of the mobility,</li><li>The institutional requirements or strategy, and the mobility's added value in the context of modernisation and internationalisation,</li><li>The activities or teaching programme content to be undertaken by the staff member, and,</li><li>The expected outcomes and impact of the mobility on the professional development of the staff member at both institutions.</li></ul><p>For this to work effectively, there needs to be dialogue and discussion between the three parties prior to the signing of the mobility agreement having agreed the common goals which are acceptable.&nbsp;</p>                      </div>

        <h2 class="eche-report-section-title eche-pdf-page-break">During the mobility</h2>
        <div class="eche-report-section-wrapper">

                        </div>
                        <div class="eche-officer-question-icon"><img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/ECHE__OFFICERS_Q10.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">

                    <div class="eche-report-title-question-text-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-officer-question"> During the mobility, your institution fosters the integration of the incoming mobile participants</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
                    </div>
                </div>
                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The institution appoints responsible person(s) to deal with practical issues (e.g. social, health, and/or psychological problems)</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution should ensure there are named, visible persons who are responsible for the practical issues associated with integrating mobile students. This visibility should be ensured through introduction to this function during the Welcome / Orientation period and be detailed on the website so all mobile students can easily access this support, throughout their stay.&nbsp;</p><p>Non-academic mentoring and support arrangements should already be outlined in the Course Catalogue of the receiving HEI, in the section on general information for students, with relevant contact persons in the respective areas. Academic advisors should have close contact with the practical services which are available to incoming participants as they are often the first line of contact to the incoming student. Further information sessions should be arranged for all staff who work with incoming students to ensure they are adequately signposted on to the appropriate services they require.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It appoints responsible person(s) to deal with academic issues (course timetables, student attendance, coursework, relationship with academic staff, etc.)</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is important that the receiving institution appoints specific named academic advisors who are responsible for dealing with problems related to academic issues (course timetables, student attendance, coursework, relationship with academic staff, etc.) of incoming students.&nbsp; Information on mentoring for thesis writing for incoming students is particularly important and clear mentoring arrangements should be agreed upon between the student, sending and receiving institutions and organised before the mobility.</p><p>For traineeships, a mentor, different from the supervisor, should be nominated to support and encourage the mobile student while in the receiving organisation. The mentor should also provide information on the culture of the enterprise and informal codes and conducts, of the receiving organisation. The contact details of both the supervisor and the mentor should be specified in the Learning Agreement.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It organises Welcome / Orientation activities at the beginning of each semester</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>An important aspect of the support arrangement is the welcome or orientation activities. These welcome / orientation activities should provide the incoming students with the necessary information on practical and administrative arrangements, to allow incoming students to meet local and other mobile students, to introduce the learning and teaching methods of the receiving institution, academic regulations, the institutional culture, health and safety issues. These activities should address any type of concern of the incoming student, and reduce any psychological pressure they might feel during their first contacts at the receiving institution. The welcome&nbsp; / orientation activities should be designed to take into account any cultural and religious sensitivities of the incoming students (ensuring a range of activities to suit different types of students).</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It organises activities to integrate them in the receiving institution and the local community, e.g. with the support of student organisations, Erasmus+ Student and Alumni Association etc.</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>As well as academic and practical support from the institution, incoming students need to feel fully integrated into the student community, something which is best done by their fellow students / peers. Local student association(s), such as Erasmus Student Network (ESN) and the other associations’ member of the ESAA - Erasmus+ Student and Alumni Association (<a href="http://esaa-eu.org/">http://esaa-eu.org/</a>), play an important role in supporting incoming students. Incoming students need to feel welcomed and included in the student organisations. To help this process, the student organisations need to be aware of their role in supporting this integration and have access to the right resources, information, guidance and incentives. As institutions often have many types of student organisations, cooperation between them is encouraged through meetings together, social activities and buddy programmes. A key aspect of these activities is to make sure they are for all students so incoming students are integrated with the local students and hence the culture. Student organisations include for example, ESN (Erasmus Student Network) or ESAA - Erasmus+ Student and Alumni Association (<a href="http://esaa-eu.org/">http://esaa-eu.org/</a>). ESAA runs a buddy system to encourage integration of incoming students with their peers inside the institution and share good practice with other member associations around Europe.</p>                      </div>

                        <div class="eche-officer-question-icon"><img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/ECHE__OFFICERS_Q11.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">
